abstract: Abstract. Previous work on nets with continuous-valued inputs led to generative procedures to construct convex decision regions with two-layer perceptrons (one hidden layer) and arbitrary decision regions with three-layer perceptrons (two hidden layers). Here we demonstrate that two-layer perceptron classifiers trained with back propagation can form both convex and disjoint decision regions. Such classifiers are robust, train rapidly, and provide good performance with simple decision regions. When complex decision regions are required, however, convergence time can be excessively long and performance is often no better than that of k-nearest neighbor classifiers. Three neural net classifiers are presented that provide more rapid training under such situations. Two use fixed weights in the first one or two layers and are similar to classifiers that estimate probability density functions using histograms. A third "feature map classifier" uses both unsupervised and supervised training. It provides good performance with little supervised training in situations such as speech recognition where much unlabeled training data is available. The architecture of this classifier can be used to implement a neural net k-nearest neighbor classifier.

paragraphs: The paper examines the decision regions neural classifiers can learn and how their training compares with traditional classification methods. It shows that perceptrons with one hidden layer, trained by backpropagation, can form both convex regions and separated regions. A category can therefore occupy disconnected portions of the input space.

These classifiers are described as robust and quick to train when the required decision regions are simple. For complex regions, convergence can take excessively long, and performance is often no better than k-nearest neighbors. The paper uses this contrast to motivate three neural classifiers intended to train more rapidly in those situations.

Two alternatives keep weights fixed in their first one or two layers and resemble histogram-based probability-density estimators. The third, a feature map classifier, combines unsupervised and supervised learning. It performs well with little supervised training where abundant unlabeled data are available, as in speech recognition. Its architecture can also implement neural k-nearest neighbors, connecting the proposed design directly to a traditional classifier.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies training difficulties for complex decision regions and presents faster neural alternatives, including a feature map classifier that uses unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper makes neural-network architecture selection depend on prediction risk: expected performance on new observations. The authors use this quantity as a precise definition of generalization ability and choose among candidate multilayer perceptron architectures according to estimated risk. The aim is to select a structure for its predictive usefulness beyond the available examples.

Because prediction risk is not directly known, the method estimates it from data. The paper considers v-fold cross-validation and asymptotic approximations based on generalized cross-validation or Akaike's final prediction error. It also proposes a heuristic search strategy for exploring possible architectures, connecting the evaluation criterion with a way to navigate the choices.

The application is corporate bond rating prediction, where data are limited and a complete prior model is unavailable to dictate network structure. Those conditions make architecture selection especially consequential. The contribution is a procedure that uses estimated generalization performance to guide the choice, bringing both the search process and the assessment of candidate networks into an explicit statistical framework.
summary.tldr: The paper selects neural architectures using estimated prediction risk and applies the approach to corporate bond rating prediction with limited data.

title: Principled Architecture Selection for Neural Networks: Application to Corporate Bond Rating Prediction

abstract: We propose a novel approach for building finite memory predictive mod(cid:173) els similar in spirit to variable memory length Markov models (VLMMs). The models are constructed by first transforming the n-block structure of the training sequence into a spatial structure of points in a unit hypercube, such that the longer is the common suffix shared by any two n-blocks, the closer lie their point representations. Such a transformation embodies a Markov assumption - n-blocks with long common suffixes are likely to produce similar continuations. Finding a set of prediction contexts is formulated as a resource allocation problem solved by vector quantizing the spatial n-block representation. We compare our model with both the classical and variable memory length Markov models on three data sets with different memory and stochastic components. Our models have a superior performance, yet, their construction is fully automatic, which is shown to be problematic in the case of VLMMs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to build finite-memory predictors for sequences of symbols. It first maps fixed-length blocks from the training sequence into points inside a unit hypercube. Blocks sharing a longer suffix receive nearby representations, turning a relationship between recent symbolic histories into a relationship between spatial locations.

This construction expresses a Markov assumption: histories with long matching endings are likely to have similar continuations. The method then treats selecting prediction contexts as a resource-allocation problem. Vector quantization of the spatial representation determines those contexts, providing an automatic route from the sequence's block structure to a predictive model.

The authors compare their models with classical Markov models and variable-memory-length Markov models on three datasets with different memory and stochastic components. Their models perform better in those comparisons, and their construction is fully automatic. The latter is a particular contribution because the abstract identifies automatic construction as problematic for the variable-memory approach. The results support the combination of suffix-based geometry and context allocation on the tested datasets.
summary.tldr: A spatial encoding of symbolic histories enables automatic predictive models that outperform classical and variable-memory Markov models on three datasets.

title: Building Predictive Models from Fractal Representations of Symbolic Sequences

abstract: Hebbian and competitive Hebbian algorithms are almost ubiquitous in modeling pattern formation in cortical development. We analyse in the(cid:173) oretical detail a particular model (adapted from Piepenbrock & Ober(cid:173) mayer, 1999) for the development of Id stripe-like patterns, which places competitive and interactive cortical influences, and free and restricted ini(cid:173) tial arborisation onto a common footing.

We analyse in the(cid:173) oretical detail a particular model (adapted from Piepenbrock & Ober(cid:173) mayer, 1999) for the development of Id stripe-like patterns, which places competitive and interactive cortical influences, and free and restricted ini(cid:173) tial arborisation onto a common footing.

paragraphs: This paper examines how stripe-like patterns can develop in a model of cortical organization. Its setting is ocular dominance, and its focus is the theoretical behavior of a particular model for one-dimensional pattern formation. The authors begin from the widespread use of Hebbian and competitive Hebbian learning in accounts of cortical development.

The analysis brings together two sets of modeling choices. One concerns competitive and interactive influences within the cortex. The other concerns initial arborization: the starting arrangement of neural branches and connections, considered under both free and restricted conditions. Treating these choices within a common framework makes their roles part of the same theoretical problem.

The contribution described is a detailed analysis of an adapted model, with these influences placed on comparable terms. Its significance lies in connecting the learning interactions that shape a developing pattern with the initial connection structure on which those interactions act. The stated scope is the one-dimensional stripe model, providing a focused setting for studying these ingredients together.
summary.tldr: A theoretical model brings cortical competition, interaction, and initial connection structure into one account of stripe formation.

title: Competition and Arbors in Ocular Dominance

abstract: We describe a computer system that provides a real-time musi(cid:173) cal accompaniment for a live soloist in a piece of non-improvised music for soloist and accompaniment. A Bayesian network is devel(cid:173) oped that represents the joint distribution on the times at which the solo and accompaniment notes are played, relating the two parts through a layer of hidden variables. The network is first con(cid:173) structed using the rhythmic information contained in the musical score. The network is then trained to capture the musical interpre(cid:173) tations of the soloist and accompanist in an off-line rehearsal phase. During live accompaniment the learned distribution of the network is combined with a real-time analysis of the soloist's acoustic sig(cid:173) nal, performed with a hidden Markov model, to generate a musi(cid:173) cally principled accompaniment that respects all available sources of knowledge. A live demonstration will be provided.

paragraphs: This paper describes a computer accompanist that responds to a live soloist performing a scored, non-improvised piece. The central problem is coordinating the timing of two musical parts while accounting for the performers’ interpretation. The system combines information from the score, a rehearsal, and the soloist’s current sound.

A Bayesian network represents the joint timing of solo and accompaniment notes. Hidden variables connect the two parts, allowing their timing to be modeled together. The score’s rhythmic structure determines the initial network. An offline rehearsal phase then trains it to capture how the soloist and accompanist interpret that structure.

During performance, a hidden Markov model analyzes the soloist’s acoustic signal in real time. The system combines that analysis with the learned timing distribution to generate accompaniment. The contribution is a probabilistic way to bring several sources of musical knowledge into one timing decision. Its stated setting is scored music with rehearsal-based learning; the abstract describes the system and announces a live demonstration without reporting a numerical evaluation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian network combines score structure, rehearsal learning, and live audio analysis to time accompaniment for a soloist.

title: A Bayesian Network for Real-Time Musical Accompaniment

abstract: In this paper we introduce new algorithms for unsupervised learn(cid:173) ing based on the use of a kernel matrix. All the information re(cid:173) quired by such algorithms is contained in the eigenvectors of the matrix or of closely related matrices. We use two different but re(cid:173) lated cost functions, the Alignment and the 'cut cost'. The first one is discussed in a companion paper [3], the second one is based on graph theoretic concepts. Both functions measure the level of clustering of a labeled dataset, or the correlation between data clus(cid:173) ters and labels. We state the problem of unsupervised learning as assigning labels so as to optimize these cost functions. We show how the optimal solution can be approximated by slightly relaxing the corresponding optimization problem, and how this corresponds to using eigenvector information. The resulting simple algorithms are tested on real world data with positive results.

paragraphs: The paper introduces clustering algorithms built around a kernel matrix. For these algorithms, the necessary information is contained in eigenvectors of that matrix or closely related matrices. The approach therefore turns unsupervised learning into a problem that can be addressed through the matrix's spectral structure.

The authors formulate clustering as assigning labels to optimize one of two related objectives, alignment and cut cost. These objectives measure how labels correspond to clusters in the data, with cut cost drawing on graph-theoretic ideas. The labels are the grouping assignments being sought, so the objective supplies a criterion for evaluating possible partitions.

A slight relaxation of the optimization problem leads to an approximation of the optimal solution using eigenvector information. This explains why the spectral calculation is relevant to the labeling objective, rather than introducing it as an unrelated heuristic. The resulting simple algorithms produce positive results on real-world data, supporting the practical usefulness of the relaxed optimization approach in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: The paper derives kernel clustering algorithms by relaxing label-assignment objectives into problems solved approximately through eigenvector information.

title: Spectral Kernel Methods for Clustering

abstract: The problem of searching for information in networks like the World Wide Web can be approached in a variety of ways, ranging from centralized indexing schemes to decentralized mechanisms that navigate the underlying network without knowledge of its global structure. The decentralized approach appears in a variety of settings: in the behavior of users browsing the Web by following hyperlinks; in the design of focused crawlers [4, 5, 8] and other agents that explore the Web's links to gather information; and in the search protocols underlying decentralized peer-to-peer sys- tems such as Gnutella [10], Freenet [7], and recent research prototypes [21, 22, 23], through which users can share resources without a central server.

paragraphs: The supplied abstract frames information search as a problem of navigating networks such as the World Wide Web. It distinguishes centralized indexing from decentralized approaches that move through the network without knowing its global structure. The central issue is how a search proceeds when the participant lacks a complete map of the available connections.

Several settings illustrate that issue. People browse by following hyperlinks, while focused crawlers and other automated agents explore links to collect information. Both involve movement through the network itself. Presenting them together highlights the shared search setting even though one involves human browsing and the other involves automated exploration.

The abstract also connects this perspective to decentralized peer-to-peer systems, where users share resources without a central server. Its stated content establishes a common problem across browsing, crawling, and distributed resource search. The explanatory emphasis is on the information available to a search process and the structure it navigates; the supplied passage sets up that perspective without presenting a particular algorithm or result.
summary.tldr: The abstract frames web browsing, crawling, and peer-to-peer resource discovery as decentralized network search without global structural knowledge.

title: Small-World Phenomena and the Dynamics of Information

abstract: The connectivity of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabdi- tis elegans has been described completely, but the analysis of the neu- ronal basis of behavior in this system is just beginning. Here, we used an optimization algorithm to search for patterns of connectivity sufﬁ- cient to compute the sensorimotor transformation underlying C. elegans chemotaxis, a simple form of spatial orientation behavior in which turn- ing probability is modulated by the rate of change of chemical concen- tration. Optimization produced differentiator networks with inhibitory feedback among all neurons. Further analysis showed that feedback reg- ulates the latency between sensory input and behavior. Common patterns of connectivity between the model and biological networks suggest new functions for previously identiﬁed connections in the C. elegans nervous system.
originalAbstract: The connectivity of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabdi- tis elegans has been described completely, but the analysis of the neu- ronal basis of behavior in this system is just beginning. Here, we used an optimization algorithm to search for patterns of connectivity sufﬁ- cient to compute the sensorimotor transformation underlying C. elegans chemotaxis, a simple form of spatial orientation behavior in which turn- ing probability is modulated by the rate of change of chemical concen- tration. Optimization produced differentiator networks with inhibitory feedback among all neurons. Further analysis showed that feedback reg- ulates the latency between sensory input and behavior. Common patterns of connectivity between the model and biological networks suggest new functions for previously identiﬁed connections in the C. elegans nervous system.

paragraphs: Knowing which neurons connect does not by itself explain how a nervous system produces behavior. This paper addresses that gap in C. elegans by studying chemotaxis, in which the animal's probability of turning changes with the rate of change of chemical concentration. The computational question is how a neural circuit can convert this sensory history into a behavioral response.

The authors use optimization to search for connection patterns sufficient to perform that transformation. The search produces differentiator networks: circuits that respond to changes in the chemical signal. These networks include inhibitory feedback among all neurons. Further analysis shows that feedback regulates the delay between sensory input and the resulting behavior, giving those connections a role in response timing.

Some connection patterns in the optimized models resemble patterns in the biological nervous system. These similarities suggest possible functions for previously identified connections. The result supplies circuit-level hypotheses grounded in a required computation; it establishes sufficient model arrangements and proposes biological interpretations, without establishing that the animal must use precisely those arrangements.
summary.tldr: Optimized circuits suggest that inhibitory feedback can support chemical-change detection and regulate behavioral response timing in C. elegans.

title: Circuit Optimization Predicts Dynamic Networks for Chemosensory Orientation in Nematode C. elegans

abstract: We present a discriminative part-based approach for the recognition of object classes from unsegmented cluttered scenes. Objects are modeled as flexible constellations of parts conditioned on local observations found by an interest operator. For each object class the probability of a given assignment of parts to local features is modeled by a Conditional Ran- dom Field (CRF). We propose an extension of the CRF framework that incorporates hidden variables and combines class conditional CRFs into a unified framework for part-based object recognition. The parameters of the CRF are estimated in a maximum likelihood framework and recogni- tion proceeds by finding the most likely class under our model. The main advantage of the proposed CRF framework is that it allows us to relax the assumption of conditional independence of the observed data (i.e. local features) often used in generative approaches, an assumption that might be too restrictive for a considerable number of object classes.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for recognizing object classes in cluttered images without first segmenting the objects. It represents each object as a flexible arrangement of parts. An interest operator identifies local image observations, and recognition involves determining how object parts could correspond to those observations.

For each class, a conditional random field models the probability of an assignment between parts and local features. The authors extend this framework with hidden variables and combine the separate class-conditioned models into one recognition system. Parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the system selects the class that is most probable under the resulting model.

The main stated benefit is flexibility in how observed features relate to one another. Many generative approaches assume conditional independence among local observations, which the authors argue may be too restrictive for a considerable number of object classes. Their discriminative framework relaxes that assumption while retaining a structured representation of object parts. The contribution is this modeling capability, rather than a reported numerical recognition gain.
summary.tldr: A part-based conditional random field recognizes objects in clutter while relaxing restrictive independence assumptions about local image features.

title: Conditional Random Fields for Object Recognition

abstract: We consider the semi-supervised learning problem, where a decision rule is to be learned from labeled and unlabeled data. In this framework, we motivate minimum entropy regularization, which enables to incorporate unlabeled data in the standard supervised learning. Our approach in- cludes other approaches to the semi-supervised problem as particular or limiting cases. A series of experiments illustrates that the proposed solu- tion benefits from unlabeled data. The method challenges mixture mod- els when the data are sampled from the distribution class spanned by the generative model. The performances are definitely in favor of minimum entropy regularization when generative models are misspecified, and the weighting of unlabeled data provides robustness to the violation of the "cluster assumption". Finally, we also illustrate that the method can also be far superior to manifold learning in high dimension spaces. 1 Introduction In the classical supervised learning classification framework, a decision rule is to be learned from a learning set Ln = {xi, yi}ni , where each example is described by a pattern =1 xi X and by the supervisor's response yi = {1, . . . , K }. We consider semi-supervised learning, where the supervisor's responses are limited to a subset of Ln. In the terminology used here, semi-supervised learning refers to learning a decision rule on X from labeled and unlabeled data. However, the related problem of transductive learning, i.e. of predicting labels on a set of predefined patterns, is addressed as a side issue. Semi- supervised problems occur in many applications where labeling is performed by human experts. They have been receiving much attention during the last few years, but some important issues are unresolved [10]. In the probabilistic framework, semi-supervised learning can be modeled as a missing data problem, which can be addressed by generative models such as mixture models thanks to the EM algorithm and extensions thereof [6].Generative models apply to the joint den- sity of patterns and class (X, Y ). abstract: We introduce a Gaussian process (GP) framework, stochastic relational models (SRM), for learning social, physical, and other relational phenomena where interactions between entities are observed. The key idea is to model the stochastic structure of entity relationships (i.e., links) via a tensor interaction of multiple GPs, each defined on one type of entities. These models in fact define a set of nonparametric priors on infinite dimensional tensor matrices, where each element represents a relationship between a tuple of entities. By maximizing the marginalized likelihood, information is exchanged between the participating GPs through the entire relational network, so that the dependency structure of links is messaged to the dependency of entities, reflected by the adapted GP kernels. The framework offers a discriminative approach to link prediction, namely, predicting the existences, strengths, or types of relationships based on the partially observed linkage network as well as the attributes of entities (if given). We discuss properties and variants of SRM and derive an efficient learning algorithm. Very encouraging experimental results are achieved on a toy problem and a user-movie preference link prediction task. In the end we discuss extensions of SRM to general relational learning tasks.

paragraphs: Relational learning predicts interactions between entities, such as preferences linking users and movies. This paper introduces stochastic relational models, a Gaussian process framework for predicting whether relationships exist, how strong they are, or what types they have. It uses a partially observed network and can also incorporate entity attributes when available.

The model combines Gaussian processes defined on different entity types through a tensor interaction. Each entry in the resulting relational representation corresponds to a relationship among a tuple of entities. This supplies nonparametric priors over potentially infinite-dimensional relational structures, allowing the model to express dependencies across linked entities.

Learning maximizes marginalized likelihood so that information passes between the participating Gaussian processes through the network. Relationship patterns influence the adapted kernels, connecting learned entity dependencies to observed links. The authors derive an efficient learning algorithm, discuss variants, and report encouraging results on a toy problem and a user–movie preference task. They also discuss extensions to broader relational learning problems.
summary.tldr: Stochastic relational models combine interacting Gaussian processes to predict links while adapting entity relationships from the observed network.

title: Stochastic Relational Models for Discriminative Link Prediction

abstract: We introduce a class of MPDs which greatly simplify Reinforcement Learning. They have discrete state spaces and continuous control spaces. The controls have the effect of rescaling the transition probabilities of an underlying Markov chain. A control cost penalizing KL divergence between controlled and uncontrolled transition probabilities makes the minimization problem convex, and allows analytical computation of the optimal controls given the optimal value function. An exponential transformation of the optimal value function makes the minimized Bellman equation linear. title: Linearly-solvable Markov decision problems

abstract: This paper introduces kernels on attributed pointsets, which are sets of vectors embedded in an euclidean space. The embedding gives the notion of neighborhood, which is used to define positive semidefinite kernels on pointsets. Two novel kernels on neighborhoods are proposed, one evaluating the attribute similarity and the other evaluating shape similarity. Shape similarity function is motivated from spectral graph matching techniques. The kernels are tested on three real life applications: face recognition, photo album tagging, and shot annotation in video sequences, with encouraging results.

paragraphs: This paper develops similarity functions for objects represented as attributed point sets. The points are vectors embedded in Euclidean space, so their positions define which points are neighbors. The approach uses this neighborhood structure to compare whole sets while taking account of information associated with their constituent points.

Two new neighborhood kernels capture different aspects of similarity. One evaluates how alike the attributes are, while the other evaluates shape. The shape comparison is motivated by spectral graph matching techniques. These neighborhood comparisons are used to define positive semidefinite kernels on point sets, giving the similarity construction the mathematical property required for use as such kernels.

The authors test the kernels in face recognition, photo album tagging, and annotation of shots in video sequences, reporting encouraging results. The applications illustrate the value of comparing structured collections through both attributes and spatial relationships. The stated finding supports the approach across these three tasks, without establishing that either neighborhood comparison is universally preferable.
summary.tldr: Neighborhood-based kernels compare attributed point sets through attribute and shape similarity, with encouraging results on three visual tasks.

title: Kernels on Attributed Pointsets with Applications

abstract: We introduce the Gamma-Exponential Process (GEP), a prior over a large family of continuous time stochastic processes. A hierarchical version of this prior (HGEP; the Hierarchical GEP) yields a useful model for analyzing complex time series. Models based on HGEPs display many attractive properties: conjugacy, exchangeability and closed-form predictive distribution for the waiting times, and exact Gibbs updates for the time scale parameters. After establishing these properties, we show how posterior inference can be carried efficiently using Particle MCMC methods [1]. This yields a MCMC algorithm that can resample entire sequences atomically while avoiding the complications of introducing slice and stick auxiliary variables of the beam sampler [2]. We applied our model to the problem of estimating the disease progression in multiple sclerosis [3], and to RNA evolutionary modeling [4]. In both domains, we found that our model outperformed the standard rate matrix estimation approach.

The approach includes uncertainty about timing within a probabilistic framework, with particular attention to predicting waiting times and inferring time-scale parameters.

The contribution combines a flexible prior with tractable inference operations and empirical evidence from two different settings. The reported comparisons support the model in those applications rather than establishing that it dominates rate-matrix approaches universally.
summary.tldr: The hierarchical Gamma-Exponential Process supports efficient continuous-time inference and outperforms standard rate-matrix estimation in two reported applications.

title: Priors over Recurrent Continuous Time Processes

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering a matrix $\mathbf{M}$ that is the sum of a low-rank matrix $\mathbf{L}$ and a sparse matrix $\mathbf{S}$ from a small set of linear measurements of the form $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{M}) = \mathcal{A}({\bf L}+{\bf S})$. This model subsumes three important classes of signal recovery problems: compressive sensing, affine rank minimization, and robust principal component analysis. We propose a natural optimization problem for signal recovery under this model and develop a new greedy algorithm called SpaRCS to solve it. SpaRCS inherits a number of desirable properties from the state-of-the-art CoSaMP and ADMiRA algorithms, including exponential convergence and efficient implementation. Simulation results with video compressive sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and robust matrix completion data sets demonstrate both the accuracy and efficacy of the algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper considers recovering a matrix from a small collection of linear measurements when the matrix combines a low-rank component and a sparse component. These two forms of structure enter the recovery problem together. The formulation encompasses compressive sensing, affine rank minimization, and robust principal component analysis within one model.

The authors propose an optimization problem for this setting and develop SpaRCS, a greedy algorithm for solving it. The algorithm inherits properties from CoSaMP and ADMiRA, including exponential convergence and efficient implementation. Its purpose is to exploit the combined structure while reconstructing from measurements that do not directly reveal every matrix entry.

Simulations cover video compressive sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and robust matrix completion. The reported results demonstrate accuracy and computational efficacy across those tested applications. The contribution brings low-rank and sparse recovery into a shared algorithmic framework, supported by convergence properties and simulation evidence, rather than treating each form of structure as a separate recovery task.
summary.tldr: SpaRCS is an efficient greedy algorithm for recovering matrices with low-rank and sparse components from limited linear measurements.

title: SpaRCS: Recovering low-rank and sparse matrices from compressive measurements

abstract: Simultaneous recordings of many neurons embedded within a recurrently-connected cortical network may provide concurrent views into the dynamical processes of that network, and thus its computational function. In principle, these dynamics might be identified by purely unsupervised, statistical means. Here, we show that a Hidden Switching Linear Dynamical Systems (HSLDS) model---in which multiple linear dynamical laws approximate a nonlinear and potentially non-stationary dynamical process---is able to distinguish different dynamical regimes within single-trial motor cortical activity associated with the preparation and initiation of hand movements. The regimes are identified without reference to behavioural or experimental epochs, but nonetheless transitions between them correlate strongly with external events whose timing may vary from trial to trial. The HSLDS model also performs better than recent comparable models in predicting the firing rate of an isolated neuron based on the firing rates of others, suggesting that it captures more of the "shared variance" of the data. Thus, the method is able to trace the dynamical processes underlying the coordinated evolution of network activity in a way that appears to reflect its computational role.

paragraphs: Simultaneous recordings from many neurons may reveal how a network's activity evolves collectively. This paper asks whether distinct dynamical regimes can be identified directly from those recordings within individual trials. It studies motor cortical activity associated with preparing and initiating hand movements, without using behavioral or experimental epochs to identify the regimes.

The method uses a Hidden Switching Linear Dynamical Systems model. Several linear dynamical laws approximate a process that may be nonlinear and may change over time. Switching between those laws allows the model to segment activity according to its dynamics. The inferred transitions correlate strongly with external events, even when those events occur at different times across trials.

The model also predicts an isolated neuron's firing rate from the others better than recent comparable models. This suggests that it captures more of the variation shared across the recorded population. Together, these findings support the method as a way to trace coordinated network activity whose changes appear related to computation, while preserving the authors' qualified interpretation of that relationship.
summary.tldr: A switching dynamical model identifies single-trial neural regimes that align with external events without using those events to define the regimes.

title: Dynamical segmentation of single trials from population neural data

abstract: Latent variable models are frequently used to identify structure in dichotomous network data, in part because they give rise to a Bernoulli product likelihood that is both well understood and consistent with the notion of exchangeable random graphs. In this article we propose conservative confidence sets that hold with respect to these underlying Bernoulli parameters as a function of any given partition of network nodes, enabling us to assess estimates of \emph{residual} network structure, that is, structure that cannot be explained by known covariates and thus cannot be easily verified by manual inspection. We demonstrate the proposed methodology by analyzing student friendship networks from the National Longitudinal Survey of Adolescent Health that include race, gender, and school year as covariates. We employ a stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm to fit a logistic regression model that includes these explanatory variables as well as a latent stochastic blockmodel component and additional node-specific effects. Although maximum-likelihood estimates do not appear consistent in this context, we are able to evaluate confidence sets as a function of different blockmodel partitions, which enables us to qualitatively assess the significance of estimated residual network structure relative to a baseline, which models covariates but lacks block structure.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to assess network structure that remains after accounting for known node characteristics. In networks with binary links, latent-variable models describe connections through underlying Bernoulli probabilities. The authors construct conservative confidence sets for these probabilities as a function of a given partition of the nodes, providing a way to evaluate inferred residual structure.

The application concerns student friendship networks with race, gender, and school year as observed covariates. A logistic regression model combines those explanatory variables with a latent stochastic blockmodel component and node-specific effects. A stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm fits the model, allowing observed characteristics and additional network organization to enter the same analysis.

Maximum-likelihood estimates do not appear consistent in this setting, a qualification the paper explicitly retains. Nevertheless, confidence sets can be evaluated for different blockmodel partitions. This enables a qualitative assessment of the significance of estimated residual structure relative to a baseline that includes the covariates but no block structure. The contribution is therefore an uncertainty-based assessment of inferred network organization.
summary.tldr: Conservative confidence sets help assess network structure left unexplained by observed covariates across different node partitions.

title: Confidence Sets for Network Structure

abstract: Mini-batch algorithms have recently received significant attention as a way to speed-up stochastic convex optimization problems. In this paper, we study how such algorithms can be improved using accelerated gradient methods. We provide a novel analysis, which shows how standard gradient methods may sometimes be insufficient to obtain a significant speed-up. We propose a novel accelerated gradient algorithm, which deals with this deficiency, and enjoys a uniformly superior guarantee. We conclude our paper with experiments on real-world datasets, which validates our algorithm and substantiates our theoretical insights.

We propose a novel accelerated gradient algorithm, which deals with this deficiency, and enjoys a uniformly superior guarantee. We conclude our paper with experiments on real-world datasets, which validates our algorithm and substantiates our theoretical insights.

paragraphs: Mini-batch algorithms process groups of examples when updating a model, with the aim of speeding up stochastic optimization. This paper studies that strategy for convex problems. Its question is whether the optimization method itself makes good enough use of mini-batches to deliver the speed-up that motivates using them.

The authors develop an analysis showing that standard gradient methods can sometimes fail to obtain a significant speed-up. They then introduce an accelerated gradient algorithm designed to address this deficiency. The proposed method has a uniformly superior theoretical guarantee in the comparison studied, making the update rule a central part of the argument for better mini-batch performance.

Experiments on real-world datasets support the algorithm and the theoretical insights. The findings connect the way examples are grouped with the way optimization progresses: changing batch organization alone may be insufficient, whereas acceleration can improve the associated guarantee. The theoretical comparison and experimental support are complementary claims; the abstract does not turn them into a claim of faster execution on every possible dataset.
summary.tldr: An accelerated gradient algorithm improves mini-batch optimization guarantees where standard gradient methods can offer insufficient speed-up.

title: Better Mini-Batch Algorithms via Accelerated Gradient Methods

abstract: We study how to automatically select and adapt multiple abstractions or representations of the world to support model-based reinforcement learning. We address the challenges of transfer learning in heterogeneous environments with varying tasks. We present an efficient, online framework that, through a sequence of tasks, learns a set of relevant representations to be used in future tasks. Without pre-defined mapping strategies, we introduce a general approach to support transfer learning across different state spaces. We demonstrate the potential impact of our system through improved jumpstart and faster convergence to near optimum policy in two benchmark domains.

Without pre-defined mapping strategies, we introduce a general approach to support transfer learning across different state spaces. We demonstrate the potential impact of our system through improved jumpstart and faster convergence to near optimum policy in two benchmark domains.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between reinforcement-learning tasks becomes difficult when environments differ in how they represent states. This paper studies how a model-based learner can automatically select and adapt multiple abstractions of the world. The aim is to retain useful representations across changing tasks and heterogeneous environments.

The authors propose an efficient online framework that learns a collection of relevant representations over a sequence of tasks. Those representations are then available to support future tasks. The approach handles transfer across different state spaces without requiring predefined mapping strategies, making the selection and adaptation of representations part of the learning process.

In two benchmark domains, the framework improves jumpstart performance, meaning how well learning begins, and reaches a near-optimal policy more quickly. These results demonstrate the potential value of learning which abstractions to carry forward. The contribution concerns both the initial benefit of previous experience and the subsequent pace of learning, with the reported evidence coming from those two domains.
summary.tldr: An online framework learns reusable representations across differing state spaces, improving initial performance and convergence in two reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

title: Transferring Expectations in Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Pedigrees, or family trees, are directed graphs used to identify sites of the genome that are correlated with the presence or absence of a disease. With the advent of genotyping and sequencing technologies, there has been an explosion in the amount of data available, both in the number of individuals and in the number of sites. Some pedigrees number in the thousands of individuals. Meanwhile, analysis methods have remained limited to pedigrees of <100 individuals which limits analyses to many small independent pedigrees. Disease models, such those used for the linkage analysis log-odds (LOD) estimator, have similarly been limited. This is because linkage anlysis was originally designed with a different task in mind, that of ordering the sites in the genome, before there were technologies that could reveal the order. LODs are difficult to interpret and nontrivial to extend to consider interactions among sites. These developments and difficulties call for the creation of modern methods of pedigree analysis. Drawing from recent advances in graphical model inference and transducer theory, we introduce a simple yet powerful formalism for expressing genetic disease models. We show that these disease models can be turned into accurate and efficient estimators. The technique we use for constructing the variational approximation has potential applications to inference in other large-scale graphical models. This method allows inference on larger pedigrees than previously analyzed in the literature, which improves disease site prediction.

summary.tldr: A disease-modeling formalism and variational inference method enable larger pedigree analyses and improve disease-site prediction.

title: Bayesian Pedigree Analysis using Measure Factorization

abstract: We propose an approximate inference algorithm for continuous time Gaussian-Markov process models with both discrete and continuous time likelihoods. We show that the continuous time limit of the expectation propagation algorithm exists and results in a hybrid fixed point iteration consisting of (1) expectation propagation updates for the discrete time terms and (2) variational updates for the continuous time term. We introduce corrections methods that improve on the marginals of the approximation. This approach extends the classical Kalman-Bucy smoothing procedure to non-Gaussian observations, enabling continuous-time inference in a variety of models, including spiking neuronal models (state-space models with point process observations) and box likelihood models. Experimental results on real and simulated data demonstrate high distributional accuracy and significant computational savings compared to discrete-time approaches in a neural application.
originalAbstract: We propose an approximate inference algorithm for continuous time Gaussian-Markov process models with both discrete and continuous time likelihoods. We show that the continuous time limit of the expectation propagation algorithm exists and results in a hybrid fixed point iteration consisting of (1) expectation propagation updates for the discrete time terms and (2) variational updates for the continuous time term. We introduce corrections methods that improve on the marginals of the approximation. This approach extends the classical Kalman-Bucy smoothing procedure to non-Gaussian observations, enabling continuous-time inference in a variety of models, including spiking neuronal models (state-space models with point process observations) and box likelihood models. Experimental results on real and simulated data demonstrate high distributional accuracy and significant computational savings compared to discrete-time approaches in a neural application.

paragraphs: This paper develops approximate inference for hidden Gaussian-Markov processes that evolve in continuous time. The observations can contribute likelihood terms at discrete times or continuously over time. The aim is to infer the hidden process while accommodating observation models beyond the Gaussian setting handled by classical Kalman-Bucy smoothing.

The authors show that expectation propagation has a continuous-time limit. The resulting algorithm combines two kinds of updates: expectation propagation for the discrete observation terms and variational updates for the continuous term. These form a hybrid fixed-point iteration. Additional correction methods improve the approximate marginal distributions, which describe uncertainty about individual portions of the hidden process.

The framework supports models including neural state-space models with point-process observations and box likelihood models. Experiments use both real and simulated data. In a neural application, the authors report accurate distributional approximations and substantial computational savings relative to discrete-time approaches. These findings support the usefulness of handling continuous-time inference directly while retaining flexibility in how observations relate to the hidden state.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time inference algorithm combines expectation propagation and variational updates to handle non-Gaussian observations of latent Gaussian-Markov processes.

title: Approximate inference in latent Gaussian-Markov models from continuous time observations

abstract: Deep learning has been a long standing pursuit in machine learning, which until recently was hampered by unreliable training methods before the discovery of improved heuristics for embedded layer training. A complementary research strategy is to develop alternative modeling architectures that admit efficient training methods while expanding the range of representable structures toward deep models. In this paper, we develop a new architecture for nested nonlinearities that allows arbitrarily deep compositions to be trained to global optimality. The approach admits both parametric and nonparametric forms through the use of normalized kernels to represent each latent layer. The outcome is a fully convex formulation that is able to capture compositions of trainable nonlinear layers to arbitrary depth.

The approach admits both parametric and nonparametric forms through the use of normalized kernels to represent each latent layer. paragraphs: The paper explores an architectural route to making deep learning easier to optimize. Its starting point is that training reliability depends partly on the model being trained. The authors therefore develop an alternative architecture that retains compositions of nonlinear layers while allowing training to be expressed as a convex optimization problem.

The architecture represents each latent layer using normalized kernels. These representations support nested, trainable nonlinearities and admit both parametric and nonparametric forms. The central result is that compositions can have arbitrary depth while the overall training formulation remains fully convex. The stated global-optimality property belongs to this particular architecture and its formulation.

This matters because the paper connects expressive depth with a global training objective that can be optimized to its best value. Its contribution is a way of constructing deep models for which that guarantee is available. The result offers a complementary research direction to improving training heuristics: designing the representation and optimization problem together so that deep composition retains favorable mathematical structure.
summary.tldr: An architecture based on normalized kernels supports arbitrarily deep nonlinear compositions within a convex training formulation.

title: Convex Deep Learning via Normalized Kernels

abstract: This paper concerns the introduction of a new Markov Chain Monte Carlo scheme for posterior sampling in Bayesian nonparametric mixture models with priors that belong to the general Poisson-Kingman class. We present a novel and compact way of representing the infinite dimensional component of the model such that while explicitly representing this infinite component it has less memory and storage requirements than previous MCMC schemes. We describe comparative simulation results demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed MCMC algorithm against existing marginal and conditional MCMC samplers.

We describe comparative simulation results demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed MCMC algorithm against existing marginal and conditional MCMC samplers.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a Markov chain Monte Carlo method for posterior sampling in Bayesian nonparametric mixture models. It targets models whose priors belong to the Poisson-Kingman class. The central computational issue is how to represent the model’s infinite-dimensional component while running a sampling procedure with practical memory and storage requirements.

The proposed sampler uses a compact representation of that infinite component. The authors emphasize that it remains explicitly represented while requiring less memory and storage than previous MCMC schemes. This is the main methodological contribution: changing how the sampler represents part of the model to reduce the resources needed for posterior computation.

The paper compares the method with existing marginal and conditional MCMC samplers through simulations. These comparisons demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in the evaluated settings. Together, the representation and simulation results offer a way to make sampling within this general prior family more economical, with the stated resource advantage specifically concerning memory and storage.
summary.tldr: A compact representation of Poisson-Kingman mixture models enables posterior sampling with lower memory and storage requirements than previous MCMC schemes.

title: A hybrid sampler for Poisson-Kingman mixture models

abstract: Existing object proposal algorithms usually search for possible object regions over multiple locations and scales \emph{ separately}, which ignore the interdependency among different objects and deviate from the human perception procedure. To incorporate global interdependency between objects into object localization, we propose an effective Tree-structured Reinforcement Learning (Tree-RL) approach to sequentially search for objects by fully exploiting both the current observation and historical search paths. The Tree-RL approach learns multiple searching policies through maximizing the long-term reward that reflects localization accuracies over all the objects. Starting with taking the entire image as a proposal, the Tree-RL approach allows the agent to sequentially discover multiple objects via a tree-structured traversing scheme. Allowing multiple near-optimal policies, Tree-RL offers more diversity in search paths and is able to find multiple objects with a single feed-forward pass. Therefore, Tree-RL can better cover different objects with various scales which is quite appealing in the context of object proposal. Experiments on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012 validate the effectiveness of the Tree-RL, which can achieve comparable recalls with current object proposal algorithms via much fewer candidate windows.

paragraphs: Object proposal methods search an image for regions that might contain objects. Searching locations and scales separately can overlook relationships among objects. This paper introduces Tree-RL, a reinforcement-learning approach that searches sequentially using both the current observation and the history of earlier search paths.

The search begins with the entire image as a proposal and branches through a tree-shaped traversal. The method learns multiple policies by maximizing a long-term reward that reflects localization accuracy across all objects. The contribution connects the organization of the search process to proposal efficiency: historical context and multiple learned paths guide where the model looks next.
summary.tldr: Tree-RL searches for multiple objects through learned branching policies, achieving comparable reported recall with substantially fewer candidate windows.

title: Tree-Structured Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Object Localization

abstract: This paper deals with finding an $n$-dimensional solution $\bm{x}$ to a system of quadratic equations $y_i=|\langle\bm{a}_i,\bm{x}\rangle|^2$, $1\le i \le m$, which in general is known to be NP-hard. We put forth a novel procedure, that starts with a \emph{weighted maximal correlation initialization} obtainable with a few power iterations, followed by successive refinements based on \emph{iteratively reweighted gradient-type iterations}. The novel techniques distinguish themselves from prior works by the inclusion of a fresh (re)weighting regularization. For certain random measurement models, the proposed procedure returns the true solution $\bm{x}$ with high probability in time proportional to reading the data $\{(\bm{a}_i;y_i)\}_{1\le i \le m}$, provided that the number $m$ of equations is some constant $c>0$ times the number $n$ of unknowns, that is, $m\ge cn$. Empirically, the upshots of this contribution are: i) perfect signal recovery in the high-dimensional regime given only an \emph{information-theoretic limit number} of equations; and, ii) (near-)optimal statistical accuracy in the presence of additive noise. Extensive numerical tests using both synthetic data and real images corroborate its improved signal recovery performance and computational efficiency relative to state-of-the-art approaches.

The authors develop a procedure with strong guarantees for certain random measurement models, using randomness in the problem structure to support efficient recovery.

summary.tldr: Weighted initialization and reweighted gradient updates enable efficient recovery for certain random quadratic systems, with strong empirical noise and sample-efficiency results.

title: Solving Most Systems of Random Quadratic Equations

abstract: We consider the analysis of Electroencephalography (EEG) and Local Field Potential (LFP) datasets, which are “big” in terms of the size of recorded data but rarely have sufficient labels required to train complex models (e.g., conventional deep learning methods). Furthermore, in many scientific applications, the goal is to be able to understand the underlying features related to the classification, which prohibits the blind application of deep networks. This motivates the development of a new model based on {\em parameterized} convolutional filters guided by previous neuroscience research; the filters learn relevant frequency bands while targeting synchrony, which are frequency-specific power and phase correlations between electrodes. This results in a highly expressive convolutional neural network with only a few hundred parameters, applicable to smaller datasets. The proposed approach is demonstrated to yield competitive (often state-of-the-art) predictive performance during our empirical tests while yielding interpretable features. Furthermore, a Gaussian process adapter is developed to combine analysis over distinct electrode layouts, allowing the joint processing of multiple datasets to address overfitting and improve generalizability. Finally, it is demonstrated that the proposed framework effectively tracks neural dynamics on children in a clinical trial on Autism Spectrum Disorder.

This paper addresses both concerns with a convolutional network whose parameterized filters are guided by neuroscience and learn frequency bands relevant to synchrony between electrodes.

Here, synchrony includes frequency-specific correlations in signal power and phase. Targeting those relationships produces an expressive network with only a few hundred parameters, making it applicable to smaller datasets while retaining interpretable features. The authors report competitive, often state-of-the-art predictive performance in their empirical evaluations.

A Gaussian process adapter allows datasets with different electrode layouts to be analyzed jointly. This supports pooling information across recordings to address overfitting and improve generalizability. That application demonstrates analysis of changing neural activity, alongside the paper's broader focus on interpretable prediction from limited labeled electrophysiological data.
summary.tldr: A compact, interpretable neural network learns electrode synchrony features, with a Gaussian process adapter enabling analysis across electrode layouts.

title: Targeting EEG/LFP Synchrony with Neural Nets

abstract: Subset selection, which is the task of finding a small subset of representative items from a large ground set, finds numerous applications in different areas. Sequential data, including time-series and ordered data, contain important structural relationships among items, imposed by underlying dynamic models of data, that should play a vital role in the selection of representatives. However, nearly all existing subset selection techniques ignore underlying dynamics of data and treat items independently, leading to incompatible sets of representatives. In this paper, we develop a new framework for sequential subset selection that finds a set of representatives compatible with the dynamic models of data. To do so, we equip items with transition dynamic models and pose the problem as an integer binary optimization over assignments of sequential items to representatives, that leads to high encoding, diversity and transition potentials. Our formulation generalizes the well-known facility location objective to deal with sequential data, incorporating transition dynamics among facilities. As the proposed formulation is non-convex, we derive a max-sum message passing algorithm to solve the problem efficiently. Experiments on synthetic and real data, including instructional video summarization, show that our sequential subset selection framework not only achieves better encoding and diversity than the state of the art, but also successfully incorporates dynamics of data, leading to compatible representatives.

paragraphs: Selecting a small representative subset becomes more complicated when items form a sequence. A collection can cover individual items well yet fail to respect the transitions that connect them. This paper develops a selection framework that explicitly accounts for those dynamics, aiming to choose representatives that fit the structure of sequential data.

The method equips items with transition models and assigns sequential items to representatives through a binary integer optimization problem. Its objective combines encoding quality, diversity, and transition compatibility. This extends the facility-location objective by including dynamics among the selected facilities. Because the formulation is nonconvex, the authors derive a max-sum message-passing algorithm for efficient solution.

Experiments on synthetic and real data, including instructional-video summarization, show better encoding and diversity than the compared state of the art. They also show that the framework incorporates sequence dynamics to produce compatible representatives. The contribution is a selection objective in which representing the content and respecting how that content evolves are addressed together.
summary.tldr: A dynamics-aware subset-selection framework chooses diverse representatives that also respect transitions in sequential data.

title: Subset Selection and Summarization in Sequential Data

abstract: We consider stochastic settings for clustering, and develop provably-good (approximation) algorithms for a number of these notions. These algorithms allow one to obtain better approximation ratios compared to the usual deterministic clustering setting. Additionally, they offer a number of advantages including providing fairer clustering and clustering which has better long-term behavior for each user. In particular, they ensure that every user is guaranteed to get good service (on average). We also complement some of these with impossibility results.

paragraphs: Clustering groups users or data points according to a service or similarity objective. This paper studies stochastic versions of clustering, where the solution is evaluated with randomness taken into account. The authors develop approximation algorithms for several such formulations, giving mathematical guarantees about how close their solutions come to the relevant optimum.

One stated benefit is better approximation ratios than those available in the usual deterministic setting. Randomness also changes how service can be distributed among users. The algorithms provide guarantees of good service on average for every user, connecting clustering quality to individual long-term outcomes. An average guarantee concerns performance across the randomness; it does not promise the same service quality in every individual outcome.

The paper therefore treats stochastic clustering as a way to improve both approximation guarantees and fairness of service. It also establishes impossibility results for some of the settings, placing boundaries around what algorithms can achieve. Together, the positive and negative results clarify both the advantages of these stochastic formulations and the limits of their guarantees.
summary.tldr: Stochastic clustering algorithms offer improved approximation guarantees and good average service for every user, alongside impossibility results.

title: Approximation algorithms for stochastic clustering

abstract: We introduce a new approach to learning in hierarchical latent-variable generative models called the “distributed distributional code Helmholtz machine”, which emphasises flexibility and accuracy in the inferential process. Like the original Helmholtz machine and later variational autoencoder algorithms (but unlike adver- sarial methods) our approach learns an explicit inference or “recognition” model to approximate the posterior distribution over the latent variables. Unlike these earlier methods, it employs a posterior representation that is not limited to a narrow tractable parametrised form (nor is it represented by samples). To train the genera- tive and recognition models we develop an extended wake-sleep algorithm inspired by the original Helmholtz machine. This makes it possible to learn hierarchical latent models with both discrete and continuous variables, where an accurate poste- rior representation is essential. We demonstrate that the new algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on synthetic, natural image patch and the MNIST data sets.

paragraphs: Hierarchical generative models describe observations through layers of hidden variables. Learning with these models requires inference about which hidden-variable configurations could explain an observation. This paper introduces the distributed distributional code Helmholtz machine, emphasizing the flexibility and accuracy of that inference process as a central part of model learning.

The approach learns an explicit recognition model that approximates the posterior distribution over hidden variables. It shares this broad strategy with Helmholtz machines and variational autoencoders, but changes how the posterior is represented. The representation is neither restricted to a narrow, tractable parameterized family nor expressed as a collection of samples.

An extended wake-sleep algorithm trains both the generative and recognition models. This enables learning hierarchical models containing discrete as well as continuous variables, where accurate posterior representations are important. Experiments on synthetic data, natural image patches, and MNIST show the algorithm outperforming the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution ties a more flexible representation of uncertainty to a training procedure capable of using it.
summary.tldr: A new Helmholtz-machine approach pairs flexible posterior representations with extended wake-sleep training for hierarchical generative models.

title: Flexible and accurate inference and learning for deep generative models

abstract: We study the problem of identifying the best action in a sequential decision-making setting when the reward distributions of the arms exhibit a non-trivial dependence structure, which is governed by the underlying causal model of the domain where the agent is deployed. In this setting, playing an arm corresponds to intervening on a set of variables and setting them to specific values. In this paper, we show that whenever the underlying causal model is not taken into account during the decision-making process, the standard strategies of simultaneously intervening on all variables or on all the subsets of the variables may, in general, lead to suboptimal policies, regardless of the number of interventions performed by the agent in the environment. We formally acknowledge this phenomenon and investigate structural properties implied by the underlying causal model, which lead to a complete characterization of the relationships between the arms' distributions. We leverage this characterization to build a new algorithm that takes as input a causal structure and finds a minimal, sound, and complete set of qualified arms that an agent should play to maximize its expected reward. We empirically demonstrate that the new strategy learns an optimal policy and leads to orders of magnitude faster convergence rates when compared with its causal-insensitive counterparts.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential action selection when actions correspond to interventions on variables in a causal system. An arm specifies which variables are set and their values. Because the system has causal structure, the reward distributions associated with different arms have relationships that can matter when deciding which interventions to consider.

The authors show that strategies ignoring this structure can produce suboptimal policies, even after arbitrarily many interventions. This can occur with standard strategies that intervene on all variables or on all subsets. The issue is therefore not necessarily resolved by collecting more experience: the structure of the intervention choices also matters.

The paper characterizes relationships among arm distributions using properties of the causal model. From a supplied causal structure, its algorithm identifies a minimal, sound, and complete set of qualified arms for reward maximization. Experiments show learning of an optimal policy and convergence improvements of orders of magnitude over causal-insensitive alternatives. These findings support using causal structure to determine the action set before learning which action is best.
summary.tldr: Causal structure identifies which intervention arms should be considered and can substantially accelerate learning an optimal policy.

title: Structural Causal Bandits: Where to Intervene?

abstract: In this work, we improve upon the stepwise analysis of noisy iterative learning algorithms initiated by Pensia, Jog, and Loh (2018) and recently extended by Bu, Zou, and Veeravalli (2019). Our main contributions are significantly improved mutual information bounds for Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics via data-dependent estimates. Our approach is based on the variational characterization of mutual information and the use of data-dependent priors that forecast the mini-batch gradient based on a subset of the training samples. Our approach is broadly applicable within the information-theoretic framework of Russo and Zou (2015) and Xu and Raginsky (2017). Our bound can be tied to a measure of flatness of the empirical risk surface. As compared with other bounds that depend on the squared norms of gradients, empirical investigations show that the terms in our bounds are orders of magnitude smaller.

paragraphs: This paper improves information-theoretic analysis of stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, a noisy iterative learning method. Such analyses connect generalization to how much information a learned model retains about its training data. The authors focus on obtaining sharper mutual information bounds by using estimates that depend on the data.

Their approach uses a variational characterization of mutual information together with data-dependent priors. These priors forecast the mini-batch gradient from a subset of training samples. By incorporating this predictive information into the analysis, the method improves on earlier stepwise bounds for noisy learning algorithms.

The resulting bound can be linked to a measure of flatness of the empirical risk surface, connecting the information analysis to the geometry of training loss. In empirical investigations, terms appearing in the new bounds are orders of magnitude smaller than those in bounds based on squared gradient norms. This finding concerns the size of the bound terms; it does not assert a corresponding improvement in the trained model's prediction accuracy.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent gradient forecasts yield sharper mutual information bounds for SGLD, with substantially smaller bound terms in empirical investigations.

title: Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds for SGLD via Data-Dependent Estimates

abstract: Given a n-by-d data matrix A, principal component projection (PCP) and principal component regression (PCR), i.e. projection and regression restricted to the top-eigenspace of A, are fundamental problems in machine learning, optimization, and numerical analysis. In this paper we provide the first algorithms that solve these problems in nearly linear time for fixed eigenvalue distribution and large n. This improves upon previous methods which had superlinear running times when either the number of top eigenvalues or gap between the eigenspaces were large. We achieve our results by applying rational polynomial approximations to reduce the problem to solving asymmetric linear systems which we solve by a variant of SVRG. We corroborate these findings with preliminary empirical experiments.

This improves upon previous methods which had superlinear running times when either the number of top eigenvalues or gap between the eigenspaces were large. We achieve our results by applying rational polynomial approximations to reduce the problem to solving asymmetric linear systems which we solve by a variant of SVRG. paragraphs: Principal component projection and regression restrict computation to the top eigenspace associated with a data matrix. These are basic operations in machine learning, optimization, and numerical analysis. This paper studies how to perform them efficiently when the matrix has many rows, focusing on the computational cost of obtaining the projection or regression result.

The authors provide algorithms with nearly linear running time for a fixed eigenvalue distribution and large row count. This improves on previous approaches that had superlinear running times when either the number of top eigenvalues or the gap between eigenspaces was large. The conditions on the eigenvalue distribution and matrix size are part of the stated result.

The method uses rational polynomial approximations to transform the original tasks into asymmetric linear-system problems. A variant of stochastic variance-reduced gradient, or SVRG, solves those systems. Preliminary empirical experiments corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore an algorithmic reduction that brings these spectral tasks within nearly linear time in the specified regime, with initial experimental support.
summary.tldr: Rational approximations and an asymmetric SVRG solver enable nearly linear-time principal component projection and regression in the stated spectral regime.

title: Principal Component Projection and Regression in Nearly Linear Time through Asymmetric SVRG

abstract: We study the relationship between the frequency of a function and the speed at which a neural network learns it. We build on recent results that show that the dynamics of overparameterized neural networks trained with gradient descent can be well approximated by a linear system. When normalized training data is uniformly distributed on a hypersphere, the eigenfunctions of this linear system are spherical harmonic functions. We derive the corresponding eigenvalues for each frequency after introducing a bias term in the model. This bias term had been omitted from the linear network model without significantly affecting previous theoretical results. However, we show theoretically and experimentally that a shallow neural network without bias cannot represent or learn simple, low frequency functions with odd frequencies. Our results lead to specific predictions of the time it will take a network to learn functions of varying frequency. These predictions match the empirical behavior of both shallow and deep networks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a function's frequency affects the speed at which a neural network learns it. It builds on a linear approximation to gradient-descent dynamics in overparameterized networks. When normalized training data is uniformly distributed over a hypersphere, the corresponding eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, providing a frequency-based way to analyze learning.

The authors introduce a bias term into the model and derive eigenvalues for the different frequencies. Although omitting bias had not substantially affected earlier theoretical results, it matters for this question. They show theoretically and experimentally that a shallow network without bias cannot represent or learn certain simple low-frequency functions with odd frequencies.

The analysis produces predictions for how long learning functions of different frequencies will take. Those predictions agree with observed behavior in both shallow and deep networks. The contribution connects frequency-dependent learning speed with the spectrum of the linearized dynamics, while showing that a seemingly minor modeling choice can affect which frequency components a shallow network can learn at all.
summary.tldr: A spectral analysis predicts frequency-dependent learning times and reveals that omitting bias prevents shallow networks from learning certain odd-frequency functions.

title: The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies

abstract: Recent works propose using the discriminator of a GAN to filter out unrealistic samples of the generator. We generalize these ideas by introducing the implicit Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. For any implicit probabilistic model and a target distribution represented by a set of samples, implicit Metropolis-Hastings operates by learning a discriminator to estimate the density-ratio and then generating a chain of samples. Since the approximation of density ratio introduces an error on every step of the chain, it is crucial to analyze the stationary distribution of such chain. For that purpose, we present a theoretical result stating that the discriminator loss upper bounds the total variation distance between the target distribution and the stationary distribution. Finally, we validate the proposed algorithm both for independent and Markov proposals on CIFAR-10, CelebA, ImageNet datasets.

For any implicit probabilistic model and a target distribution represented by a set of samples, implicit Metropolis-Hastings operates by learning a discriminator to estimate the density-ratio and then generating a chain of samples. Since the approximation of density ratio introduces an error on every step of the chain, it is crucial to analyze the stationary distribution of such chain.
