paragraphs: A generative model may produce samples without providing an explicit probability density that can be evaluated directly. This paper develops implicit Metropolis–Hastings for such models when the target distribution is represented by examples. It generalizes earlier ideas that use a GAN discriminator to screen out unrealistic generator outputs.

The method learns a discriminator to estimate a density ratio and uses that estimate to generate a chain of samples. Because the ratio is approximate, each step can introduce error. The important question is therefore what distribution the chain approaches over time, rather than whether individual generated samples appear plausible.

The authors provide a theoretical result linking discriminator loss to the total variation distance between the target and the chain's stationary distribution. The loss supplies an upper bound on this discrepancy, connecting discriminator quality to the eventual sampling distribution. They validate the algorithm with both independent and Markov proposals on CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, demonstrating its application beyond a single proposal mechanism.
summary.tldr: Implicit Metropolis–Hastings uses learned density ratios for sampling and bounds stationary-distribution error through discriminator loss.

title: The Implicit Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm

abstract: We study epsilon-best-arm identification, in a setting where during the exploration phase, the cost of each arm pull is proportional to the expected future reward of that arm. We term this setting Pay-Per-Reward. We provide an algorithm for this setting, that with a high probability returns an epsilon-best arm, while incurring a cost that depends only linearly on the total expected reward of all arms, and does not depend at all on the number of arms. Under mild assumptions, the algorithm can be applied also to problems with infinitely many arms.
originalAbstract: We study epsilon-best-arm identification, in a setting where during the exploration phase, the cost of each arm pull is proportional to the expected future reward of that arm. We term this setting Pay-Per-Reward. We provide an algorithm for this setting, that with a high probability returns an epsilon-best arm, while incurring a cost that depends only linearly on the total expected reward of all arms, and does not depend at all on the number of arms. Under mild assumptions, the algorithm can be applied also to problems with infinitely many arms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a nearly best option when trying different options has unequal costs. In its Pay-Per-Reward setting, the cost of exploring an arm is proportional to that arm's expected future reward. The objective is to return an arm whose expected reward lies within epsilon of the best available one.

The authors give an algorithm with a high-probability guarantee of finding such an arm. Its exploration cost depends only linearly on the sum of expected rewards across all arms, with no separate dependence on the number of arms. This shifts the cost characterization from counting available choices to measuring their combined expected reward under the specified payment rule.

That distinction does not imply that adding arms can never change the cost: additional arms can change the total expected reward. The result instead removes arm count as an independent factor in the stated bound. Under mild assumptions, the authors also extend the algorithm's applicability to problems with infinitely many arms, broadening the setting beyond a finite list of choices.
summary.tldr: A Pay-Per-Reward bandit algorithm identifies an epsilon-best arm with high probability at a cost linear in total expected reward, without separate arm-count dependence.

title: Epsilon-Best-Arm Identification in Pay-Per-Reward Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: The study on improving the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial examples grows rapidly in recent years. Among them, adversarial training is the most promising one, which flattens the \textit{input loss landscape} (loss change with respect to input) via training on adversarially perturbed examples. However, how the widely used \textit{weight loss landscape} (loss change with respect to weight) performs in adversarial training is rarely explored. In this paper, we investigate the weight loss landscape from a new perspective, and identify a clear correlation between the flatness of weight loss landscape and robust generalization gap. Several well-recognized adversarial training improvements, such as early stopping, designing new objective functions, or leveraging unlabeled data, all implicitly flatten the weight loss landscape. Based on these observations, we propose a simple yet effective \textit{Adversarial Weight Perturbation (AWP)} to explicitly regularize the flatness of weight loss landscape, forming a \textit{double-perturbation} mechanism in the adversarial training framework that adversarially perturbs both inputs and weights. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AWP indeed brings flatter weight loss landscape and can be easily incorporated into various existing adversarial training methods to further boost their adversarial robustness.

This paper examines a second source of sensitivity: changes to the network’s weights. It studies the weight loss landscape, meaning how much the training loss changes as model parameters move, and its relationship to robust generalization.

The authors identify a clear correlation between flatter weight loss landscapes and the robust generalization gap. They also find that several established improvements to adversarial training implicitly flatten this landscape, including early stopping, alternative objectives, and use of unlabeled data. These observations motivate directly encouraging the same property during training.

Their method, Adversarial Weight Perturbation, adds adversarial changes to weights alongside the usual adversarial changes to inputs. This creates a training procedure that addresses sensitivity in both spaces. Extensive experiments show that AWP produces flatter weight loss landscapes and improves adversarial robustness when incorporated into various existing training methods. The empirical improvements support its practical value, while the motivating relationship between flatness and generalization is described as a correlation.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Weight Perturbation adds weight attacks to input attacks during training, empirically flattening the weight loss landscape and improving robustness.

title: Adversarial Weight Perturbation Helps Robust Generalization

abstract: This paper presents a new matching-based framework for semi-supervised video object segmentation (VOS). Recently, state-of-the-art VOS performance has been achieved by matching-based algorithms, in which feature banks are created to store features for region matching and classification. However, how to effectively organize information in the continuously growing feature bank remains under-explored, and this leads to an inefficient design of the bank. We introduced an adaptive feature bank update scheme to dynamically absorb new features and discard obsolete features. We also designed a new confidence loss and a fine-grained segmentation module to enhance the segmentation accuracy in uncertain regions. On public benchmarks, our algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-arts.

As a video continues, that bank can keep growing. The authors identify organization of this accumulated information as an underexplored source of inefficiency.

Their framework updates the feature bank adaptively, incorporating new features while removing obsolete ones. This makes information management an explicit part of the segmentation method. The bank can respond to new observations without simply preserving every feature accumulated earlier, addressing the storage design problem described in the paper.

A second part targets regions where segmentation is uncertain. The authors introduce a confidence loss and a fine-grained segmentation module to improve accuracy in those areas. Together, the changes address both the information used for matching and the refinement of uncertain predictions. On public benchmarks, the complete algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined framework's effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Adaptive feature-bank updates and targeted refinement of uncertain regions improve matching-based video object segmentation.

title: Video Object Segmentation with Adaptive Feature Bank and Uncertain-Region Refinement

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations are an attractive option for modelling temporal dynamics. However, a fundamental issue is that the solution to an ordinary differential equation is determined by its initial condition, and there is no mechanism for adjusting the trajectory based on subsequent observations. Here, we demonstrate how this may be resolved through the well-understood mathematics of \emph{controlled differential equations}. The resulting \emph{neural controlled differential equation} model is directly applicable to the general setting of partially-observed irregularly-sampled multivariate time series, and (unlike previous work on this problem) it may utilise memory-efficient adjoint-based backpropagation even across observations. We demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance against similar (ODE or RNN based) models in empirical studies on a range of datasets. Finally we provide theoretical results demonstrating universal approximation, and that our model subsumes alternative ODE models.

This creates a problem for time series, where new measurements should influence the evolving representation.

The paper uses controlled differential equations to introduce that influence. The resulting neural controlled differential equation model handles multivariate observations that may be incomplete and arrive at irregular times. It also permits memory-efficient adjoint-based backpropagation across observations, connecting the ability to absorb incoming data with an efficient way to train the model.

Empirical studies across several datasets report state-of-the-art performance relative to similar ODE- and recurrent-network-based models. The paper also establishes universal approximation results and shows that its formulation subsumes alternative ODE models. These theoretical findings address expressive scope, while the experiments support its practical usefulness for the irregular time-series settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: Neural controlled differential equations incorporate incoming irregular observations into continuous-time models while supporting memory-efficient training.

title: Neural Controlled Differential Equations for Irregular Time Series

abstract: Partial label learning assumes inaccurate supervision where each training example is associated with a set of candidate labels, among which only one is valid. In many real-world scenarios, however, it is costly and time-consuming to assign candidate label sets to all the training examples. To circumvent this difficulty, the problem of semi-supervised partial label learning is investigated in this paper, where unlabeled data is utilized to facilitate model induction along with partial label training examples. Specifically, label propagation is adopted to instantiate the labeling confidence of partial label examples. After that, maximum margin formulation is introduced to jointly enable the induction of predictive model and the estimation of labeling confidence over unlabeled data. The derived formulation enforces confidence-rated margin maximization and confidence manifold preservation over partial label examples and unlabeled data. We show that the predictive model and labeling confidence can be solved via alternating optimization which admits QP solutions in either alternating step. Extensive experiments on synthetic as well as real-world data sets clearly validate the effectiveness of the proposed semi-supervised partial label learning approach.

paragraphs: Partial label learning gives each training example several candidate labels, exactly one of which is correct. Even creating these candidate sets can be expensive. This paper studies a semi-supervised setting in which examples with candidate sets are combined with completely unlabeled examples, allowing the latter to contribute to learning.

The method first uses label propagation to establish confidence values for the partially labeled examples. It then introduces a maximum-margin formulation that jointly learns a predictive model and estimates labeling confidence for unlabeled data. The objective incorporates confidence into margin maximization and preserves the manifold structure of confidence across both kinds of examples.

The resulting optimization alternates between the predictive model and labeling confidences, with each step admitting a quadratic programming solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution connects uncertainty about candidate labels with the use of additional unlabeled data, treating confidence estimation and prediction as coupled parts of the same learning process.
summary.tldr: The method combines partial labels and unlabeled data through joint confidence estimation and confidence-rated margin maximization.

title: Semi-Supervised Partial Label Learning via Confidence-Rated Margin Maximization

abstract: A prominent technique for self-supervised representation learning has been to contrast semantically similar and dissimilar pairs of samples. Without access to labels, dissimilar (negative) points are typically taken to be randomly sampled datapoints, implicitly accepting that these points may, in reality, actually have the same label. Perhaps unsurprisingly, we observe that sampling negative examples from truly different labels improves performance, in a synthetic setting where labels are available. Motivated by this observation, we develop a debiased contrastive objective that corrects for the sampling of same-label datapoints, even without knowledge of the true labels. Empirically, the proposed objective consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art for representation learning in vision, language, and reinforcement learning benchmarks. Theoretically, we establish generalization bounds for the downstream classification task.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning trains representations by distinguishing similar examples from examples treated as dissimilar. Without labels, negative examples are commonly sampled at random. Some of those random examples can actually belong to the same class, so the training objective can push apart items that share the semantic category it should help recover.

The authors first demonstrate in a synthetic setting with available labels that choosing negatives from genuinely different classes improves performance. They then develop a debiased contrastive objective that corrects for the inclusion of same-label examples without requiring the true labels. The intervention targets the sampling bias in the learning objective rather than assuming every randomly chosen negative is appropriate.

Across the reported vision, language, and reinforcement learning benchmarks, the objective consistently outperforms state-of-the-art representation-learning methods. The paper also establishes generalization bounds for downstream classification. These contributions connect an identifiable source of misleading training signals to both empirical improvements and a theoretical analysis of how the resulting representations support classification.
summary.tldr: A debiased contrastive objective corrects for randomly sampled negatives that share a class, improving representation learning without needing true labels.

title: Debiased Contrastive Learning

abstract: It is well-known that given a smooth, bounded-from-below, and possibly nonconvex function, standard gradient-based methods can find $\epsilon$-stationary points (with gradient norm less than $\epsilon$) in $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations. However, many important nonconvex optimization problems, such as those associated with training modern neural networks, are inherently not smooth, making these results inapplicable. In this paper, we study nonsmooth nonconvex optimization from an oracle complexity viewpoint, where the algorithm is assumed to be given access only to local information about the function at various points. We provide two main results (under mild assumptions): First, we consider the problem of getting \emph{near} $\epsilon$-stationary points. This is perhaps the most natural relaxation of \emph{finding} $\epsilon$-stationary points, which is impossible in the nonsmooth nonconvex case. We prove that this relaxed goal cannot be achieved efficiently, for any distance and $\epsilon$ smaller than some constants. Our second result deals with the possibility of tackling nonsmooth nonconvex optimization by reduction to smooth optimization: Namely, applying smooth optimization methods on a smooth approximation of the objective function. For this approach, we prove an inherent trade-off between oracle complexity and smoothness: On the one hand, smoothing a nonsmooth nonconvex function can be done very efficiently (e.g., by randomized smoothing), but with dimension-dependent factors in the smoothness parameter, which can strongly affect iteration complexity when plugging into standard smooth optimization methods. On the other hand, these dimension factors can be eliminated with suitable smoothing methods, but only by making the oracle complexity of the smoothing process exponentially large.

paragraphs: Smooth nonconvex optimization has established guarantees for finding points with small gradients, but these guarantees do not directly cover nonsmooth objectives. This paper studies what is possible when an algorithm accesses an objective only through local information at queried points. Its results concern the fundamental cost of optimization in that oracle setting.

summary.tldr: Oracle lower bounds show that approaching stationary points and obtaining dimension-independent smoothing can be fundamentally expensive in nonsmooth nonconvex optimization.

title: Oracle Complexity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: We study solution methods for (strongly-)convex-(strongly)-concave Saddle-Point Problems (SPPs) over networks of two type--master/workers (thus centralized) architectures and mesh (thus decentralized) networks. The local functions at each node are assumed to be \textit{similar}, due to statistical data similarity or otherwise. We establish lower complexity bounds for a fairly general class of algorithms solving the SPP. We show that a given suboptimality $\epsilon>0$ is achieved over master/workers networks in $\Omega\big(\Delta\cdot \delta/\mu\cdot \log (1/\varepsilon)\big)$ rounds of communications, where $\delta>0$ measures the degree of similarity of the local functions, $\mu$ is their strong convexity constant, and $\Delta$ is the diameter of the network. The lower communication complexity bound over mesh networks reads $\Omega\big(1/{\sqrt{\rho}} \cdot {\delta}/{\mu}\cdot\log (1/\varepsilon)\big)$, where $\rho$ is the (normalized) eigengap of the gossip matrix used for the communication between neighbouring nodes. We then propose algorithms matching the lower bounds over either types of networks (up to log-factors). We assess the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms on a robust regression problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies distributed saddle-point optimization, where an objective is minimized in some variables and maximized in others. It considers convex-concave problems, including strongly convex-concave cases, across both centralized master-worker systems and decentralized mesh networks. A central assumption is that the local functions held by different nodes are similar, possibly because their data are statistically similar.

The authors establish lower bounds on the communication needed by a fairly general class of algorithms. In the strongly convex setting described, these bounds depend on the function-similarity parameter relative to strong convexity and logarithmically on the desired accuracy. Network structure also matters: the master-worker bound involves network diameter, while the mesh bound involves the communication matrix’s normalized eigengap.

They then propose algorithms that match the respective lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. This connects achievable performance to a theoretical communication limit for each network type. An evaluation on robust regression assesses the proposed methods in an application. The main implication is that local-function similarity and network connectivity can be incorporated explicitly into near-optimal communication guarantees.
summary.tldr: Distributed saddle-point algorithms exploit similar local functions to match communication lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: Distributed Saddle-Point Problems Under Data Similarity

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can match or exceed convolutional networks on image classification, but similar predictive performance does not reveal whether their internal representations work alike. This paper compares the representations learned by the two architectures on image classification benchmarks, asking how their processing of visual information differs.

The analysis finds substantial differences, including more uniform representations across transformer layers. Self-attention plays an important role by combining global information early in processing. Residual connections also strongly carry features from lower layers to higher ones. Together, these findings help explain why the transformer’s internal organization differs from that of the convolutional models studied.

The authors also examine spatial localization and show that Vision Transformers preserve information about input locations, with noticeable effects from the classification method used. They investigate how pretraining dataset size affects intermediate features and transfer learning, and discuss connections with MLP-Mixer. The contribution is an empirical account of representation structure: classification success can arise through different patterns of information aggregation, feature propagation, and spatial preservation.
summary.tldr: Representation analyses reveal that Vision Transformers and CNNs organize visual information differently, with important roles for attention and residual connections.

title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?

abstract: Nowadays, there is an explosive growth of screen contents due to the wide application of screen sharing, remote cooperation, and online education. To match the limited terminal bandwidth, high-resolution (HR) screen contents may be downsampled and compressed. At the receiver side, the super-resolution (SR)of low-resolution (LR) screen content images (SCIs) is highly demanded by the HR display or by the users to zoom in for detail observation. However, image SR methods mostly designed for natural images do not generalize well for SCIs due to the very different image characteristics as well as the requirement of SCI browsing at arbitrary scales. To this end, we propose a novel Implicit Transformer Super-Resolution Network (ITSRN) for SCISR. For high-quality continuous SR at arbitrary ratios, pixel values at query coordinates are inferred from image features at key coordinates by the proposed implicit transformer and an implicit position encoding scheme is proposed to aggregate similar neighboring pixel values to the query one. We construct benchmark SCI1K and SCI1K-compression datasets withLR and HR SCI pairs. Extensive experiments show that the proposed ITSRN significantly outperforms several competitive continuous and discrete SR methods for both compressed and uncompressed SCIs.

Methods designed mainly for natural photographs do not generalize well to this setting, where image characteristics differ and users may zoom to arbitrary scales. This paper develops ITSRN specifically for continuous super-resolution of screen content.

The network predicts pixel values at requested coordinates using image features associated with key coordinates. This coordinate-based formulation supports arbitrary enlargement ratios. An implicit position-encoding scheme also combines similar neighboring pixel values when estimating a query pixel, contributing local information to the reconstruction.

The authors create SCI1K and SCI1K-compression benchmarks containing paired low- and high-resolution screen images. Experiments show significant improvements over several competitive methods that support either continuous or discrete scaling, for both compressed and uncompressed inputs. The contribution combines a reconstruction architecture suited to flexible zooming with evaluation data for screen-specific restoration. The findings support treating screen content and arbitrary output scale as central design requirements when building super-resolution methods for this use.
summary.tldr: ITSRN reconstructs screen images at arbitrary enlargement ratios and improves results on compressed and uncompressed screen-content benchmarks.

title: Implicit Transformer Network for Screen Content Image Continuous Super-Resolution

abstract: Given an optimization problem, the Hessian matrix and its eigenspectrum can be used in many ways, ranging from designing more efficient second-order algorithms to performing model analysis and regression diagnostics. When nonlinear models and non-convex problems are considered, strong simplifying assumptions are often made to make Hessian spectral analysis more tractable.This leads to the question of how relevant the conclusions of such analyses are for realistic nonlinear models. In this paper, we exploit tools from random matrix theory to make a *precise* characterization of the Hessian eigenspectra for a broad family of nonlinear models that extends the classical generalized linear models, without relying on strong simplifying assumptions used previously. We show that, depending on the data properties, the nonlinear response model, and the loss function, the Hessian can have *qualitatively* different spectral behaviors: of bounded or unbounded support, with single- or multi-bulk, and with isolated eigenvalues on the left- or right-hand side of the main eigenvalue bulk. By focusing on such a simple but nontrivial model, our analysis takes a step forward to unveil the theoretical origin of many visually striking features observed in more realistic machine learning models.

paragraphs: The Hessian describes an objective's local curvature, and its eigenvalues reveal how that curvature varies across directions. These quantities support optimization and model analysis, but studying them for nonlinear models often requires strong simplifications.

The paper uses random matrix theory to characterize Hessian eigenvalue distributions for a broad family of nonlinear models extending classical generalized linear models. Its aim is to retain meaningful nonlinear structure while avoiding strong simplifying assumptions used in earlier analyses.

The resulting spectra can differ qualitatively depending on the data, response model, and loss function. Eigenvalues may occupy bounded or unbounded ranges, form one main cluster or several, and include isolated values to either side of the main cluster.

These distinctions show that the shape of a Hessian spectrum depends on several parts of the learning problem, rather than following one uniform pattern. By analyzing a relatively simple but nontrivial model family precisely, the work helps explain possible theoretical origins of striking spectral features observed in more realistic machine-learning models.
summary.tldr: Random matrix analysis shows how data, nonlinear responses, and loss functions produce qualitatively different Hessian spectra.

title: Hessian Eigenspectra of More Realistic Nonlinear Models

abstract: Deep Metric Learning (DML) aims to find representations suitable for zero-shot transfer to a priori unknown test distributions. However, common evaluation protocols only test a single, fixed data split in which train and test classes are assigned randomly. More realistic evaluations should consider a broad spectrum of distribution shifts with potentially varying degree and difficulty.In this work, we systematically construct train-test splits of increasing difficulty and present the ooDML benchmark to characterize generalization under out-of-distribution shifts in DML. ooDML is designed to probe the generalization performance on much more challenging, diverse train-to-test distribution shifts. Based on our new benchmark, we conduct a thorough empirical analysis of state-of-the-art DML methods. We find that while generalization tends to consistently degrade with difficulty, some methods are better at retaining performance as the distribution shift increases. Finally, we propose few-shot DML as an efficient way to consistently improve generalization in response to unknown test shifts presented in ooDML.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning seeks representations that transfer to test distributions and classes that were unknown during training. Yet a common evaluation uses just one randomly assigned split between training and test classes. The paper argues that this gives too narrow a picture of generalization because deployment can involve shifts with very different levels of difficulty.

The authors introduce ooDML, a benchmark built from systematically constructed training and test splits of increasing difficulty. This creates a broader range of distribution shifts on which to compare methods. The resulting evaluation asks both how well a method transfers and how its performance changes as the mismatch between training and testing becomes more demanding.

Their empirical analysis finds that generalization tends to deteriorate as difficulty rises, while some methods preserve performance better than others. They also propose few-shot metric learning as an efficient response to unknown test shifts and report consistent improvements on ooDML. The findings make robustness across different shifts a central comparison, rather than relying on a single split's result.
summary.tldr: ooDML evaluates metric learning across increasingly difficult distribution shifts and finds that few-shot learning consistently improves generalization.

title: Characterizing Generalization under Out-Of-Distribution Shifts in Deep Metric Learning

abstract: Learning in stochastic games is a notoriously difficult problem because, in addition to each other's strategic decisions, the players must also contend with the fact that the game itself evolves over time, possibly in a very complicated manner. Because of this, the convergence properties of popular learning algorithms — like policy gradient and its variants — are poorly understood, except in specific classes of games (such as potential or two-player, zero-sum games). In view of this, we examine the long-run behavior of policy gradient methods with respect to Nash equilibrium policies that are second-order stationary (SOS) in a sense similar to the type of sufficiency conditions used in optimization. Our first result is that SOS policies are locally attracting with high probability, and we show that policy gradient trajectories with gradient estimates provided by the REINFORCE algorithm achieve an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ distance-squared convergence rate if the method's step-size is chosen appropriately. Subsequently, specializing to the class of deterministic Nash policies, we show that this rate can be improved dramatically and, in fact, policy gradient methods converge within a finite number of iterations in that case.

Subsequently, specializing to the class of deterministic Nash policies, we show that this rate can be improved dramatically and, in fact, policy gradient methods converge within a finite number of iterations in that case.

paragraphs: In stochastic games, players learn while responding both to one another and to an environment that changes over time. This makes policy-gradient convergence harder to understand than in some special game classes. The paper studies behavior near Nash equilibrium policies satisfying a second-order stationarity condition related to sufficient conditions in optimization.

The first result shows that these policies attract nearby learning trajectories with high probability. For policy gradients estimated using REINFORCE, the authors establish a squared-distance convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(n)) when the step size is selected appropriately. The result describes local convergence under the stated equilibrium and step-size conditions, rather than convergence from every possible starting policy.

For the more specialized class of deterministic Nash policies, the analysis gives a substantially stronger conclusion: policy-gradient methods converge in finitely many iterations. Together, these findings distinguish general local attraction from faster behavior in a particular policy class. They extend understanding of policy-gradient learning beyond the special classes of stochastic games where convergence had been better understood.
summary.tldr: Policy gradients locally approach second-order stationary Nash policies with high probability, with finite-iteration convergence in the studied deterministic-policy case.

title: On the convergence of policy gradient methods to Nash equilibria in general stochastic games

abstract: The combinatorial problem of learning directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from data was recently framed as a purely continuous optimization problem by leveraging a differentiable acyclicity characterization of DAGs based on the trace of a matrix exponential function. Existing acyclicity characterizations are based on the idea that powers of an adjacency matrix contain information about walks and cycles. In this work, we propose a new acyclicity characterization based on the log-determinant (log-det) function, which leverages the nilpotency property of DAGs. To deal with the inherent asymmetries of a DAG, we relate the domain of our log-det characterization to the set of $\textit{M-matrices}$, which is a key difference to the classical log-det function defined over the cone of positive definite matrices.Similar to acyclicity functions previously proposed, our characterization is also exact and differentiable. However, when compared to existing characterizations, our log-det function: (1) Is better at detecting large cycles; (2) Has better-behaved gradients; and (3) Its runtime is in practice about an order of magnitude faster. From the optimization side, we drop the typically used augmented Lagrangian scheme and propose DAGMA ($\textit{Directed Acyclic Graphs via M-matrices for Acyclicity}$), a method that resembles the central path for barrier methods. Each point in the central path of DAGMA is a solution to an unconstrained problem regularized by our log-det function, then we show that at the limit of the central path the solution is guaranteed to be a DAG. Finally, we provide extensive experiments for $\textit{linear}$ and $\textit{nonlinear}$ SEMs and show that our approach can reach large speed-ups and smaller structural Hamming distances against state-of-the-art methods. Code implementing the proposed method is open-source and publicly available at https://github.com/kevinsbello/dagma.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph requires finding directed relationships without introducing cycles. Differentiable tests for acyclicity make it possible to approach this discrete structural problem through continuous optimization. This paper introduces an exact, differentiable test based on a log-determinant function and the nilpotency property of acyclic graphs.

The construction uses M-matrices to accommodate the asymmetry of directed graphs, rather than the positive-definite matrix domain associated with the classical log-determinant. The authors report that their test detects large cycles better, has better-behaved gradients, and runs about an order of magnitude faster in practice than existing characterizations. These properties matter because the acyclicity test guides optimization as well as checking the resulting structure.

DAGMA combines this test with a sequence of unconstrained optimization problems regularized by the log-determinant function. The sequence resembles a barrier method's central path, and the authors prove that its limiting solution is acyclic. Experiments with linear and nonlinear structural equation models show that the approach can achieve substantial speedups and smaller structural Hamming distances than leading methods.
summary.tldr: DAGMA combines an exact log-determinant acyclicity test with an optimization path whose limiting solution is guaranteed to be a DAG.

title: DAGMA: Learning DAGs via M-matrices and a Log-Determinant Acyclicity Characterization

abstract: In recommendation systems, global positioning, system identification and mobile social networks, it is a fundamental routine that a server completes a low-rank matrix from an observed subset of its entries. However, sending data to a cloud server raises up the data privacy concern due to eavesdropping attacks and the single-point failure problem, e.g., the Netflix prize contest was canceled after a privacy lawsuit. In this paper, we propose a homomorphic matrix completion algorithm for privacy-preserving data completion. First, we formulate a \textit{homomorphic matrix completion} problem where a server performs matrix completion on cyphertexts, and propose an encryption scheme that is fast and easy to implement. Secondly, we prove that the proposed scheme satisfies the \textit{homomorphism property} that decrypting the recovered matrix on cyphertexts will obtain the target complete matrix in plaintext. Thirdly, we prove that the proposed scheme satisfies an $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy property. While with similar level of privacy guarantee, we reduce the best-known error bound $O(\sqrt[10]{n_1^3n_2})$ to EXACT recovery at a price of more samples. Finally, on numerical data and real-world data, we show that both homomorphic nuclear-norm minimization and alternating minimization algorithms achieve accurate recoveries on cyphertexts, verifying the homomorphism property.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix from only some of its entries, a task used in recommendation and other applications. Sending those entries to a server creates privacy concerns. This paper proposes an encryption scheme and completion procedure that let the server perform the reconstruction on encrypted data.

The key mathematical property connects encrypted computation with the intended plaintext result: decrypting the recovered encrypted matrix yields the target complete matrix. The authors prove this homomorphism property and also establish an epsilon-delta differential privacy guarantee. These results address both whether the encrypted procedure produces the desired answer and the stated privacy behavior of the scheme.

At a similar level of privacy guarantee, the paper replaces a previously known nonzero error bound with exact recovery, at the cost of requiring more observed samples. Experiments on numerical and real-world data show accurate encrypted-domain recovery using nuclear-norm minimization and alternating minimization. The contribution combines encrypted computation with recovery guarantees while making the additional sample requirement an explicit part of the trade-off.
summary.tldr: The paper enables low-rank matrix completion on encrypted data, proving privacy and exact-recovery properties with an increased sample requirement.

title: Homomorphic Matrix Completion

abstract: Large transformer-based models are able to perform in-context few-shot learning, without being explicitly trained for it. This observation raises the question: what aspects of the training regime lead to this emergent behavior? Here, we show that this behavior is driven by the distributions of the training data itself. In-context learning emerges when the training data exhibits particular distributional properties such as burstiness (items appear in clusters rather than being uniformly distributed over time) and having a large number of rarely occurring classes. In-context learning also emerges more strongly when item meanings or interpretations are dynamic rather than fixed. These properties are exemplified by natural language, but are also inherent to naturalistic data in a wide range of other domains. They also depart significantly from the uniform, i.i.d. training distributions typically used for standard supervised learning. In our initial experiments, we found that in-context learning traded off against more conventional weight-based learning, and models were unable to achieve both simultaneously. However, our later experiments uncovered that the two modes of learning could co-exist in a single model when it was trained on data following a skewed Zipfian distribution -- another common property of naturalistic data, including language. In further experiments, we found that naturalistic data distributions were only able to elicit in-context learning in transformers, and not in recurrent models. Our findings indicate how the transformer architecture works together with particular properties of the training data to drive the intriguing emergent in-context learning behaviour of large language models, and indicate how future work might encourage both in-context and in-weights learning in domains beyond language.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why transformers can learn from examples supplied in their current context without being explicitly trained for that ability. It examines the training data distribution as a source of this behavior. The experiments identify burstiness, where items occur in clusters, and large numbers of rare classes as properties that encourage in-context learning.

The behavior becomes stronger when an item's meaning or interpretation can change. These properties resemble naturalistic data, including language, and differ from the uniform, independently sampled distributions often used in supervised learning. The findings connect adaptation within a context to regularities encountered during training, rather than treating the ability as a consequence of architecture alone.

Together, these results point to an interaction between architecture and data distribution, and suggest ways to encourage both learning modes beyond language.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that particular training-data distributions encourage transformer in-context learning and can allow it to coexist with learning stored in weights.

title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers

abstract: Structured kernel interpolation (SKI) accelerates Gaussian processes (GP) inference by interpolating the kernel covariance function using a dense grid of inducing points, whose corresponding kernel matrix is highly structured and thus amenable to fast linear algebra. Unfortunately, SKI scales poorly in the dimension of the input points, since the dense grid size grows exponentially with the dimension. To mitigate this issue, we propose the use of sparse grids within the SKI framework. These grids enable accurate interpolation, but with a number of points growing more slowly with dimension. We contribute a novel nearly linear time matrix-vector multiplication algorithm for the sparse grid kernel matrix. We also describe how sparse grids can be combined with an efficient interpolation scheme based on simplicial complexes. With these modifications, we demonstrate that SKI can be scaled to higher dimensions while maintaining accuracy, for both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Structured kernel interpolation accelerates Gaussian process inference by approximating a covariance function using inducing points arranged on a grid. A dense grid supports efficient matrix operations, but its size grows exponentially with input dimension. This paper tackles that growth by replacing the dense grid with a sparse one.

Sparse grids retain accurate interpolation while requiring a number of points that grows more slowly with dimension. Using fewer points is only part of the challenge, because the resulting kernel matrix must still support fast computation. The authors therefore develop a nearly linear-time algorithm for multiplying that matrix by a vector.

The paper also combines sparse grids with an efficient interpolation scheme based on simplicial complexes. Together, these changes adapt both the grid representation and the operations needed to use it. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that structured kernel interpolation can reach higher dimensions while maintaining accuracy. The contribution is a coordinated approach to reducing grid growth without giving up the computational advantages that motivate the framework.
summary.tldr: Sparse grids and fast matrix operations extend structured kernel interpolation to higher-dimensional Gaussian process problems while maintaining accuracy.

title: Kernel Interpolation with Sparse Grids

abstract: On-device training enables the model to adapt to new data collected from the sensors by fine-tuning a pre-trained model. Users can benefit from customized AI models without having to transfer the data to the cloud, protecting the privacy. However, the training memory consumption is prohibitive for IoT devices that have tiny memory resources. We propose an algorithm-system co-design framework to make on-device training possible with only 256KB of memory. On-device training faces two unique challenges: (1) the quantized graphs of neural networks are hard to optimize due to low bit-precision and the lack of normalization; (2) the limited hardware resource (memory and computation) does not allow full backpropagation. To cope with the optimization difficulty, we propose Quantization- Aware Scaling to calibrate the gradient scales and stabilize 8-bit quantized training. To reduce the memory footprint, we propose Sparse Update to skip the gradient computation of less important layers and sub-tensors. The algorithm innovation is implemented by a lightweight training system, Tiny Training Engine, which prunes the backward computation graph to support sparse updates and offload the runtime auto-differentiation to compile time. Our framework is the first practical solution for on-device transfer learning of visual recognition on tiny IoT devices (e.g., a microcontroller with only 256KB SRAM), using less than 1/1000 of the memory of PyTorch and TensorFlow while matching the accuracy. Our study enables IoT devices not only to perform inference but also to continuously adapt to new data for on-device lifelong learning. A video demo can be found here: https://youtu.be/XaDCO8YtmBw.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained model on a device lets it adapt to locally collected sensor data without sending that data to the cloud. This paper combines algorithm and system changes to make visual recognition transfer learning practical with only 256KB of memory.

The result demonstrates on-device adaptation on tiny microcontrollers and provides a practical basis for devices to keep learning from new data after deployment.
summary.tldr: Gradient scaling, selective updates, and a specialized training engine enable visual transfer learning on devices with only 256KB of memory.

title: On-Device Training Under 256KB Memory

abstract: We study semi-supervised learning (SSL) for vision transformers (ViT), an under-explored topic despite the wide adoption of the ViT architectures to different tasks. To tackle this problem, we use a SSL pipeline, consisting of first un/self-supervised pre-training, followed by supervised fine-tuning, and finally semi-supervised fine-tuning. At the semi-supervised fine-tuning stage, we adopt an exponential moving average (EMA)-Teacher framework instead of the popular FixMatch, since the former is more stable and delivers higher accuracy for semi-supervised vision transformers. In addition, we propose a probabilistic pseudo mixup mechanism to interpolate unlabeled samples and their pseudo labels for improved regularization, which is important for training ViTs with weak inductive bias. Our proposed method, dubbed Semi-ViT, achieves comparable or better performance than the CNN counterparts in the semi-supervised classification setting. Semi-ViT also enjoys the scalability benefits of ViTs that can be readily scaled up to large-size models with increasing accuracy. For example, Semi-ViT-Huge achieves an impressive 80\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet using only 1\% labels, which is comparable with Inception-v4 using 100\% ImageNet labels. The code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/semi-vit.

paragraphs: Semi-ViT studies how vision transformers can learn image classification from a mixture of labeled and unlabeled data. Its pipeline begins with unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining, continues with supervised fine-tuning, and finishes with semi-supervised fine-tuning. This sequence combines an initial representation-learning stage with later use of both label sources.

For the final stage, the authors use an exponential-moving-average teacher framework because they find it more stable and accurate than FixMatch for these transformers. They also introduce probabilistic pseudo mixup, which interpolates unlabeled examples and their predicted labels. This supplies regularization, an important concern for vision transformers with weak inductive bias.

Semi-ViT matches or exceeds the studied convolutional-network counterparts in semi-supervised classification and gains accuracy as model size increases. Semi-ViT-Huge reaches 80% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with only 1% of labels, comparable to Inception-v4 using all ImageNet labels. The result illustrates the reported label efficiency of this training pipeline and its ability to benefit from larger transformer models.
summary.tldr: Semi-ViT combines staged training, an EMA teacher, and pseudo mixup to scale semi-supervised vision transformers effectively.

title: Semi-supervised Vision Transformers at Scale

abstract: Imitation learning (IL) is a general learning paradigm for sequential decision-making problems. Interactive imitation learning, where learners can interactively query for expert annotations, has been shown to achieve provably superior sample efficiency guarantees compared with its offline counterpart or reinforcement learning. In this work, we study classification-based online imitation learning (abbrev. COIL) and the fundamental feasibility to design oracle-efficient regret-minimization algorithms in this setting, with a focus on the general non-realizable case. We make the following contributions: (1) we show that in the COIL problem, any proper online learning algorithm cannot guarantee a sublinear regret in general; (2) we propose Logger, an improper online learning algorithmic framework, that reduces COIL to online linear optimization, by utilizing a new definition of mixed policy class; (3) we design two oracle-efficient algorithms within the Logger framework that enjoy different sample and interaction round complexity tradeoffs, and show their improvements over behavior cloning; (4) we show that under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, efficient dynamic regret minimization is infeasible in the Logger framework.

paragraphs: Interactive imitation learning lets a learner request expert annotations while learning sequential decisions. This paper examines classification-based online imitation learning, focusing on the general non-realizable case, where the chosen policy class need not perfectly represent the expert. It asks which regret guarantees can be achieved by algorithms that efficiently use optimization oracles.

The first result rules out a broad approach: proper online algorithms, which remain within the original policy class, cannot guarantee sublinear regret in general. The authors respond with Logger, an improper learning framework built around a new mixed policy class. Logger reduces the imitation-learning problem to online linear optimization, expanding the available algorithmic tools.

Within this framework, two oracle-efficient algorithms offer different tradeoffs between sample requirements and interaction rounds, with improvements over behavior cloning. The paper also establishes a boundary: under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, efficient dynamic-regret minimization is infeasible within Logger. The contribution combines constructive guarantees with impossibility results, clarifying both the value of mixed policies and the limits of stronger performance requirements.
summary.tldr: Logger uses mixed policies to enable efficient online imitation learning while the paper establishes limits for proper learners and dynamic regret.

title: On Efficient Online Imitation Learning via Classification

abstract: The level of autonomy is increasing in systems spanning multiple domains, but these systems still experience failures. One way to mitigate the risk of failures is to integrate human oversight of the autonomous systems and rely on the human to take control when the autonomy fails. In this work, we formulate a method of collaborative decision making through action suggestions that improves action selection without taking control of the system. Our approach uses each suggestion efficiently by incorporating the implicit information shared through suggestions to modify the agent's belief and achieves better performance with fewer suggestions than naively following the suggested actions. We assume collaborative agents share the same objective and communicate through valid actions. By assuming the suggested action is dependent only on the state, we can incorporate the suggested action as an independent observation of the environment. The assumption of a collaborative environment enables us to use the agent's policy to estimate the distribution over action suggestions. We propose two methods that use suggested actions and demonstrate the approach through simulated experiments. The proposed methodology results in increased performance while also being robust to suboptimal suggestions.

paragraphs: An autonomous system can benefit from another agent's advice without handing over control. This paper studies collaboration through action suggestions: a collaborator recommends a valid action, and the receiving agent uses that recommendation to improve its decision. The central idea is that advice conveys information about the environment as well as a proposed move.

The method assumes that the agents share an objective and that the suggested action depends only on the environment's state. Under this assumption, the suggestion can be incorporated as an independent observation, updating the receiving agent's beliefs. The collaborative setting also lets the method use the agent's own policy to estimate how suggestions are distributed.

The authors propose two methods and evaluate them in simulations. They report better performance with fewer suggestions than a strategy that simply follows the recommended actions, together with robustness to suboptimal advice. These results support interpreting suggestions as evidence: even imperfect recommendations can inform the agent's understanding and help it choose subsequent actions.
summary.tldr: Treating collaborative action suggestions as information about the environment improves simulated decision making with fewer recommendations.

title: Collaborative Decision Making Using Action Suggestions

abstract: Equivariances provide useful inductive biases in neural network modeling, with the translation equivariance of convolutional neural networks being a canonical example. Equivariances can be embedded in architectures through weight-sharing and place symmetry constraints on the functions a neural network can represent. The type of symmetry is typically fixed and has to be chosen in advance. Although some tasks are inherently equivariant, many tasks do not strictly follow such symmetries. In such cases, equivariance constraints can be overly restrictive. In this work, we propose a parameter-efficient relaxation of equivariance that can effectively interpolate between a (i) non-equivariant linear product, (ii) a strict-equivariant convolution, and (iii) a strictly-invariant mapping. The proposed parameterisation can be thought of as a building block to allow adjustable symmetry structure in neural networks. In addition, we demonstrate that the amount of equivariance can be learned from the training data using backpropagation. Gradient-based learning of equivariance achieves similar or improved performance compared to the best value found by cross-validation and outperforms baselines with partial or strict equivariance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image classification tasks.

paragraphs: Equivariance builds a symmetry into a neural network: a transformation of the input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. Convolutional networks provide the familiar translation example. Such constraints can be helpful, but choosing them in advance may restrict a model too much when the task only partly follows the assumed symmetry.

This paper proposes a parameter-efficient construction that makes symmetry adjustable. It can interpolate between a non-equivariant linear product, a strictly equivariant convolution, and a strictly invariant mapping. These alternatives represent different requirements on how outputs respond to transformations, allowing one building block to cover a range of symmetry structures.

The authors also show that backpropagation can learn the amount of equivariance from training data. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 classification, this learning achieves similar or better performance than the best setting found through cross-validation and outperforms the compared partial- and strict-equivariance baselines. The findings support treating symmetry strength as something to learn alongside model parameters when a fixed architectural choice may be too restrictive.
summary.tldr: A parameter-efficient neural building block learns how strongly to enforce equivariance and improves or matches symmetry choices selected by cross-validation.

title: Relaxing Equivariance Constraints with Non-stationary Continuous Filters

abstract: Large and diverse datasets have been the cornerstones of many impressive advancements in artificial intelligence. Intelligent creatures, however, learn by interacting with the environment, which changes the input sensory signals and the state of the environment. In this work, we aim to bring the best of both worlds and propose an algorithm that exhibits an exploratory behavior whilst it utilizes large diverse datasets. Our key idea is to leverage deep generative models that are pretrained on static datasets and introduce a dynamic model in the latent space. The transition dynamics simply mixes an action and a random sampled latent. It then applies an exponential moving average for temporal persistency, the resulting latent is decoded to image using pretrained generator. We then employ an unsupervised reinforcement learning algorithm to explore in this environment and perform unsupervised representation learning on the collected data. We further leverage the temporal information of this data to pair data points as a natural supervision for representation learning. Our experiments suggest that the learned representations can be successfully transferred to downstream tasks in both vision and reinforcement learning domains.

paragraphs: Large static datasets provide diverse examples, while interaction provides sequences shaped by an agent's actions. This paper combines those sources of learning by turning a pretrained generative model into an environment for exploration. The generator supplies images, and a new dynamical model determines how its latent input changes.

Each transition mixes an action with a randomly sampled latent and then uses an exponential moving average to provide temporal persistence. The pretrained generator decodes the resulting latent into an image. This creates an evolving visual environment from a model originally trained on static data, allowing exploration without requiring the original dataset itself to be interactive.

An unsupervised reinforcement learning algorithm explores the environment, and the collected observations support unsupervised representation learning. Their temporal relationships also provide a natural way to pair examples for supervision. Experiments suggest that the learned representations transfer successfully to downstream tasks in both vision and reinforcement learning. The contribution is a concrete mechanism for combining dataset diversity with action-dependent, temporally connected experience.
summary.tldr: Palm up turns a pretrained image generator into an explorable latent-space environment for learning transferable representations.

title: Palm up: Playing in the Latent Manifold for Unsupervised Pretraining

abstract: The conclusions of randomized controlled trials may be biased when the outcome of one unit depends on the treatment status of other units, a problem known as \textit{interference}. In this work, we study interference in the setting of one-sided bipartite experiments in which the experimental units---where treatments are randomized and outcomes are measured---do not interact directly. Instead, their interactions are mediated through their connections to \textit{interference units} on the other side of the graph. Examples of this type of interference are common in marketplaces and two-sided platforms. The \textit{cluster-randomized design} is a popular method to mitigate interference when the graph is known, but it has not been well-studied in the one-sided bipartite experiment setting. In this work, we formalize a natural model for interference in one-sided bipartite experiments using the exposure mapping framework. We first exhibit settings under which existing cluster-randomized designs fail to properly mitigate interference under this model. We then show that minimizing the bias of the difference-in-means estimator under our model results in a balanced partitioning clustering objective with a natural interpretation. We further prove that our design is minimax optimal over the class of linear potential outcomes models with bounded interference. We conclude by providing theoretical and experimental evidence of the robustness of our design to a variety of interference graphs and potential outcomes models.

paragraphs: A randomized experiment can give biased conclusions when treating one unit changes another unit’s outcome. This paper studies a particular network structure: treatments and outcomes belong to units on one side of a bipartite graph, while connections through units on the other side transmit interference. Such indirect interactions arise in marketplaces and two-sided platforms.

The authors formalize this setting using exposure mappings, which describe how treatment assignments translate into the treatment conditions a unit experiences. They identify situations where existing methods for assigning whole clusters to treatment fail to adequately control interference. They then derive a balanced graph-partitioning objective by minimizing the bias of the difference between treatment and control means.

Under their model, the resulting design is minimax optimal within a class of linear potential-outcome models with bounded interference. This is a worst-case guarantee within that specified class, rather than across every possible outcome mechanism. The paper also supplies theoretical and experimental evidence that the design remains robust across varied interference graphs and outcome models.
summary.tldr: A balanced clustering objective yields experimental designs that control indirect interference and have a specified minimax optimality guarantee.

title: Cluster Randomized Designs for One-Sided Bipartite Experiments

abstract: Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a unifying framework that generalizes both linear programming and quadratically-constrained quadratic programming, while also yielding efficient solvers, both in theory and in practice. However, there exist known impossibility results for approximating the optimal solution when constraints for covering SDPs arrive in an online fashion. In this paper, we study online covering linear and semidefinite programs in which the algorithm is augmented with advice from a possibly erroneous predictor. We show that if the predictor is accurate, we can efficiently bypass these impossibility results and achieve a constant-factor approximation to the optimal solution, i.e., consistency. On the other hand, if the predictor is inaccurate, under some technical conditions, we achieve results that match both the classical optimal upper bounds and the tight lower bounds up to constant factors, i.e., robustness. More broadly, we introduce a framework that extends both (1) the online set cover problem augmented with machine-learning predictors, studied by Bamas, Maggiori, and Svensson (NeurIPS 2020), and (2) the online covering SDP problem, initiated by Elad, Kale, and Naor (ICALP 2016). Specifically, we obtain general online learning-augmented algorithms for covering linear programs with fractional advice and constraints, and initiate the study of learning-augmented algorithms for covering SDP problems. Our techniques are based on the primal-dual framework of Buchbinder and Naor (Mathematics of Operations Research, 34, 2009) and can be further adjusted to handle constraints where the variables lie in a bounded region, i.e., box constraints.

paragraphs: Online covering optimization requires an algorithm to respond as constraints arrive. For semidefinite programs, known impossibility results restrict how closely online methods can approximate the optimal solution. This paper studies what becomes possible when the algorithm also receives advice from a predictor that may sometimes be wrong.

The proposed framework aims for two guarantees. With accurate predictions, it achieves a constant-factor approximation, a property called consistency. With inaccurate predictions, it matches classical optimal bounds up to constant factors under stated technical conditions, providing robustness. Accurate advice supplies additional information that allows the method to bypass the impossibility results of the original online setting.

The authors develop general algorithms for covering linear programs with fractional advice and constraints, and extend learning-augmented optimization to covering semidefinite programs. Their techniques use a primal-dual framework and can be adjusted for box constraints that restrict variables to bounded regions. The contribution is a way to benefit from reliable predictions while retaining conditional worst-case protection when advice is poor.
summary.tldr: Prediction-augmented online covering algorithms achieve constant-factor guarantees with accurate advice and retain classical robustness bounds under technical conditions.

title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms for Online Linear and Semidefinite Programming

abstract: Motion planning, which aims to find a high-quality collision-free path in the configuration space, is a fundamental task in robotic systems. Recently, learning-based motion planners, especially the graph neural network-powered, have shown promising planning performance. However, though the state-of-the-art GNN planner can efficiently extract and learn graph information, its inherent mechanism is not well suited for graph search process, hindering its further performance improvement. To address this challenge and fully unleash the potential of GNN in motion planning, this paper proposes GraphMP, a neural motion planner for both low and high-dimensional planning tasks. With the customized model architecture and training mechanism design, GraphMP can simultaneously perform efficient graph pattern extraction and graph search processing, leading to strong planning performance. Experiments on a variety of environments, ranging from 2D Maze to 14D dual KUKA robotic arm, show that our proposed GraphMP achieves significant improvement on path quality and planning speed over the state-of-the-art learning-based and classical planners; while preserving the competitive success rate.

paragraphs: Motion planning seeks a high-quality path through a robot's possible configurations while avoiding collisions. Graph neural networks can learn useful information from the graph used for planning, but extracting graph patterns and searching for a route are different requirements. The authors identify a mismatch between the mechanism of an existing leading GNN planner and the graph-search process.

GraphMP addresses that mismatch through a customized network architecture and training mechanism. It is designed to combine efficient graph-pattern extraction with graph-search processing in one neural planner. The intended scope includes both low-dimensional problems and higher-dimensional tasks involving more complex robotic configurations.

Experiments range from a two-dimensional maze to a 14-dimensional dual KUKA robotic arm. Across the evaluated environments, the authors report significant improvements in path quality and planning speed over leading learning-based and classical planners, while maintaining a competitive success rate. The findings suggest that adapting the network to the search process can improve planning efficiency without giving up competitive reliability in finding a path.
summary.tldr: GraphMP combines graph feature learning with search-oriented processing to improve robotic path quality and planning speed.

title: GraphMP: Graph Neural Network-based Motion Planning with Efficient Graph Search

abstract: We study a two-stage scenario for learning to defer with multiple experts, which is crucial in practice for many applications. In this scenario, a predictor is derived in a first stage by training with a common loss function such as cross-entropy. In the second stage, a deferral function is learned to assign the most suitable expert to each input. We design a new family of surrogate loss functions for this scenario both in the score-based and the predictor-rejector settings and prove that they are supported by $H$-consistency bounds, which implies their Bayes-consistency. Moreover, we show that, for a constant cost function, our two-stage surrogate losses are realizable $H$-consistent. While the main focus of this work is a theoretical analysis, we also report the results of several experiments on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets.

In the second stage, a deferral function is learned to assign the most suitable expert to each input. paragraphs: A predictive system may need to decide which expert should handle a particular input. This paper studies a two-stage version of that problem: first train a predictor using an ordinary loss such as cross-entropy, then learn a deferral function that assigns inputs to suitable experts. The separation makes the deferral problem distinct from initial predictor training.

The authors design a family of surrogate losses for both score-based and predictor-rejector formulations. These losses provide trainable objectives for the second stage. Their theoretical analysis establishes H-consistency bounds, linking surrogate optimization to the desired decision objective within a hypothesis class, and shows that these bounds imply Bayes consistency.

A further result establishes realizable H-consistency when the cost function is constant. That condition is part of the guarantee and determines its scope. Although the paper centers on theory, it also reports experiments on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. Its main contribution is therefore a theoretically supported set of objectives for learning expert deferral after a predictor has already been trained.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theoretically consistent losses for learning which expert should receive an input after a predictor is trained.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts

abstract: We introduce MQ-Det, an efficient architecture and pre-training strategy design to utilize both textual description with open-set generalization and visual exemplars with rich description granularity as category queries, namely, Multi-modal Queried object Detection, for real-world detection with both open-vocabulary categories and various granularity. MQ-Det incorporates vision queries into existing well-established language-queried-only detectors. A plug-and-play gated class-scalable perceiver module upon the frozen detector is proposed to augment category text with class-wise visual information. To address the learning inertia problem brought by the frozen detector, a vision conditioned masked language prediction strategy is proposed. MQ-Det's simple yet effective architecture and training strategy design is compatible with most language-queried object detectors, thus yielding versatile applications. Experimental results demonstrate that multi-modal queries largely boost open-world detection. For instance, MQ-Det significantly improves the state-of-the-art open-set detector GLIP by +7.8% AP on the LVIS benchmark via multi-modal queries without any downstream finetuning, and averagely +6.3% AP on 13 few-shot downstream tasks, with merely additional 3% modulating time required by GLIP. Code is available at https://github.com/YifanXu74/MQ-Det.

paragraphs: Text descriptions and example images offer complementary ways to specify which objects a detector should find. Text supports open-vocabulary categories, while visual examples can express finer distinctions in appearance. MQ-Det combines both forms of category query to support detection across unfamiliar categories and different levels of descriptive detail.

The method adds a gated, class-scalable perceiver module to an existing frozen language-queried detector. This module supplements category text with visual information for each class. A vision-conditioned masked-language prediction strategy addresses the learning inertia associated with the frozen detector. The architecture is designed to work with most language-queried detectors, making the addition broadly reusable.

The experiments show substantial benefits from multimodal queries. For GLIP, the authors report a 7.8% AP improvement on LVIS without downstream fine-tuning and an average 6.3% AP improvement across 13 few-shot downstream tasks. They report only 3% additional modulating time relative to GLIP. These results support adding visual exemplars as an efficient way to enrich what category queries communicate.
summary.tldr: MQ-Det enriches text-queried detectors with visual examples, improving open-world and few-shot detection with modest additional modulating time.

title: Multi-modal Queried Object Detection in the Wild

abstract: Visual localization is a fundamental task in computer vision and robotics. Training existing visual localization methods requires a large number of posed images to generalize to novel views, while state-of-the-art methods generally require dense ground truth 3D labels for supervision. However, acquiring a large number of posed images and dense 3D labels in the real world is challenging and costly. In this paper, we present a novel visual localization method that achieves accurate localization while using only a few posed images compared to other localization methods. To achieve this, we first use a few posed images with coarse pseudo-3D labels provided by NeRF to train a coordinate regression network. Then a coarse pose is estimated from the regression network with PNP. Finally, we use the image-based visual servo (IBVS) with the scene prior provided by NeRF for pose optimization. Furthermore, our method can provide effective navigation prior, which enable navigation based on IBVS without using custom markers and depth sensor. Extensive experiments on 7-Scenes and 12-Scenes datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods under the same setting, with only 5\% to 25\% training data. Furthermore, our framework can be naturally extended to the visual navigation task based on IBVS, and its effectiveness is verified in simulation experiments.
