paragraphs: Some decisions require a probability distribution over several related outputs, conditioned on observed inputs. A poorly calibrated joint distribution can make those predictions unreliable. Existing recalibration methods mostly address individual outputs, while multivariate conformal prediction supplies coverage regions without explicitly specifying the full probability distribution inside and outside those regions.

This paper introduces latent calibration for conditional invertible generative models, including normalizing flows and flow matching. It evaluates calibration in the model’s latent representation. The proposed latent recalibration method then learns a transformation of that space after the original model has been trained, producing a revised distribution with an explicit multivariate density.

The method includes finite-sample bounds on latent calibration and is designed to remain computationally efficient. Experiments on tabular and image datasets consistently improve both latent calibration error and negative log-likelihood. These findings support correcting probability models through their latent spaces while retaining a usable density. The theoretical bounds concern the introduced latent-calibration notion, and the reported empirical improvements also address how well the recalibrated models assign probability to observed data.
summary.tldr: Latent recalibration adjusts a trained generative model’s latent space to improve multivariate probabilistic calibration while preserving an explicit density.

title: Multivariate Latent Recalibration for Conditional Normalizing Flows

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations without labeled data, often by enforcing invariance to input transformations such as rotations or blurring. Recent studies have highlighted two pivotal properties for effective representations: (i) avoiding dimensional collapse-where the learned features occupy only a low-dimensional subspace, and (ii) enhancing uniformity of the induced distribution. In this work, we introduce T-REGS, a simple regularization framework for SSL based on the length of the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) over the learned representation. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that T-REGS simultaneously mitigates dimensional collapse and promotes distribution uniformity on arbitrary compact Riemannian manifolds. Several experiments on synthetic data and on classical SSL benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our approach at enhancing representation quality.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning builds representations without labeled examples, often by encouraging transformed versions of an input to receive similar representations. This paper focuses on two properties that help those representations remain useful: avoiding dimensional collapse, where features occupy only a small subspace, and distributing representations more uniformly across the space available to them.

T-REGS introduces a regularization framework based on the length of a minimum spanning tree over learned representations. Such a tree connects the represented points with minimal total edge length. Using its length gives the framework a geometric quantity that reflects relationships across the collection of representations, tying the learning objective to how those points occupy their space.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that T-REGS both mitigates dimensional collapse and promotes uniformity on arbitrary compact Riemannian manifolds. Experiments on synthetic data and standard self-supervised learning benchmarks support improvements in representation quality. The contribution is a simple shared mechanism for addressing both geometric properties, with theory extending beyond an exclusively flat representation-space setting.
summary.tldr: T-REGS uses minimum-spanning-tree length to mitigate representation collapse and encourage uniformity, with theoretical analysis and experimental support.

title: T-REGS: Minimum Spanning Tree Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Recent advances in operating system (OS) agents have enabled vision-language models (VLMs) to directly control a user’s computer. Unlike conventional VLMs that passively output text, OS agents autonomously perform computer-based tasks in response to a single user prompt. OS agents do so by capturing, parsing, and analysing screenshots and executing low-level actions via application programming interfaces (APIs), such as mouse clicks and keyboard inputs. This direct interaction with the OS significantly raises the stakes, as failures or manipulations can have immediate and tangible consequences. In this work, we uncover a novel attack vector against these OS agents: Malicious Image Patches (MIPs), adversarially perturbed screen regions that, when captured by an OS agent, induce it to perform harmful actions by exploiting specific APIs. For instance, a MIP can be embedded in a desktop wallpaper or shared on social media to cause an OS agent to exfiltrate sensitive user data. We show that MIPs generalise across user prompts and screen configurations, and that they can hijack multiple OS agents even during the execution of benign instructions. These findings expose critical security vulnerabilities in OS agents that have to be carefully addressed before their widespread deployment.

paragraphs: Operating-system agents use screenshots to understand a computer interface and then act through APIs that control inputs such as clicks and keystrokes. This connects visual interpretation directly to actions on a user's machine. The paper investigates how manipulating a small visible region can redirect that behavior even while the agent is carrying out a legitimate task.

The attack uses Malicious Image Patches: adversarially modified screen regions that induce harmful actions through particular APIs when the agent captures them. The authors describe placements such as desktop wallpaper or social-media content and identify sensitive-data exfiltration as a possible consequence. The security implication is that an agent's visual inputs can become a route to unauthorized computer actions, making the connection between perception and API execution a consequential vulnerability.
summary.tldr: Malicious image patches can redirect screenshot-driven computer agents into harmful API actions across different prompts and screen configurations.

title: MIP against Agent: Malicious Image Patches Hijacking Multimodal OS Agents

abstract: Predicting future neural activity is a core challenge in modeling brain dynamics, with applications ranging from scientific investigation to closed-loop neurotechnology. While recent models of population activity emphasize interpretability and behavioral decoding, neural forecasting—particularly across multi-session, spontaneous recordings—remains underexplored. We introduce POCO, a unified forecasting model that combines a lightweight univariate forecaster with a population-level encoder to capture both neuron-specific and brain-wide dynamics. Trained across five calcium imaging datasets spanning zebrafish, mice, and *C. elegans*, POCO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy at cellular resolution in spontaneous behaviors. After pre-training, POCO rapidly adapts to new recordings with minimal fine-tuning. Notably, POCO's learned unit embeddings recover biologically meaningful structure—such as brain region clustering—without any anatomical labels. Our comprehensive analysis reveals several key factors influencing performance, including context length, session diversity, and preprocessing. Together, these results position POCO as a scalable and adaptable approach for cross-session neural forecasting and offer actionable insights for future model design. By enabling accurate, generalizable forecasting models of neural dynamics across individuals and species, POCO lays the groundwork for adaptive neurotechnologies and large-scale efforts for neural foundation models. Code is available at [https://github.com/yuvenduan/POCO](https://github.com/yuvenduan/POCO).

It targets cellular-resolution prediction, particularly for spontaneous recordings collected across multiple sessions, an area the paper identifies as less explored than behavioral decoding or interpretability.

title: POCO: Scalable Neural Forecasting through Population Conditioning

abstract: Missing values, frequently encountered in time series data, can significantly impair the effectiveness of analytical methods. While deep imputation models have emerged as the predominant approach due to their superior performance, explicitly incorporating inductive biases aligned with time-series characteristics offers substantial improvement potential. Taking advantage of non-stationarity and periodicity in time series, two domain-specific inductive biases are designed: (1) Non-Stationary Guidance, which operationalizes the proximity principle to address highly non-stationary series by emphasizing temporal neighbors, and (2) Periodic Guidance, which exploits periodicity patterns through learnable weight allocation across historical periods. Building upon these complementary mechanisms, the overall module, named Meta Guidance, dynamically fuses both guidances through data-adaptive weights learned from the specific input sample. Experiments on nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that integrating Meta Guidance into existing deep imputation architectures achieves an average 27.39\% reduction in imputation error compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Building upon these complementary mechanisms, the overall module, named Meta Guidance, dynamically fuses both guidances through data-adaptive weights learned from the specific input sample. Experiments on nine benchmark datasets demonstrate that integrating Meta Guidance into existing deep imputation architectures achieves an average 27.39\% reduction in imputation error compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Meta Guidance improves models that fill missing values in time series by explicitly incorporating two kinds of temporal structure. The paper focuses on non-stationarity, where a series’ behavior changes over time, and periodicity, where patterns recur. These properties offer complementary clues about which observations are useful for estimating a missing value.

Non-Stationary Guidance emphasizes nearby observations, applying the idea that temporal neighbors can be especially informative when the series changes substantially. Periodic Guidance learns how much weight to assign to historical periods, drawing on repeated patterns. The overall module learns sample-specific weights that dynamically combine these two sources of guidance.

The authors integrate Meta Guidance into existing deep imputation architectures and evaluate it on nine benchmark datasets. They report an average 27.39% reduction in imputation error relative to state-of-the-art baselines. The result supports explicitly supplying temporal preferences while allowing the model to adapt their relative influence to each input. The reported percentage is an average across the evaluation, rather than an identical improvement for every dataset.
summary.tldr: Meta Guidance adaptively combines nearby observations and recurring temporal patterns to improve missing-value estimation in time series.

title: Meta Guidance: Incorporating Inductive Biases into Deep Time Series Imputers

abstract: The widespread use of diffusion models has led to an abundance of AI-generated data, raising concerns about model collapse---a phenomenon in which recursive iterations of training on synthetic data lead to performance degradation. Prior work primarily characterizes this collapse via variance shrinkage or distribution shift, but these perspectives miss practical manifestations of model collapse. This paper identifies a transition from generalization to memorization during model collapse in diffusion models, where models increasingly replicate training data instead of generating novel content during iterative training on synthetic samples. This transition is directly driven by the declining entropy of the synthetic training data produced in each training cycle, which serves as a clear indicator of model degradation. Motivated by this insight, we propose an entropy-based data selection strategy to mitigate the transition from generalization to memorization and alleviate model collapse. Empirical results show that our approach significantly enhances visual quality and diversity in recursive generation, effectively preventing collapse.

paragraphs: When a diffusion model trains on images generated by an earlier model, repeated cycles can gradually damage its output. This paper studies that process through the distinction between generalization and memorization: producing new content versus increasingly reproducing examples from the training data. That perspective connects model collapse to a recognizable change in what the generator actually creates.

The authors identify declining entropy in the synthetic training data as the direct driver of this transition. Entropy here captures the diversity or uncertainty present in the data. As successive synthetic datasets lose that richness, the models move toward memorization. The paper therefore treats entropy as an indicator of degradation and as a basis for deciding which generated examples to retain.

The proposed intervention selects training data using entropy. In the reported experiments, this improves both visual quality and diversity during recursive generation and effectively prevents collapse. The findings support managing the composition of synthetic training data as a way to preserve generation quality across repeated training cycles.
summary.tldr: The paper links diffusion-model collapse to declining synthetic-data entropy and uses entropy-based data selection to preserve quality and diversity.

title: A Closer Look at Model Collapse: From a Generalization-to-Memorization Perspective

abstract: Physical phenomena in the real world are often described by energy-based modeling theories, such as Hamiltonian mechanics or the Landau theory. It is known that physical phenomena based on these theories have an energy conservation law or a dissipation law. Therefore, in the simulations of such physical phenomena, numerical methods that preserve the energy-conservation or dissipation laws are desirable. However, because various energy-behavior-preserving numerical methods have been proposed, it is difficult to discover the best one. In this study, we propose a method for learning highly accurate energy-behavior-preserving integrators from data. Numerical results show that our approach certainly learns energy-behavior-preserving numerical methods that are more accurate than existing numerical methods for various differential equations, including chaotic Hamiltonian systems, dissipative systems, and a nonlinear partial differential equation. We also provide universal approximation theorems for the proposed approach.

Numerical simulations should respect that behavior as they approximate the underlying differential equations. This paper addresses the difficulty of choosing among numerous numerical methods that preserve such laws.

The object being learned is the numerical integration method itself. This connects data-driven adaptation with a structural requirement supplied by the physical model, so accuracy and energy behavior are considered together.

The reported numerical studies find learned integrators more accurate than existing numerical methods across several differential equations, including chaotic Hamiltonian systems, dissipative systems, and a nonlinear partial differential equation. The authors also establish universal approximation theorems for their approach. The numerical findings demonstrate its performance on the tested systems, while the theorems supply complementary support for the expressive capacity of the proposed learning framework.
summary.tldr: UEPI learns accurate numerical integrators from data while preserving the energy conservation or dissipation behavior of the modeled system.

title: UEPI: Universal Energy-Behavior-Preserving Integrators for Energy Conservative/Dissipative Differential Equations

abstract: Recently, Gaussian Splatting (GS) has shown great potential for urban scene reconstruction in the field of autonomous driving. However, current urban scene reconstruction methods often depend on multimodal sensors as inputs, $\textit{i.e.}$ LiDAR and images. Though the geometry prior provided by LiDAR point clouds can largely mitigate ill-posedness in reconstruction, acquiring such accurate LiDAR data is still challenging in practice: i) precise spatiotemporal calibration between LiDAR and other sensors is required, as they may not capture data simultaneously; ii) reprojection errors arise from spatial misalignment when LiDAR and cameras are mounted at different locations. To avoid the difficulty of acquiring accurate LiDAR depth, we propose ${D}^2GS$, a LiDAR-free urban scene reconstruction framework. In this work, we obtain geometry priors that are as effective as LiDAR while being denser and more accurate. $\textbf{First}$, we initialize a dense point cloud by back-projecting multi-view metric depth predictions. This point cloud is then optimized by a Progressive Pruning strategy to improve the global consistency. $\textbf{Second}$, we jointly refine Gaussian geometry and predicted dense metric depth via a Depth Enhancer. Specifically, we leverage diffusion priors from a depth foundation model to enhance the depth maps rendered by Gaussians. In turn, the enhanced depths provide stronger geometric constraints during Gaussian training. $\textbf{Finally}$, we improve the accuracy of ground geometry by constraining the shape and normal attributes of Gaussians within road regions. Extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, producing more accurate geometry even when compared with those using ground-truth LiDAR data.

The authors also report that their geometric priors are denser and more accurate while being as effective as LiDAR guidance. summary.tldr: D²GS reconstructs urban scenes without LiDAR by jointly refining Gaussian geometry and dense predicted depth.

title: D$^2$GS: Dense Depth Regularization for LiDAR-free Urban Scene Reconstruction

abstract: This paper presents $\mathbf{OLinear}$, a $\mathbf{linear}$-based multivariate time series forecasting model that operates in an $\mathbf{o}$rthogonally transformed domain. Recent forecasting models typically adopt the temporal forecast (TF) paradigm, which directly encode and decode time series in the time domain. However, the entangled step-wise dependencies in series data can hinder the performance of TF. To address this, some forecasters conduct encoding and decoding in the transformed domain using fixed, dataset-independent bases (e.g., sine and cosine signals in the Fourier transform). In contrast, we propose $\mathbf{OrthoTrans}$, a data-adaptive transformation based on an orthogonal matrix that diagonalizes the series' temporal Pearson correlation matrix. This approach enables more effective encoding and decoding in the decorrelated feature domain and can serve as a plug-in module to enhance existing forecasters. To enhance the representation learning for multivariate time series, we introduce a customized linear layer, $\mathbf{NormLin}$, which employs a normalized weight matrix to capture multivariate dependencies. Empirically, the NormLin module shows a surprising performance advantage over multi-head self-attention, while requiring nearly half the FLOPs. Extensive experiments on 24 benchmarks and 140 forecasting tasks demonstrate that OLinear consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance with high efficiency. Notably, as a plug-in replacement for self-attention, the NormLin module consistently enhances Transformer-based forecasters. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/jackyue1994/OLinear.

summary.tldr: OLinear combines a data-adaptive orthogonal transformation with a normalized linear layer for accurate, efficient time-series forecasting.

title: OLinear: A Linear Model for Time Series Forecasting in Orthogonally Transformed Domain

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved impressive results across diverse network modeling tasks, but accurately estimating uncertainty on graphs remains difficult—especially under distributional shifts. Unlike traditional uncertainty estimation, graph-based uncertainty must account for randomness arising from both the graph’s structure and its label distribution, which adds complexity. In this paper, making an analogy between the evolution of a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) driven by Mat\'ern Gaussian Process and message passing using GNN layers, we present a principled way to design a novel message passing scheme that incorporates spatial-temporal noises motivated by the Gaussian Process approach to SPDE. Our method simultaneously captures uncertainty across space and time and allows explicit control over the covariance kernel’s smoothness, thereby enhancing uncertainty estimates on graphs with both low and high label informativeness. Our extensive experiments on Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection on graph datasets with varying label informativeness demonstrate the soundness and superiority of our model to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Uncertainty on a graph involves both its connectivity and the distribution of its labels. This makes confidence estimation particularly difficult when data shift away from the conditions seen during training. The paper develops a graph message-passing scheme that explicitly draws on a mathematical model of randomness evolving across space and time.

The design connects layers of a graph neural network to the evolution of a stochastic partial differential equation driven by a Matérn Gaussian process. This analogy motivates spatial and temporal noise within message passing. It also provides explicit control over the smoothness of the covariance kernel, which describes how random variation is related across locations.

The resulting method captures uncertainty across both space and time and is evaluated on graphs with low and high label informativeness. Out-of-distribution detection experiments report better performance than existing approaches across the tested datasets. These findings support using structured, controllable noise to improve graph uncertainty estimates across different levels of label informativeness, rather than treating graph uncertainty as a single undifferentiated source.
summary.tldr: A graph message-passing method inspired by stochastic differential equations uses structured noise to improve uncertainty estimation and out-of-distribution detection.

title: Uncertainty Estimation on Graphs with Structure Informed Stochastic Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Graph generation models play pivotal roles in many real-world applications, from data augmentation to privacy-preserving. Despite their deployment successes, existing approaches often exhibit fairness issues, limiting their adoption in high-risk decision-making applications. Most existing fair graph generation works are based on autoregressive models that suffer from ordering sensitivity, while primarily addressing structural bias and overlooking the critical issue of feature bias. To this end, we propose FairGEM, a novel one-shot graph generation framework designed to mitigate both graph structural bias and node feature bias simultaneously. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis establishes that FairGEM delivers substantially stronger fairness guarantees than existing models while preserving generation quality. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that FairGEM achieves superior performance in both generation quality and fairness.

paragraphs: Graph generators create data containing entities and the connections between them. Their outputs can carry unfairness through both connection patterns and attributes attached to individual nodes. The paper argues that existing fair graph generation methods mainly address structural bias, leaving node feature bias insufficiently addressed. Many also generate graphs sequentially, making their behavior sensitive to the ordering used.

FairGEM is a one-shot generation framework designed to mitigate both sources of bias together. Its central contribution is to treat the fairness of graph structure and node attributes as parts of the same generation problem. This matters because improving one component alone can leave the other component biased.

The authors provide theoretical results establishing stronger fairness guarantees than existing models while preserving generation quality. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets also report improvements in both fairness and output quality. Together, these findings support the framework's joint treatment of the two biases within the generation settings studied.
summary.tldr: FairGEM jointly addresses bias in graph connections and node features, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements in fairness and generation quality.

title: A Unified Framework for Fair Graph Generation: Theoretical Guarantees and Empirical Advances

abstract: For any black-box model, conformal prediction (CP) returns prediction *sets* guaranteed to include the true label with high adjustable probability. Robust CP (RCP) extends the guarantee to the worst case noise up to a pre-defined magnitude. For RCP, a well-established approach is to use randomized smoothing since it is applicable to any black-box model and provides smaller sets compared to deterministic methods. However, smoothing-based robustness requires many model forward passes per each input which is computationally expensive. We show that conformal prediction attains some robustness even with *a single forward pass on a randomly perturbed input*. Using any binary certificate we propose a single sample robust CP (RCP1). Our approach returns robust sets with smaller average set size compared to SOTA methods which use many (e.g. $\sim 100$) passes per input. Our key insight is to certify the conformal procedure itself rather than individual conformity scores. Our approach is agnostic to the task (classification and regression). We further extend our approach to smoothing-based robust conformal risk control.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with a chosen high probability of containing the truth. Robust conformal prediction extends this protection to worst-case noise within a specified magnitude. Randomized smoothing is useful for black-box models, but conventional smoothing-based approaches require many model evaluations for each input.

This paper shows that some robustness is possible with just one evaluation of a randomly perturbed input. Its method, RCP1, uses a binary certificate and changes what gets certified: it targets the conformal procedure as a whole instead of certifying individual conformity scores. This shift is the central reason the method can pursue robust prediction sets with far fewer forward passes.

The reported results give smaller average robust sets than state-of-the-art methods using many evaluations, including approaches requiring roughly 100 passes per input. The framework applies to both classification and regression and extends to smoothing-based conformal risk control. The single-sample result concerns robustness within this certification framework and the specified noise setting, rather than unrestricted resistance to arbitrary input changes.
summary.tldr: RCP1 certifies the conformal procedure itself to obtain some robustness from a single randomly perturbed model evaluation.

title: One Sample is Enough to Make Conformal Prediction Robust

abstract: Self-play constitutes a fundamental paradigm for autonomous skill acquisition, whereby agents iteratively enhance their capabilities through self-directed environmental exploration. Conventional self-play frameworks exploit agent symmetry within zero-sum competitive settings, yet this approach proves inadequate for open-ended learning scenarios characterized by inherent asymmetry. Human pedagogical systems exemplify asymmetric instructional frameworks wherein educators systematically construct challenges calibrated to individual learners' developmental trajectories. The principal challenge resides in operationalizing these asymmetric, adaptive pedagogical mechanisms within artificial systems capable of autonomously synthesizing appropriate curricula without predetermined task hierarchies. Here we present Heterogeneous Adversarial Play (HAP), an adversarial Automatic Curriculum Learning framework that formalizes teacher-student interactions as a minimax optimization wherein task-generating instructor and problem-solving learner co-evolve through adversarial dynamics. In contrast to prevailing automatic curriculum learning methodologies that employ static curricula or unidirectional task selection mechanisms, HAP establishes a bidirectional feedback system wherein instructors continuously recalibrate task complexity in response to real-time learner performance metrics. Experimental validation across multi-task learning domains demonstrates that our framework achieves performance parity with SOTA baselines while generating curricula that enhance learning efficacy in both artificial agents and human subjects.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous Adversarial Play, or HAP, develops an automatic curriculum through interaction between a teacher and a learner. The paper argues that conventional self-play, built around symmetric competitors, is poorly matched to open-ended settings with different instructional and problem-solving roles. Its motivating question is how an artificial teacher can construct suitable challenges without a predefined hierarchy of tasks.

HAP models the teacher and learner as participants in a minimax optimization process. The teacher generates tasks, the learner attempts to solve them, and their adversarial interaction changes both over time. A bidirectional feedback mechanism lets the teacher continually adjust task complexity using the learner’s current performance. The curriculum therefore responds to the learner’s development during training.

Experiments across multi-task learning domains show performance on par with state-of-the-art baselines. The generated curricula also improve learning efficacy in the reported studies involving artificial agents and human participants. These findings support adaptive teacher–learner interaction as a way to construct useful curricula while maintaining competitive task performance.
summary.tldr: HAP co-trains a task-generating teacher and a problem-solving learner to produce adaptive curricula with competitive reported performance.

title: Heterogeneous Adversarial Play in Interactive Environments

abstract: State-of-the-art membership inference attacks (MIAs) typically require training many reference models, making it difficult to scale these attacks to large pre-trained language models (LLMs). As a result, prior research has either relied on weaker attacks that avoid training references (e.g., fine-tuning attacks), or on stronger attacks applied to small models and datasets. However, weaker attacks have been shown to be brittle and insights from strong attacks in simplified settings do not translate to today's LLMs. These challenges prompt an important question: are the limitations observed in prior work due to attack design choices, or are MIAs fundamentally ineffective on LLMs? We address this question by scaling LiRA--one of the strongest MIAs--to GPT-2 architectures ranging from 10M to 1B parameters, training references on over 20B tokens from the C4 dataset. Our results advance the understanding of MIAs on LLMs in four key ways. While (1) strong MIAs can succeed on pre-trained LLMs, (2) their effectiveness, remains limited (e.g., AUC<0.7) in practical settings. (3) Even when strong MIAs achieve better-than-random AUC, aggregate success metrics conceal per-sample prediction instability; many individual predictions are so unstable that they are statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip. Finally, (4) the relationship between MIA success and related privacy metrics is not as straightforward as prior work has suggested.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example appeared in a model's training data. Strong attacks often need many reference models, making them expensive to study at language-model scale. This paper investigates whether previously observed weaknesses reflect compromises in attack design or deeper limits on membership inference in pretrained language models.

The authors scale LiRA, a strong membership-inference method, to GPT-2 architectures with 10 million to 1 billion parameters. They train reference models on more than 20 billion C4 tokens. This setup examines a strong attack beyond the small models and simplified datasets that had constrained some earlier investigations.

The results show that strong attacks can succeed, but effectiveness remains limited in practical settings, with reported examples having AUC below 0.7. More importantly, above-random aggregate performance can hide unstable decisions about individual examples: many predictions are statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip. The authors also find a less straightforward relationship between attack success and related privacy measures than prior work suggested. These findings qualify how confidently aggregate attack scores can support claims about specific training examples.
summary.tldr: Scaled-up LiRA attacks can detect training membership, but practical accuracy and the stability of individual predictions remain limited.

title: Exploring the limits of strong membership inference attacks on large language models

abstract: Topological descriptors have been increasingly utilized for capturing multiscale structural information in relational data. In this work, we consider various filtrations on the (box) product of graphs and the effect on their outputs on the topological descriptors - the Euler characteristic (EC) and persistent homology (PH). In particular, we establish a complete characterization of the expressive power of EC on general color-based filtrations. We also show that the PH descriptors of (virtual) graph products contain strictly more information than the computation on individual graphs, whereas EC does not. Additionally, we provide algorithms to compute the PH diagrams of the product of vertex- and edge-level filtrations on the graph product. We also substantiate our theoretical analysis with empirical investigations on runtime analysis, expressivity, and graph classification performance. Overall, this work paves way for powerful graph persistent descriptors via product filtrations. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/tda_graph_product.

It focuses on two summaries: the Euler characteristic and persistent homology.

The authors fully characterize the expressive power of the Euler characteristic for general color-based filtrations. They also establish a distinction between the two descriptors: persistent homology of virtual graph products contains strictly more information than computing persistent homology on the individual graphs, while the Euler characteristic does not gain that additional information. The choice of descriptor therefore determines whether the product construction increases what can be distinguished.

The paper also provides algorithms for computing persistence diagrams for products of vertex-level and edge-level filtrations. Empirical studies examine runtime, expressivity, and graph classification, supporting the theoretical analysis. The contribution connects a representational advantage to concrete computation: product filtrations can enrich persistent graph descriptors, and the proposed algorithms provide a way to calculate those enriched summaries.
summary.tldr: Persistent homology on graph products captures additional information unavailable from individual graphs, while Euler characteristic descriptors do not gain the same expressivity.

title: On topological descriptors for graph products

abstract: Multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning (MAIRL) aims to recover agent reward functions from expert demonstrations. We characterize the feasible reward set in Markov games, identifying all reward functions that rationalize a given equilibrium. However, equilibrium-based observations are often ambiguous: a single Nash equilibrium can correspond to many reward structures, potentially changing the game's nature in multi-agent systems. We address this by introducing entropy-regularized Markov games, which yield a unique equilibrium while preserving strategic incentives. For this setting, we provide a sample complexity analysis detailing how errors affect learned policy performance. Our work establishes theoretical foundations and practical insights for MAIRL.

paragraphs: Multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning asks what rewards could explain the behavior of interacting experts. The difficulty is that observing an equilibrium does not uniquely reveal those rewards. Several different reward structures can justify the same behavior, and those structures may imply different kinds of strategic interaction.

The paper characterizes the feasible reward set in Markov games: all reward functions that make a given equilibrium rational. This turns ambiguity into an explicit mathematical object to study. It then introduces entropy-regularized Markov games, which, in the setting developed by the authors, produce a unique equilibrium while preserving strategic incentives.

For this regularized setting, the authors analyze sample complexity and how estimation errors influence the performance of learned policies. The contribution connects three questions: which rewards fit observed behavior, how equilibrium ambiguity can be addressed, and how imperfect learning affects subsequent decisions. Its uniqueness claim concerns equilibrium in the proposed setting; the starting observation remains that a single observed equilibrium can be compatible with many reward structures.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes rewards compatible with multi-agent equilibria and analyzes learning in an entropy-regularized setting with a unique equilibrium.

title: On Feasible Rewards in Multi-Agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning disentangled representations in sequential data is a key goal in deep learning, with broad applications in vision, audio, and time series. While real-world data involves multiple interacting semantic factors over time, prior work has mostly focused on simpler two-factor static and dynamic settings, primarily because such settings make data collection easier, thereby overlooking the inherently multi-factor nature of real-world data. We introduce the first standardized benchmark for evaluating multi-factor sequential disentanglement across six diverse datasets spanning video, audio, and time series. Our benchmark includes modular tools for dataset integration, model development, and evaluation metrics tailored to multi-factor analysis. We additionally propose a post-hoc Latent Exploration Stage to automatically align latent dimensions with semantic factors, and introduce a Koopman-inspired model that achieves state-of-the-art results. Moreover, we show that Vision-Language Models can automate dataset annotation and serve as zero-shot disentanglement evaluators, removing the need for manual labels and human intervention. Together, these contributions provide a robust and scalable foundation for advancing multi-factor sequential disentanglement. Our code is available on GitHub, and the datasets and trained models are available on Hugging Face.

paragraphs: Sequential data often contains several interacting sources of variation. Yet research on disentangled representations has frequently reduced the problem to separating static information from dynamic information. This paper expands evaluation to multiple semantic factors, asking whether learned representations can separate the different meaningful influences present across a sequence.

The authors introduce a standardized benchmark covering six datasets across video, audio, and time series. Its modular tools support adding datasets, developing models, and measuring disentanglement across multiple factors. A separate Latent Exploration Stage then aligns learned latent dimensions with semantic factors after training. This helps connect the model’s internal coordinates with the properties those coordinates represent.

The paper also introduces a Koopman-inspired model and reports state-of-the-art results. In addition, it demonstrates that vision-language models can generate dataset annotations and evaluate disentanglement without task-specific evaluator training, removing manual labeling and intervention in the demonstrated workflow. Together, these contributions broaden both the modeling target and the evaluation machinery beyond the familiar static-versus-dynamic split.
summary.tldr: This work benchmarks multi-factor sequential disentanglement and introduces tools, a model, and automated evaluation beyond the static-versus-dynamic setting.

title: Disentanglement Beyond Static vs. Dynamic: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Multi-Factor Sequential Representations

abstract: Quality analysis of weather forecasts is an essential topic in meteorology. Although traditional score-based evaluation metrics can quantify certain forecast errors, they are still far from meteorological experts in terms of descriptive capability, interpretability, and understanding of dynamic evolution. With the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), these models become potential tools to overcome the above challenges. In this work, we introduce an MLLM-based weather forecast analysis method, RadarQA, integrating key physical attributes with detailed assessment reports. We introduce a novel and comprehensive task paradigm for multi-modal quality analysis, encompassing both single frame and sequence, under both rating and assessment scenarios. To support training and benchmarking, we design a hybrid annotation pipeline that combines human expert labeling with automated heuristics. With such an annotation method, we construct RQA-70K, a large-scale dataset with varying difficulty levels for radar forecast quality evaluation. We further design a multi-stage training strategy that iteratively improves model performance at each stage. Extensive experiments show that RadarQA outperforms existing general MLLMs across all evaluation settings, highlighting its potential for advancing quality analysis in weather prediction.

paragraphs: Weather forecast quality is difficult to communicate with a numerical score alone. Traditional metrics capture some errors but offer less descriptive detail and understanding of changing weather patterns than expert assessment. RadarQA explores using a multimodal language model to connect key physical attributes of radar forecasts with detailed evaluation reports.

The paper defines tasks for both individual frames and sequences, with settings that require ratings or written assessments. The contribution centers on evaluating and describing forecast quality, with a task framework and dataset that make these capabilities measurable.
summary.tldr: RadarQA combines specialized training and expert-informed data to rate and describe weather radar forecast quality.

title: RadarQA: Multi-modal Quality Analysis of Weather Radar Forecasts

abstract: We present LeMiCa, a training-free and efficient acceleration framework for diffusion-based video generation. While existing caching strategies primarily focus on reducing local heuristic errors, they often overlook the accumulation of global errors, leading to noticeable content degradation between accelerated and original videos. To address this issue, we formulate cache scheduling as a directed graph with error-weighted edges and introduce a Lexicographic Minimax Path Optimization strategy that explicitly bounds the worst-case path error. This approach substantially improves the consistency of global content and style across generated frames. Extensive experiments on multiple text-to-video benchmarks demonstrate that LeMiCa delivers dual improvements in both inference speed and generation quality. Notably, our method achieves a 2.9× speedup on the Latte model and reaches an LPIPS score of 0.05 on Open-Sora, outperforming prior caching techniques. Importantly, these gains come with minimal perceptual quality degradation, making LeMiCa a robust and generalizable paradigm for accelerating diffusion-based video generation. We believe this approach can serve as a strong foundation for future research on efficient and reliable video synthesis.

paragraphs: LeMiCa accelerates diffusion-based video generation without additional training. It addresses a problem in caching strategies that reduce computation: locally reasonable reuse decisions can accumulate errors across generation. The resulting video may drift in content or style from the output of the original, unaccelerated process.

The authors represent cache scheduling as a directed graph whose edges carry error weights. They then use lexicographic minimax path optimization to explicitly bound the worst-case path error. This makes the accumulated consequences of a schedule central to the decision, supporting greater consistency of content and style across the generated frames.

Specific results include a 2.9-fold speedup on Latte and an LPIPS score of 0.05 on Open-Sora. The abstract reports minimal perceptual degradation from the acceleration. These findings support treating caching as a global scheduling problem, because the quality of a sequence depends on how errors combine across the generation process.
summary.tldr: LeMiCa accelerates diffusion video generation by optimizing cache schedules around accumulated worst-case error.

title: LeMiCa: Lexicographic Minimax Path Caching for Efficient Diffusion-Based Video Generation

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) often relies on manually designed reward functions, which are difficult to specify and can lead to issues such as reward hacking and suboptimal behavior. Alternatives like inverse RL and preference-based RL attempt to infer surrogate rewards from demonstrations or preferences but suffer from ambiguity and distribution mismatch. A more direct approach, inspired by imitation learning, avoids reward modeling by leveraging expert demonstrations. However, most existing methods align actions only at individual states, failing to capture the coherence of long-horizon trajectories. In this work, we study the problem of directly aligning policies with expert-labeled trajectories to preserve long-horizon behavior without relying on reward signals. Specifically, we aim to learn a policy that maximizes the probability of generating the expert trajectories. Nevertheless, we prove that, in its general form, this trajectory alignment problem is NP-complete. To address this, we propose Trajectory Graph Learning (TGL), a framework that leverages structural assumptions commonly satisfied in practice—such as bounded realizability of expert trajectories or a tree-structured MDP. These enable a graph-based policy planning algorithm that computes optimal policies in polynomial time under known dynamics. For settings with unknown dynamics, we develop a sample-efficient algorithm based on UCB-style exploration and establish sub-linear regret. Experiments on grid-world tasks demonstrate that TGL substantially outperforms standard imitation learning methods for long-trajectory planning.

paragraphs: Learning from expert demonstrations can avoid manually specifying a reward, but matching actions at individual states may miss the coherence of a long sequence. This paper instead aims to learn a policy that maximizes the probability of producing expert-labeled trajectories. The objective makes whole-trajectory behavior central to learning.

Under the relevant assumptions and with known dynamics, its graph-based planning algorithm computes optimal policies in polynomial time. Those conditions are essential to the stated tractability result.

For unknown dynamics, the paper develops an algorithm using upper-confidence-bound-style exploration and establishes sublinear regret. Grid-world experiments show substantial improvements over standard imitation-learning methods for planning long trajectories. The contribution joins a direct trajectory objective with structural conditions that make planning manageable, then extends the approach to learning when the environment's dynamics are initially unknown.
summary.tldr: Trajectory Graph Learning directly aligns policies with expert trajectories, with efficient optimal planning under stated structural assumptions and known dynamics.

title: Trajectory Graph Learning: Aligning with Long Trajectories in Reinforcement Learning Without Reward Design

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) excel at multimodal tasks but are prone to misinterpreting visual inputs, often resulting in hallucinations and unreliable outputs. We present Dropout Decoding, a novel inference-time approach that quantifies the uncertainty of visual tokens and selectively masks uncertain tokens to improve decoding. Our method measures the uncertainty of each visual token by projecting it onto the text space and decomposing it into aleatoric and epistemic components. Specifically, we focus on epistemic uncertainty, which captures perception-related errors more effectively. Inspired by dropout regularization, we introduce uncertainty-guided token dropout, which applies the dropout principle to input visual tokens instead of model parameters, and during inference rather than training. By aggregating predictions from an ensemble of masked decoding contexts, we can robustly mitigate errors arising from visual token misinterpretations. Evaluations on benchmarks including CHAIR, THRONE, and MMBench demonstrate that Dropout Decoding significantly reduces object hallucinations (OH) and enhances both reliability and quality of LVLM outputs across diverse visual contexts.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can generate plausible descriptions based on misinterpreted image features. Dropout Decoding targets that perception uncertainty at inference, deciding which visual tokens may be unreliable before they influence the final response.

The method projects each visual token into text space and separates aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. It focuses on the epistemic component because it better captures the studied perception errors. Uncertainty-guided dropout then masks selected input tokens, and an ensemble of these masked contexts supplies aggregated predictions.

Evaluations on CHAIR, THRONE, and MMBench show fewer object hallucinations and improved response quality and reliability across visual settings. The contribution applies dropout to visual inputs during decoding rather than to parameters during training. Its benefit comes from reducing dependence on questionable perceptual evidence while combining the information retained by multiple contexts.
summary.tldr: Dropout Decoding masks uncertain visual tokens and aggregates predictions to reduce hallucinations.

title: Enhancing Vision-Language Model Reliability with Uncertainty-Guided Dropout Decoding

abstract: We show that low-rank adaptation of large-scale models suffers from a low stable rank that is well below the linear algebraic rank of the subspace, degrading fine-tuning performance. To mitigate the underutilization of the allocated subspace, we propose PoLAR, a parameterization inspired by the polar decomposition that factorizes the low-rank update into two direction matrices constrained to Stiefel manifolds and an unconstrained scale matrix. Our theory shows that PoLAR yields an exponentially faster convergence rate on a canonical low-rank adaptation problem. Pairing the parameterization with Riemannian optimization leads to consistent gains on three different benchmarks testing general language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and mathematical problem solving with base model sizes ranging from 350M to 27B.

To mitigate the underutilization of the allocated subspace, we propose PoLAR, a parameterization inspired by the polar decomposition that factorizes the low-rank update into two direction matrices constrained to Stiefel manifolds and an unconstrained scale matrix. paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation allocates a restricted subspace for updating a large model during fine-tuning. This paper finds that the update can use that space poorly: its stable rank is substantially below its algebraic rank. In practical terms, the allocated dimensions do not contribute evenly enough to realize the subspace's potential, and fine-tuning performance suffers.

PoLAR changes the representation of the update using a factorization inspired by polar decomposition. Two matrices describe directions and are constrained to Stiefel manifolds, while a separate unconstrained matrix controls scale. The method pairs this representation with Riemannian optimization, which handles the geometry of the constrained direction matrices during learning.

The theory establishes an exponentially faster convergence rate for a canonical low-rank adaptation problem. Experiments provide complementary evidence, showing consistent gains on benchmarks covering language understanding, commonsense reasoning, and mathematical problem solving for base models from 350 million to 27 billion parameters. The theoretical claim applies to the analyzed problem, while the broader evaluations support the usefulness of separating direction and scale in practical adaptation.
summary.tldr: PoLAR separates low-rank updates into constrained directions and unconstrained scale to better use adaptation capacity and improve fine-tuning.

title: PoLAR: Polar-Decomposed Low-Rank Adapter Representation

abstract: We present Fin3R, a simple, effective, and general fine-tuning method for feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. The family of feed-forward reconstruction model regresses pointmap of all input images to a reference frame coordinate system, along with other auxiliary outputs, in a single forward pass. However, we find that current models struggle with fine geometry and robustness due to (\textit{i}) the scarcity of high-fidelity depth and pose supervision and (\textit{ii}) the inherent geometric misalignment from multi-view pointmap regression. Fin3R jointly tackles two issues with an extra lightweight fine-tuning step. We freeze the decoder, which handles view matching, and fine-tune only the image encoder—the component dedicated to feature extraction. The encoder is enriched with fine geometric details distilled from a strong monocular teacher model on large, unlabeled datasets, using a custom, lightweight LoRA adapter. We validate our method on a wide range of models, including DUSt3R, MASt3R, CUT3R, and VGGT. The fine-tuned models consistently deliver sharper boundaries, recover complex structures, and achieve higher geometric accuracy in both single- and multi-view settings, while adding only the tiny LoRA weights, which leave test-time memory and latency virtually unchanged. Project page: \href{http://visual-ai.github.io/fin3r}{https://visual-ai.github.io/fin3r}

paragraphs: Feed-forward reconstruction models turn input images into 3D point maps in a shared reference frame in one forward pass. Their speed does not remove difficulties with fine geometry and robustness. This paper identifies two sources of those difficulties: limited high-quality depth and camera-pose supervision, and geometric misalignment arising when point maps are predicted across multiple views.

Fin3R adds a lightweight fine-tuning step focused on the image encoder, which extracts visual features. It freezes the decoder responsible for view matching. A strong model that learns geometry from single images acts as a teacher, transferring fine geometric information through large unlabeled datasets. A small, customized LoRA adapter provides the trainable additions to the encoder.

Tests on DUSt3R, MASt3R, CUT3R, and VGGT report consistently sharper boundaries, better recovery of complex structures, and higher geometric accuracy. These improvements appear in both single-view and multi-view settings. The results suggest that enriching image features can improve several reconstruction systems while preserving their existing matching component. Only small adapter weights are added, leaving inference memory and latency virtually unchanged.
summary.tldr: Fin3R transfers geometric knowledge from a single-image teacher into reconstruction encoders, improving detail with virtually unchanged inference costs.

title: Fin3R: Fine-tuning Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction Models via Monocular Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Modern foundation models often undergo iterative ``bootstrapping'' in their post-training phase: a model generates synthetic data, an external verifier filters out low-quality samples, and the high-quality subset is used for further fine-tuning. Over multiple iterations, the model performance improves, raising a crucial question: How should the total budget for generation and training be allocated across iterations to maximize final performance? In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing budget allocation strategies. Specifically, we show that constant policies fail to converge with high probability, while increasing policies---particularly exponential growth policies---exhibit significant theoretical advantages. Experiments on image denoising with diffusion probabilistic models and math reasoning with large language models show that both exponential and polynomial growth policies consistently outperform constant policies, with exponential policies often providing more stable performance.

paragraphs: Iterative synthetic-data bootstrapping alternates between generating examples, filtering them with an external verifier, and fine-tuning on the accepted subset. As the model improves, the usefulness of spending resources at different iterations can change. This paper asks how a total generation and training budget should be distributed across that process to maximize final performance.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for comparing allocation policies. Within that framework, constant policies fail to converge with high probability, while policies that increase spending over iterations have theoretical advantages. Exponential growth receives particular attention, making the timing of computation a central part of the learning procedure rather than treating every iteration identically.

Experiments investigate image denoising with diffusion probabilistic models and mathematical reasoning with language models. Both polynomial and exponential growth policies consistently outperform constant policies in those tests, and exponential policies often behave more stably. The findings support allocating progressively larger resources as bootstrapping advances, with the empirical comparison complementing the theoretical analysis of how spending schedules affect learning.
summary.tldr: Increasing generation and training budgets across bootstrapping iterations outperforms constant spending in reported experiments, with theoretical advantages for growing policies.

title: Spend Wisely: Maximizing Post-Training Gains in Iterative Synthetic Data Bootstrapping

abstract: We present MetaFind, a scene-aware multi-modal retrieval framework designed to enhance scene generation in the metaverse by retrieving 3D assets from large-scale repositories. MetaFind addresses two core challenges: (i) inconsistent asset retrieval that overlooks spatial, semantic, and stylistic constraints, and (ii) the absence of a standardized retrieval paradigm specifically tailored for 3D asset retrieval, as existing approaches predominantly rely on general-purpose 3D shape representation models. Our key innovation is a retrieval mechanism that enhances both spatial reasoning and style consistency by jointly modeling object-level features (including appearance) and scene-level layout structures. Methodologically, MetaFind introduces a plug-and-play layout encoder that captures both spatial relationships and object appearance features, ensuring retrieved 3D assets are contextually and stylistically coherent with the existing scene. The framework supports iterative scene construction by continuously adapting retrieval results to current scene updates. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the improved spatial and stylistic consistency of MetaFind in various retrieval tasks compared to baseline methods.

paragraphs: Choosing a 3D object for a scene involves more than finding the right category or shape. The object also needs to fit the scene’s spatial arrangement, meaning, and visual style. MetaFind addresses retrieval methods that overlook these constraints by using the surrounding scene to guide searches through large repositories of 3D assets.

The framework jointly represents individual objects, including their appearance, and the layout of the scene. A plug-and-play layout encoder captures spatial relationships together with appearance features. This lets retrieval account for how an asset relates to what is already present, making scene context part of the selection process rather than relying only on general-purpose shape representations.

MetaFind also supports building a scene iteratively: as the scene changes, retrieval results adapt to the updated context. Evaluations across several retrieval tasks report better spatial and stylistic consistency than baseline methods. The contribution is therefore a scene-aware retrieval framework whose selections can remain coordinated with an evolving composition throughout the construction process.
summary.tldr: MetaFind retrieves 3D assets using object appearance and scene layout to improve spatial and stylistic consistency.

title: MetaFind: Scene-Aware 3D Asset Retrieval for Coherent Metaverse Scene Generation

abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude has significantly increased the presence of AI-generated text in digital communication. This trend has heightened the need for reliable detection methods to distinguish between human-authored and machine-generated content. Existing approaches both zero-shot methods and supervised classifiers largely conceptualize this task as a binary classification problem, often leading to poor generalization across domains and models. In this paper, we argue that such a binary formulation fundamentally mischaracterizes the detection task by assuming a coherent representation of human-written texts. In reality, human texts do not constitute a unified distribution, and their diversity cannot be effectively captured through limited sampling. This causes previous classifiers to memorize observed OOD characteristics rather than learn the essence of `non-ID' behavior, limiting generalization to unseen human-authored inputs. Based on this observation, we propose reframing the detection task as an out-of-distribution (OOD) detection problem, treating human-written texts as distributional outliers while machine-generated texts are in-distribution (ID) samples. To this end, we develop a detection framework using one-class learning method including DeepSVDD and HRN, and score-based learning techniques such as energy-based method, enabling robust and generalizable performance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets validate the effectiveness of our OOD-based approach. Specifically, the OOD-based method achieves 98.3\% AUROC and AUPR with only 8.9\% FPR95 on DeepFake dataset. Moreover, we test our detection framework on multilingual, attacked, and unseen-model and -domain text settings, demonstrating the robustness and generalizability of our framework. Code will be released openly and also available in the supplementary materials.
originalAbstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude has significantly increased the presence of AI-generated text in digital communication. This trend has heightened the need for reliable detection methods to distinguish between human-authored and machine-generated content. Existing approaches both zero-shot methods and supervised classifiers largely conceptualize this task as a binary classification problem, often leading to poor generalization across domains and models. In this paper, we argue that such a binary formulation fundamentally mischaracterizes the detection task by assuming a coherent representation of human-written texts. In reality, human texts do not constitute a unified distribution, and their diversity cannot be effectively captured through limited sampling. This causes previous classifiers to memorize observed OOD characteristics rather than learn the essence of `non-ID' behavior, limiting generalization to unseen human-authored inputs. Based on this observation, we propose reframing the detection task as an out-of-distribution (OOD) detection problem, treating human-written texts as distributional outliers while machine-generated texts are in-distribution (ID) samples. To this end, we develop a detection framework using one-class learning method including DeepSVDD and HRN, and score-based learning techniques such as energy-based method, enabling robust and generalizable performance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets validate the effectiveness of our OOD-based approach. Specifically, the OOD-based method achieves 98.3\% AUROC and AUPR with only 8.9\% FPR95 on DeepFake dataset. Moreover, we test our detection framework on multilingual, attacked, and unseen-model and -domain text settings, demonstrating the robustness and generalizability of our framework. Code will be released openly and also available in the supplementary materials.

paragraphs: Most detectors frame human and machine writing as two classes to distinguish. This paper argues that the human class is too diverse to represent adequately with a limited training sample. A detector may consequently learn quirks of the sampled human texts and generalize poorly to different writers, domains, or generating models.

The authors instead treat machine-generated text as the reference distribution and human writing as out-of-distribution input. Their framework explores one-class learning methods, including DeepSVDD and HRN, alongside energy-based scoring. The conceptual shift is to characterize machine writing and detect departures from it, rather than assume that sampled human writing captures a coherent opposing class.

On the DeepFake dataset, the approach reports 98.3% for both AUROC and AUPR, with 8.9% FPR95. Additional experiments cover multilingual text, attacked inputs, unseen generating models, and unseen domains, supporting robustness and generalization in those settings. The title's description of human texts as outliers is therefore a detection formulation relative to the learned machine-text distribution, not a claim about the intrinsic quality of human writing.
summary.tldr: Treating human writing as outside a learned machine-text distribution improves detection generalization in the reported evaluations.

title: Human Texts Are Outliers: Detecting LLM-generated Texts via Out-of-distribution Detection

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have made remarkable strides in generating and editing high-fidelity images from text. Yet, these models remain fundamentally generic, failing to adapt to the nuanced aesthetic preferences of individual users. In this work, we present the first framework for personalized image editing in diffusion models, introducing Collaborative Direct Preference Optimization (C-DPO), a novel method that aligns image edits with user-specific preferences while leveraging collaborative signals from like-minded individuals. Our approach encodes each user as a node in a dynamic preference graph and learns embeddings via a lightweight graph neural network, enabling information sharing across users with overlapping visual tastes. We enhance a diffusion model's editing capabilities by integrating these personalized embeddings into a novel DPO objective, which jointly optimizes for individual alignment and neighborhood coherence. Comprehensive experiments, including user studies and quantitative benchmarks, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms baselines in generating edits that are aligned with user preferences.

paragraphs: A diffusion model can produce convincing image edits while still missing an individual user’s aesthetic preferences. This paper introduces personalized editing through Collaborative Direct Preference Optimization, or C-DPO. Its central idea is to learn from both a user’s own preferences and signals from other people whose visual tastes overlap.

The method represents users as nodes in a dynamic preference graph. A lightweight graph neural network learns user embeddings while sharing information between related users. These embeddings enter a new preference-optimization objective for the diffusion model. The objective jointly encourages alignment with each individual and coherence with their preference neighborhood, connecting personalization to collaborative learning.

User studies and quantitative benchmarks show that the method consistently outperforms the compared baselines in preference-aligned editing. The result concerns whether edits match users’ tastes, which is distinct from simply producing high-fidelity images. The approach provides a concrete way to incorporate relationships among users into an image editor while retaining a separate learned representation for each person.
summary.tldr: C-DPO personalizes diffusion-based image edits by combining individual preference embeddings with signals from users who share similar tastes.

title: Personalized Image Editing in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Collaborative Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: We propose a new stochastic alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm, which incrementally approximates the full gradient in the linearized ADMM formulation. Besides having a low per-iteration complexity as existing stochastic ADMM algorithms, it improves the convergence rate on convex problems from \mO(1/\sqrtT) to \mO(1/T), where T is the number of iterations. This matches the convergence rate of the batch ADMM algorithm, but without the need to visit all the samples in each iteration. Experiments on the graph-guided fused lasso demonstrate that the new algorithm is significantly faster than state-of-the-art stochastic and batch ADMM algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper develops a stochastic version of the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, aimed at combining inexpensive iterations with faster convergence. Existing stochastic methods have low per-iteration cost, while batch ADMM visits all samples during each iteration. The proposed method seeks the convergence rate of the batch approach without that repeated full-data work.

Its central mechanism incrementally approximates the full gradient within a linearized ADMM formulation. On convex problems, the convergence rate improves from O(1/√T) to O(1/T), where T counts iterations. This matches the stated batch ADMM rate while preserving low per-iteration complexity. The distinction matters because iteration count and the cost of each iteration jointly determine computational usefulness.

Experiments on graph-guided fused lasso show that the algorithm is significantly faster than the compared state-of-the-art stochastic and batch ADMM methods. The empirical finding complements the rate analysis: the proposed gradient approximation yields a practical speed advantage on the reported application as well as a stronger theoretical convergence rate.
summary.tldr: Incremental gradient approximation gives stochastic ADMM an O(1/T) convex convergence rate with inexpensive iterations.

title: Fast Stochastic Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers

abstract: We propose a method to aggregate noisy ordinal labels collected from a crowd of workers or annotators. Eliciting ordinal labels is important in tasks such as judging web search quality and consumer satisfaction. Our method is motivated by the observation that workers usually have difficulty distinguishing between two adjacent ordinal classes whereas distinguishing between two classes which are far away from each other is much easier. We develop the method through minimax conditional entropy subject to constraints which encode this observation. Empirical evaluations on real datasets demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods.

Eliciting ordinal labels is important in tasks such as judging web search quality and consumer satisfaction. Our method is motivated by the observation that workers usually have difficulty distinguishing between two adjacent ordinal classes whereas distinguishing between two classes which are far away from each other is much easier. We develop the method through minimax conditional entropy subject to constraints which encode this observation. Empirical evaluations on real datasets demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods.

paragraphs: When people judge search quality or consumer satisfaction, their answers often belong to ordered categories. Combining those answers requires handling disagreement among annotators. The paper focuses on a particular structure in that disagreement: workers commonly struggle to distinguish neighboring categories, while categories farther apart are easier to tell apart.

The authors build an aggregation method around this observation. They use minimax conditional entropy with constraints that encode the different difficulty of nearby and distant distinctions. The ordering therefore contributes information to the aggregation procedure. A disagreement between adjacent categories carries a different interpretation from a disagreement spanning a large part of the rating scale.

Evaluations on real datasets show significant improvements over existing methods. These findings support using the geometry of an ordered label scale when combining noisy judgments. The contribution is both a method for producing aggregate labels and a concrete modeling principle: the pattern of likely annotation errors should reflect how workers distinguish the available categories.
summary.tldr: An ordinal-label aggregation method improves crowd judgments by modeling neighboring categories as harder to distinguish than distant ones.

title: Aggregating Ordinal Labels from Crowds by Minimax Conditional Entropy

abstract: We introduce Markov latent feature models (MLFM), a sparse latent feature model that arises naturally from a simple sequential construction. The key idea is to interpret each state of a sequential process as corresponding to a latent feature, and the set of states visited between two null-state visits as picking out features for an observation. We show that, given some natural constraints, we can represent this stochastic process as a mixture of recurrent Markov chains. In this way we can perform correlated latent feature modeling for the sparse coding problem. We demonstrate two cases in which we define finite and infinite latent feature models constructed from first-order Markov chains, and derive their associated scalable inference algorithms. We show empirical results on a genome analysis task and an image denoising task.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a sparse latent-feature model built from a sequential process. Each state represents a hidden feature. To generate the features associated with an observation, the process records the states visited between two visits to a designated null state. This creates a direct link between movement through states and feature selection.

The sequential construction supports correlations among latent features, which the authors use for sparse coding. Under stated natural constraints, they show that the process can be represented as a mixture of recurrent Markov chains. That representation gives a mathematical foundation for treating the selected features as the outcome of a structured stochastic process.

The authors develop both finite and infinite latent-feature models using first-order Markov chains and derive scalable inference algorithms for each case. They present empirical results on genome analysis and image denoising. The contribution combines a feature-generation mechanism, a conditional representation result, and practical inference methods, showing how sequential structure can organize correlated sparse features across different applications.
summary.tldr: Markov latent feature models use state visits to construct correlated sparse features, with finite and infinite variants.

title: Markov Latent Feature Models

abstract: In this paper we analyze the robustness of stochastic variants of the greedy algorithm for submodular maximization. Our main result shows that for maximizing a monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint, iteratively selecting an element whose marginal contribution is approximately maximal in expectation is a sufficient condition to obtain the optimal approximation guarantee with exponentially high probability, assuming the cardinality is sufficiently large. One consequence of our result is that the linear-time STOCHASTIC-GREEDY algorithm recently proposed in (Mirzasoleiman et al.,2015) achieves the optimal running time while maintaining an optimal approximation guarantee. We also show that high probability guarantees cannot be obtained for stochastic greedy algorithms under matroid constraints, and prove an approximation guarantee which holds in expectation. In contrast to the guarantees of the greedy algorithm, we show that the approximation ratio of stochastic local search is arbitrarily bad, with high probability, as well as in expectation.

One consequence of our result is that the linear-time STOCHASTIC-GREEDY algorithm recently proposed in (Mirzasoleiman et al.,2015) achieves the optimal running time while maintaining an optimal approximation guarantee.
