In contrast to the guarantees of the greedy algorithm, we show that the approximation ratio of stochastic local search is arbitrarily bad, with high probability, as well as in expectation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how reliably stochastic greedy algorithms maximize submodular objectives. Its main result concerns monotone objectives with a cardinality constraint, which limits the number of selected elements. Selecting an element whose added contribution is approximately best in expectation is sufficient for an optimal approximation guarantee with exponentially high probability, provided the cardinality is sufficiently large.

This establishes that the analyzed greedy procedure can tolerate randomness in its successive choices while retaining a strong final guarantee. One consequence is that the linear-time STOCHASTIC-GREEDY algorithm achieves optimal running time while maintaining an optimal approximation guarantee. The sufficient condition concerns expected contribution, rather than requiring an exactly best choice at every step.

The conclusions change under other settings. For matroid constraints, the authors rule out high-probability guarantees for stochastic greedy algorithms and instead prove a guarantee in expectation. They also show that stochastic local search can have an arbitrarily poor approximation ratio, both with high probability and in expectation.
summary.tldr: Stochastic greedy selection has strong conditional approximation guarantees under cardinality constraints, with weaker or negative results in other analyzed settings.

title: Robust Guarantees of Stochastic Greedy Algorithms

abstract: Deep generative models have been wildly successful at learning coherent latent representations for continuous data such as natural images, artwork, and audio. However, generative modeling of discrete data such as arithmetic expressions and molecular structures still poses significant challenges. Crucially, state-of-the-art methods often produce outputs that are not valid. We make the key observation that frequently, discrete data can be represented as a parse tree from a context-free grammar. We propose a variational autoencoder which directly encodes from and decodes to these parse trees, ensuring the generated outputs are always syntactically valid. Surprisingly, we show that not only does our model more often generate valid outputs, it also learns a more coherent latent space in which nearby points decode to similar discrete outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our learned models by showing their improved performance in Bayesian optimization for symbolic regression and molecule generation.

paragraphs: Generating discrete structures creates a problem that visual plausibility alone cannot solve: an output may violate the rules of its representation. Arithmetic expressions and molecular structures are examples where validity matters. This paper uses the observation that such data can often be expressed as parse trees governed by a context-free grammar.

The proposed variational autoencoder encodes these trees into a latent representation and decodes directly back into parse trees. Building the grammar into this process ensures syntactic validity of generated outputs. That guarantee concerns conformity to the grammar. The authors also report a more coherent latent space, meaning nearby latent points decode into similar discrete outputs.

This organization matters when the latent space is used to search for useful structures. If nearby locations correspond to related outputs, optimization can operate over a representation with meaningful local relationships. The paper demonstrates improved Bayesian optimization performance for symbolic regression and molecule generation. Its findings connect grammatical constraints with both valid generation and a latent representation that better supports the reported search tasks.
summary.tldr: A variational autoencoder operating on grammar parse trees ensures syntactic validity and learns a latent space useful for optimizing discrete structures.

title: Grammar Variational Autoencoder

abstract: Clustering data with both continuous and discrete attributes is a challenging task. Existing methods lack a principled probabilistic formulation. In this paper, we propose a clustering method based on a tree-structured graphical model to describe the generation process of mixed-type data. Our tree-structured model factorized into a product of pairwise interactions, and thus localizes the interaction between feature variables of different types. To provide a robust clustering method based on the tree-model, we adopt a topographical view and compute peaks of the density function and their attractive basins for clustering. Furthermore, we leverage the theory from topology data analysis to adaptively merge trivial peaks into large ones in order to achieve meaningful clusterings. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on mixed-type data.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes difficult when each observation combines continuous measurements with discrete attributes. The paper addresses this setting through a probabilistic model of how such mixed data is generated. Its tree-structured graphical model expresses the joint distribution as a product of pairwise interactions, localizing relationships between variables of different types.

The method then treats the estimated density as a landscape. Density peaks serve as centers, and their attractive basins organize observations into clusters. This connects the probabilistic description of the data to a geometric account of grouping: clusters correspond to regions associated with peaks in the modeled distribution.

Small peaks can create divisions that do not yield meaningful clusters. To address this, the approach uses ideas from topological data analysis to adaptively merge trivial peaks into larger ones. The authors report that the resulting method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on mixed-type data. Its contribution combines a model for heterogeneous attributes with a way to simplify the density landscape when forming clusters.
summary.tldr: A tree-based probabilistic model and topology-guided peak merging produce clusters for data containing both continuous and discrete attributes.

title: Composing Tree Graphical Models with Persistent Homology Features for Clustering Mixed-Type Data

abstract: Recent work by Nesterov and Stich (2016) showed that momentum can be used to accelerate the rate of convergence for block Gauss-Seidel in the setting where a fixed partitioning of the coordinates is chosen ahead of time. We show that this setting is too restrictive, constructing instances where breaking locality by running non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel with randomly sampled coordinates substantially outperforms accelerated Gauss-Seidel with any fixed partitioning. Motivated by this finding, we analyze the accelerated block Gauss-Seidel algorithm in the random coordinate sampling setting. Our analysis captures the benefit of acceleration with a new data-dependent parameter which is well behaved when the matrix sub-blocks are well-conditioned. Empirically, we show that accelerated Gauss-Seidel with random coordinate sampling provides speedups for large scale machine learning tasks when compared to non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel and the classical conjugate-gradient algorithm.

We show that this setting is too restrictive, constructing instances where breaking locality by running non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel with randomly sampled coordinates substantially outperforms accelerated Gauss-Seidel with any fixed partitioning. Motivated by this finding, we analyze the accelerated block Gauss-Seidel algorithm in the random coordinate sampling setting. Our analysis captures the benefit of acceleration with a new data-dependent parameter which is well behaved when the matrix sub-blocks are well-conditioned. Empirically, we show that accelerated Gauss-Seidel with random coordinate sampling provides speedups for large scale machine learning tasks when compared to non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel and the classical conjugate-gradient algorithm.

paragraphs: Block Gauss-Seidel updates groups of coordinates while solving an optimization problem. Momentum can accelerate this procedure, but earlier analysis considered coordinate groups fixed before optimization begins. This paper asks whether that grouping choice itself restricts performance, even when the updates within those groups use an accelerated method.

The authors construct instances where ordinary Gauss-Seidel with randomly sampled coordinates substantially outperforms accelerated Gauss-Seidel under every fixed partition. This establishes that acceleration alone does not resolve the disadvantages of fixed groups in those instances. It motivates analyzing an accelerated algorithm that also samples coordinates randomly, combining the two sources of improvement.

The resulting analysis describes acceleration through a new parameter that depends on the data and behaves well when matrix sub-blocks are well-conditioned. Experiments on large machine learning tasks report speedups over non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel and conjugate gradients. Together, the construction and experiments show why coordinate selection deserves attention alongside the choice of acceleration mechanism.
summary.tldr: Random coordinate sampling can overcome fixed-block bottlenecks and make accelerated Gauss-Seidel faster on the tasks studied.

title: Breaking Locality Accelerates Block Gauss-Seidel

abstract: We introduce the problem of grouping a finite ground set into blocks where each block is a subset of the ground set and where: (i) the blocks are individually highly valued by a submodular function (both robustly and in the average case) while satisfying block-specific matroid constraints; and (ii) block scores interact where blocks are jointly scored highly, thus making the blocks mutually non-redundant. Submodular functions are good models of information and diversity; thus, the above can be seen as grouping the ground set into matroid constrained blocks that are both intra- and inter-diverse. Potential applications include forming ensembles of classification/regression models, partitioning data for parallel processing, and summarization. In the non-robust case, we reduce the problem to non-monotone submodular maximization subject to multiple matroid constraints. In the mixed robust/average case, we offer a bi-criterion guarantee for a polynomial time deterministic algorithm and a probabilistic guarantee for randomized algorithm, as long as the involved submodular functions (including the inter-block interaction terms) are monotone. We close with a case study in which we use these algorithms to find high quality diverse ensembles of classifiers, showing good results.

paragraphs: Selecting several useful groups requires more than making each group strong on its own. The groups may also need to avoid repeating one another’s information. This paper formalizes that problem using submodular scores for individual blocks, constraints specific to each block, and interaction scores that reward a collection of mutually nonredundant blocks.

The formulation captures diversity both within groups and between them. For the non-robust version, the authors reduce the task to non-monotone submodular maximization under multiple matroid constraints. For a version combining robust and average performance, they provide a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with a bi-criterion guarantee and a randomized algorithm with a probabilistic guarantee.

Those latter guarantees require the relevant submodular functions, including the interaction terms, to be monotone. The framework has potential uses in model ensembles, parallel data processing, and summarization. A classifier-ensemble case study reports good results, illustrating how jointly selecting diverse groups can produce useful collections rather than merely several individually appealing choices.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms for forming constrained groups that are valuable individually and diverse collectively, with guarantees for specified cases.

title: Constrained Interacting Submodular Groupings

abstract: Microbes are everywhere, including in and on our bodies, and have been shown to play key roles in a variety of prevalent human diseases. Consequently, there has been intense interest in the design of bacteriotherapies or "bugs as drugs," which are communities of bacteria administered to patients for specific therapeutic applications. Central to the design of such therapeutics is an understanding of the causal microbial interaction network and the population dynamics of the organisms. In this work we present a Bayesian nonparametric model and associated efficient inference algorithm that addresses the key conceptual and practical challenges of learning microbial dynamics from time series microbe abundance data. These challenges include high-dimensional (300+ strains of bacteria in the gut) but temporally sparse and non-uniformly sampled data; high measurement noise; and, nonlinear and physically non-negative dynamics. Our contributions include a new type of dynamical systems model for microbial dynamics based on what we term interaction modules, or learned clusters of latent variables with redundant interaction structure (reducing the expected number of interaction coefficients from O(n^2) to O((log n)^2)); a fully Bayesian formulation of the stochastic dynamical systems model that propagates measurement and latent state uncertainty throughout the model; and introduction of a temporally varying auxiliary variable technique to enable efficient inference by relaxing the hard non-negativity constraint on states. We apply our method to simulated and real data, and demonstrate the utility of our technique for system identification from limited data and gaining new biological insights into bacteriotherapy design.

paragraphs: Designing bacterial communities for therapeutic use requires understanding how microbial populations interact and change over time. Learning these dynamics is difficult when abundance measurements are noisy, irregularly spaced, and sparse relative to hundreds of bacterial strains. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric dynamical model and an efficient inference algorithm for that setting.

Its central organizing idea is an interaction module: a learned cluster of latent variables with redundant interaction structure. Sharing structure through these modules reduces the expected number of interaction coefficients from O(n²) to O((log n)²). This provides a way to represent complex communities without separately estimating every possible pairwise coefficient.

The Bayesian formulation carries measurement and hidden-state uncertainty through the model. A time-varying auxiliary-variable technique makes inference more efficient by relaxing the hard constraint that population states remain nonnegative. Applications to simulated and real data demonstrate usefulness for identifying dynamics from limited observations and obtaining biological insights relevant to bacteriotherapy design. The contribution addresses model size, uncertainty, and physical constraints within one inference framework.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian microbial-dynamics model shares interaction structure across learned modules to support inference from sparse, noisy abundance measurements.

title: Robust and Scalable Models of Microbiome Dynamics

abstract: We consider deep linear networks with arbitrary convex differentiable loss. We provide a short and elementary proof of the fact that all local minima are global minima if the hidden layers are either 1) at least as wide as the input layer, or 2) at least as wide as the output layer. This result is the strongest possible in the following sense: If the loss is convex and Lipschitz but not differentiable then deep linear networks can have sub-optimal local minima.
originalAbstract: We consider deep linear networks with arbitrary convex differentiable loss. We provide a short and elementary proof of the fact that all local minima are global minima if the hidden layers are either 1) at least as wide as the input layer, or 2) at least as wide as the output layer. This result is the strongest possible in the following sense: If the loss is convex and Lipschitz but not differentiable then deep linear networks can have sub-optimal local minima.

paragraphs: A deep linear network stacks linear transformations, creating a layered parameterization even though the resulting input-output mapping remains linear. This paper examines whether that parameterization can introduce local minima with worse objective values than the best possible solution. The analysis applies to loss functions that are both convex and differentiable.

The authors give a short, elementary proof that every local minimum is global under either of two width conditions. All hidden layers may be at least as wide as the input layer, or they may all be at least as wide as the output layer. Under these assumptions, a locally optimal set of network parameters cannot have a suboptimal loss value.

The paper also establishes why differentiability matters. If the loss remains convex and Lipschitz but is no longer differentiable, suboptimal local minima can occur. This counterpoint defines the stated sense in which the result is strongest possible. The guarantee concerns the structure of local minima under the given assumptions, rather than an asserted convergence rate for a training algorithm.
summary.tldr: For convex differentiable losses and specified hidden-layer widths, every local minimum of a deep linear network is global.

title: Deep Linear Networks with Arbitrary Loss: All Local Minima Are Global

abstract: High sensitivity of neural architecture search (NAS) methods against their input such as step-size (i.e., learning rate) and search space prevents practitioners from applying them out-of-the-box to their own problems, albeit its purpose is to automate a part of tuning process. Aiming at a fast, robust, and widely-applicable NAS, we develop a generic optimization framework for NAS. We turn a coupled optimization of connection weights and neural architecture into a differentiable optimization by means of stochastic relaxation. It accepts arbitrary search space (widely-applicable) and enables to employ a gradient-based simultaneous optimization of weights and architecture (fast). We propose a stochastic natural gradient method with an adaptive step-size mechanism built upon our theoretical investigation (robust). Despite its simplicity and no problem-dependent parameter tuning, our method exhibited near state-of-the-art performances with low computational budgets both on image classification and inpainting tasks.

We propose a stochastic natural gradient method with an adaptive step-size mechanism built upon our theoretical investigation (robust). Despite its simplicity and no problem-dependent parameter tuning, our method exhibited near state-of-the-art performances with low computational budgets both on image classification and inpainting tasks.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search aims to automate the choice of a network’s structure, but the search procedure can itself require careful tuning. This paper targets sensitivity to choices such as learning rate and search space. Its goal is a framework that searches efficiently while requiring less adjustment for each new problem.

The authors use stochastic relaxation to turn the coupled selection of network architecture and connection weights into a differentiable optimization problem. This makes it possible to update both through gradients within one framework. The formulation accepts arbitrary search spaces, while a stochastic natural gradient method supplies the architecture updates. A theoretically motivated mechanism adapts the step size during optimization.

On image classification and image inpainting tasks, the method achieved performance close to the state of the art with small computational budgets and without problem-dependent parameter tuning. These findings support the practical value of combining a flexible search formulation with automatic step-size adjustment. They demonstrate the intended efficiency and robustness on the evaluated tasks, without establishing that every possible search space will be equally easy to optimize.
summary.tldr: Stochastic relaxation and adaptive natural-gradient updates enable efficient joint optimization of network weights and architecture with little task-specific tuning.

title: Adaptive Stochastic Natural Gradient Method for One-Shot Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We introduce a new model for online ranking in which the click probability factors into an examination and attractiveness function and the attractiveness function is a linear function of a feature vector and an unknown parameter. Only relatively mild assumptions are made on the examination function. A novel algorithm for this setup is analysed, showing that the dependence on the number of items is replaced by a dependence on the dimension, allowing the new algorithm to handle a large number of items. When reduced to the orthogonal case, the regret of the algorithm improves on the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an online ranking model that learns from clicks while using features describing the available items. It separates the probability of a click into two parts: whether an item is examined and how attractive it is. This distinction allows the model to account for exposure as well as item appeal.

Attractiveness is assumed to be a linear function of an item’s feature vector and an unknown parameter. The examination function is subject to assumptions described as relatively mild. The authors develop and analyze an algorithm for this setting, using the feature-based structure to change how the learning problem scales.

The analysis replaces dependence on the number of items with dependence on the feature dimension. This matters when a large collection can be described through a comparatively compact set of features. In the special orthogonal case, the algorithm also improves on the state-of-the-art regret guarantee. That stronger comparison is specific to the stated reduction, while the broader contribution is a feature-based framework for handling many items.
summary.tldr: A feature-based online ranking algorithm replaces item-count dependence with feature-dimension dependence and improves regret in the orthogonal case.

title: Online Learning to Rank with Features

abstract: Kernel methods are effective but do not scale well to large scale data, especially in high dimensions where the geometric data structures used to accelerate kernel evaluation suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Recent theoretical advances have proposed fast kernel evaluation algorithms leveraging hashing techniques with worst-case asymptotic improvements. However, these advances are largely confined to the theoretical realm due to concerns such as super-linear preprocessing time and diminishing gains in non-worst case datasets. In this paper, we close the gap between theory and practice by addressing these challenges via provable and practical procedures for adaptive sample size selection, preprocessing time reduction, and refined variance bounds that quantify the data-dependent performance of random sampling and hashing-based kernel evaluation methods. Our experiments show that these new tools offer up to $10\times$ improvement in evaluation time on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Kernel evaluation can become expensive on large, high-dimensional datasets. Geometric data structures lose effectiveness as dimension grows, while hashing-based algorithms offer promising theoretical improvements. This paper addresses why those theoretical gains may fail to translate into practical speed: preprocessing can cost more than linear time, and advantages established for worst-case inputs can shrink on other datasets.

The authors develop procedures for choosing sample sizes adaptively and reducing preprocessing time. They also derive refined variance bounds that describe how the particular dataset affects random-sampling and hashing-based evaluation methods. These tools connect the computation needed for an estimate to the behavior of the data, helping move beyond a comparison based only on worst-case asymptotic bounds.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report evaluation-time improvements of up to tenfold. That is a maximum observed improvement across the evaluated range, rather than a uniform guarantee for every dataset. The contribution combines practical algorithmic changes with theoretical analysis to make fast kernel evaluation more useful under the conditions encountered in actual data.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling, cheaper preprocessing, and data-dependent analysis make hashing-based kernel evaluation practical, with observed speedups of up to tenfold.

title: Rehashing Kernel Evaluation in High Dimensions

abstract: The causal relationships among a set of random variables are commonly represented by a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), where there is a directed edge from variable $X$ to variable $Y$ if $X$ is a direct cause of $Y$. From the purely observational data, the true causal graph can be identified up to a Markov Equivalence Class (MEC), which is a set of DAGs with the same conditional independencies between the variables. The size of an MEC is a measure of complexity for recovering the true causal graph by performing interventions. We propose a method for efficient iteration over possible MECs given intervention results. We utilize the proposed method for computing MEC sizes and experiment design in active and passive learning settings. Compared to previous work for computing the size of MEC, our proposed algorithm reduces the time complexity by a factor of $O(n)$ for sparse graphs where $n$ is the number of variables in the system. Additionally, integrating our approach with dynamic programming, we design an optimal algorithm for passive experiment design. Experimental results show that our proposed algorithms for both computing the size of MEC and experiment design outperform the state of the art.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several directed causal graphs consistent with the same conditional independencies. Such graphs form a Markov equivalence class. Counting the graphs in that class measures the remaining ambiguity and helps characterize the difficulty of identifying the true causal graph through interventions. This paper makes that counting and experiment-design process more efficient.

LazyIter efficiently iterates over possible equivalence classes given intervention results. The authors use this procedure both to compute class sizes and to design experiments in active and passive learning settings. For sparse graphs, the counting algorithm improves time complexity over previous work by a factor proportional to the number of variables.

Combining the approach with dynamic programming also produces an optimal algorithm for passive experiment design. Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art methods for both class-size computation and experiment design. The contribution matters because handling the remaining graph ambiguity efficiently supports two related operations: measuring how much uncertainty remains and choosing experiments intended to resolve causal structure.
summary.tldr: LazyIter accelerates counting observationally equivalent causal graphs and supports improved intervention design, including optimal passive design.

title: LazyIter: A Fast Algorithm for Counting Markov Equivalent DAGs and Designing Experiments

abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-level controls over the global structure of generated sequences, particularly in the context of symbolic music generation with complex language models. In this work, we present the Transformer autoencoder, which aggregates encodings of the input data across time to obtain a global representation of style from a given performance. We show it is possible to combine this global representation with other temporally distributed embeddings, enabling improved control over the separate aspects of performance style and melody. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various music generation tasks on the MAESTRO dataset and a YouTube dataset with 10,000+ hours of piano performances, where we achieve improvements in terms of log-likelihood and mean listening scores as compared to baselines.

paragraphs: Generating a musical sequence involves more than choosing each next event: a performance also has style and structure that extend across time. This paper addresses how to provide high-level control over those longer-range properties in symbolic music generation. Its goal is to make aspects of a generated performance more separately controllable.

The proposed Transformer autoencoder combines input encodings across time into a global representation of a performance's style. The authors show that this summary can be used alongside embeddings distributed throughout the sequence. Combining these forms of representation enables improved control over performance style and melody, which operate at different levels of the musical sequence.

The method is evaluated on multiple music generation tasks using MAESTRO and a YouTube collection containing more than 10,000 hours of piano performances. It improves both log-likelihood and average listening scores over the compared baselines. Those results support the usefulness of the representation through both a model-based measure and listeners' assessments.
summary.tldr: A Transformer autoencoder combines global style summaries with sequence-level embeddings to improve musical control and generation quality in the reported evaluations.

title: Encoding Musical Style with Transformer Autoencoders

abstract: Thompson sampling for multi-armed bandit problems is known to enjoy favorable performance in both theory and practice. However, its wider deployment is restricted due to a significant computational limitation: the need for samples from posterior distributions at every iteration. In practice, this limitation is alleviated by making use of approximate sampling methods, yet provably incorporating approximate samples into Thompson Sampling algorithms remains an open problem. In this work we address this by proposing two efficient Langevin MCMC algorithms tailored to Thompson sampling. The resulting approximate Thompson Sampling algorithms are efficiently implementable and provably achieve optimal instance-dependent regret for the Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem. To prove these results we derive novel posterior concentration bounds and MCMC convergence rates for log-concave distributions which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling has strong theoretical and practical performance in multi-armed bandit problems, but each decision requires sampling from a posterior distribution. Repeating that computation can make the method difficult to deploy. Approximate sampling is a practical response, yet its approximation error must be accounted for when establishing guarantees about the decisions it produces.

The paper develops two efficient Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms specifically for Thompson sampling. The resulting methods use approximate posterior samples while retaining a provable optimal instance-dependent regret guarantee for the bandit problem. Regret describes the loss from choosing actions instead of consistently choosing the best one; instance-dependent analysis reflects the particular problem being solved.

The proof develops new bounds on posterior concentration and on how quickly the sampling procedures converge for log-concave distributions. These results connect the quality of approximate sampling to the quality of sequential decisions. The contribution therefore addresses computational implementation and statistical guarantees together, rather than treating approximate posterior sampling as an unexamined substitute.
summary.tldr: Two Langevin sampling algorithms make approximate Thompson sampling efficiently implementable while preserving optimal instance-dependent regret guarantees.

title: On Approximate Thompson Sampling with Langevin Algorithms

abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are a promising avenue for probabilistic modeling, as they permit a wide range of exact and efficient inference routines. Recent “deep-learning-style” implementations of PCs strive for a better scalability, but are still difficult to train on real-world data, due to their sparsely connected computational graphs. In this paper, we propose Einsum Networks (EiNets), a novel implementation design for PCs, improving prior art in several regards. At their core, EiNets combine a large number of arithmetic operations in a single monolithic einsum-operation, leading to speedups and memory savings of up to two orders of magnitude, in comparison to previous implementations. As an algorithmic contribution, we show that the implementation of Expectation-Maximization (EM) can be simplified for PCs, by leveraging automatic differentiation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that EiNets scale well to datasets which were previously out of reach, such as SVHN and CelebA, and that they can be used as faithful generative image models.

Yet their sparse computational connections can make implementations difficult to train on realistic datasets. This paper tackles that implementation bottleneck with Einsum Networks, or EiNets, aiming to make the existing probabilistic modeling framework more scalable.

The core design combines many arithmetic operations into one large einsum operation. This consolidates computation that would otherwise be spread across a sparsely connected graph. Compared with earlier implementations, the paper reports speed improvements and memory savings reaching two orders of magnitude. These are reported upper-end improvements, rather than a fixed gain for every use.

The contribution links a computational redesign with a simpler training implementation, making tractable probabilistic models usable at larger data scales.
summary.tldr: EiNets consolidate probabilistic-circuit computation into einsum operations, substantially improving scalability while simplifying Expectation-Maximization training.

title: Einsum Networks: Fast and Scalable Learning of Tractable Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: This paper studies an entropy-based multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MBO). Existing entropy-based MBO methods need complicated approximations to evaluate entropy or employ over-simplification that ignores trade-off among objectives. We propose a novel entropy-based MBO called Pareto-frontier entropy search (PFES), which is based on the information gain of Pareto-frontier. We show that our entropy evaluation can be reduced to a closed form whose computation is quite simple while capturing the trade-off relation in Pareto-frontier. We further propose an extension for the “decoupled” setting, in which each objective function can be observed separately, and show that the PFES-based approach derives a natural extension of the original acquisition function which can also be evaluated simply. Our numerical experiments show effectiveness of PFES through several benchmark datasets, and real-word datasets from materials science.

paragraphs: Optimizing several objectives requires understanding trade-offs: improving one objective may come at the expense of another. The Pareto frontier describes these competing possibilities. This paper proposes Pareto-frontier entropy search, or PFES, to choose evaluations according to how much they reveal about that frontier.

Existing entropy-based approaches can require complicated approximations or simplify the problem in ways that discard objective trade-offs. PFES reduces its entropy evaluation to a closed-form expression with straightforward computation while retaining the trade-off relation. This matters because the information used to guide the search should reflect the multi-objective structure being sought.

The authors also extend the method to a decoupled setting, where objectives can be observed separately. They derive a natural extension of the acquisition function that remains simple to evaluate, allowing the search to accommodate separate objective observations. Numerical experiments on benchmarks and materials science datasets support the effectiveness of PFES in the tested problems, linking its computational formulation to practical multi-objective search.
summary.tldr: PFES guides multi-objective optimization with tractable information-gain calculations that preserve Pareto trade-offs and allow separately observed objectives.

title: Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization using Pareto-frontier Entropy

abstract: Balancing exploration and exploitation is crucial in reinforcement learning (RL). In this paper, we study model-based posterior sampling for reinforcement learning (PSRL) in continuous state-action spaces theoretically and empirically. First, we show the first regret bound of PSRL in continuous spaces which is polynomial in the episode length to the best of our knowledge. With the assumption that reward and transition functions can be modeled by Bayesian linear regression, we develop a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(H^{3/2}d\sqrt{T})$, where $H$ is the episode length, $d$ is the dimension of the state-action space, and $T$ indicates the total time steps. This result matches the best-known regret bound of non-PSRL methods in linear MDPs. Our bound can be extended to nonlinear cases as well with feature embedding: using linear kernels on the feature representation $\phi$, the regret bound becomes $\tilde{O}(H^{3/2}d_{\phi}\sqrt{T})$, where $d_\phi$ is the dimension of the representation space. Moreover, we present MPC-PSRL, a model-based posterior sampling algorithm with model predictive control for action selection. To capture the uncertainty in models, we use Bayesian linear regression on the penultimate layer (the feature representation layer $\phi$) of neural networks. Empirical results show that our algorithm achieves the state-of-the-art sample efficiency in benchmark continuous control tasks compared to prior model-based algorithms, and matches the asymptotic performance of model-free algorithms.

title: Model-based Reinforcement Learning for Continuous Control with Posterior Sampling

abstract: The convergence rate of Value Iteration (VI), a fundamental procedure in dynamic programming and reinforcement learning, for solving MDPs can be slow when the discount factor is close to one. We propose modifications to VI in order to potentially accelerate its convergence behaviour. The key insight is the realization that the evolution of the value function approximations $(V_k)_{k \geq 0}$ in the VI procedure can be seen as a dynamical system. This opens up the possibility of using techniques from \emph{control theory} to modify, and potentially accelerate, this dynamics. We present such modifications based on simple controllers, such as PD (Proportional-Derivative), PI (Proportional-Integral), and PID. We present the error dynamics of these variants of VI, and provably (for certain classes of MDPs) and empirically (for more general classes) show that the convergence rate can be significantly improved. We also propose a gain adaptation mechanism in order to automatically select the controller gains, and empirically show the effectiveness of this procedure.

paragraphs: Value iteration repeatedly updates estimates of how valuable states are in a Markov decision process. Its convergence can be slow when the discount factor is close to one, so distant rewards remain influential. This paper explores whether ideas from control theory can accelerate that iterative calculation.

The key move is to view the sequence of value estimates as a dynamical system. Once the updates are understood this way, controllers can modify how the estimates evolve. The authors develop proportional-derivative, proportional-integral, and proportional-integral-derivative variants of value iteration and analyze their error dynamics. This provides a framework for studying how controller choices affect progress toward the solution.

The paper proves improved convergence rates for certain classes of MDPs and demonstrates improvements empirically for broader classes. These are qualified acceleration results, rather than a claim that every controller speeds up every problem. The authors also propose automatically adapting controller gains and show experimentally that this mechanism is effective, addressing the practical task of selecting the controller’s numerical settings.
summary.tldr: Control-inspired modifications can accelerate value iteration, with proofs for certain MDP classes and broader empirical support.

title: PID Accelerated Value Iteration Algorithm

abstract: Decentralized training of deep learning models is a key element for enabling data privacy and on-device learning over networks. In realistic learning scenarios, the presence of heterogeneity across different clients’ local datasets poses an optimization challenge and may severely deteriorate the generalization performance. In this paper, we investigate and identify the limitation of several decentralized optimization algorithms for different degrees of data heterogeneity. We propose a novel momentum-based method to mitigate this decentralized training difficulty. We show in extensive empirical experiments on various CV/NLP datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and AG News) and several network topologies (Ring and Social Network) that our method is much more robust to the heterogeneity of clients’ data than other existing methods, by a significant improvement in test performance (1%-20%).

paragraphs: Decentralized learning trains models across a network of clients, a setting relevant to on-device learning and data privacy. A major difficulty is that clients can hold different kinds of local data. This heterogeneity complicates optimization and can substantially harm how well the resulting model performs on unseen examples.

The paper investigates several decentralized optimization algorithms across different levels of data heterogeneity and identifies their limitations. It proposes a momentum-based method called quasi-global momentum to mitigate the training difficulty. The method’s purpose is to make optimization more resilient when local datasets differ, addressing a central obstacle in realistic decentralized learning.

Experiments cover computer vision and language data, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and AG News, as well as ring and social-network communication topologies. The authors report substantially greater robustness to heterogeneous client data than existing methods, with test-performance improvements ranging from 1% to 20%. These empirical findings show benefits across the studied datasets and network structures, connecting the optimization change to better generalization under client differences.
summary.tldr: Quasi-global momentum improves decentralized training’s empirical robustness when clients have heterogeneous local datasets.

title: Quasi-global Momentum: Accelerating Decentralized Deep Learning on Heterogeneous Data

abstract: Replay buffers are a key component in many reinforcement learning schemes. Yet, their theoretical properties are not fully understood. In this paper we analyze a system where a stochastic process X is pushed into a replay buffer and then randomly sampled to generate a stochastic process Y from the replay buffer. We provide an analysis of the properties of the sampled process such as stationarity, Markovity and autocorrelation in terms of the properties of the original process. Our theoretical analysis sheds light on why replay buffer may be a good de-correlator. Our analysis provides theoretical tools for proving the convergence of replay buffer based algorithms which are prevalent in reinforcement learning schemes.

paragraphs: Replay buffers store observations from a running process and later supply randomly selected observations to a learning algorithm. They are common in reinforcement learning, but their mathematical effects are not fully understood. This paper studies the buffer as a transformation between two stochastic processes: the original sequence entering storage and the sampled sequence leaving it.

The analysis relates properties of the sampled process to properties of the original one. It considers stationarity, whether statistical behavior stays stable over time; Markovity, whether the present state suffices to describe dependence on the past; and autocorrelation, the relationship between values at different times. These properties describe different aspects of the data a learner receives.

The results help explain why replay buffers may reduce correlations between observations. They also provide theoretical tools for analyzing convergence of algorithms that use replay. The contribution is therefore a mathematical account of how storage and random sampling reshape sequential data, supporting more principled analysis of a widely used learning component.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how replay-buffer sampling changes a stochastic process and explains why it may reduce temporal correlations.

title: Analysis of Stochastic Processes through Replay Buffers

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a critical task for deploying machine learning models in the open world. Distance-based methods have demonstrated promise, where testing samples are detected as OOD if they are relatively far away from in-distribution (ID) data. However, prior methods impose a strong distributional assumption of the underlying feature space, which may not always hold. In this paper, we explore the efficacy of non-parametric nearest-neighbor distance for OOD detection, which has been largely overlooked in the literature. Unlike prior works, our method does not impose any distributional assumption, hence providing stronger flexibility and generality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of nearest-neighbor-based OOD detection on several benchmarks and establish superior performance. Under the same model trained on ImageNet-1k, our method substantially reduces the false positive rate (FPR@TPR95) by 24.77% compared to a strong baseline SSD+, which uses a parametric approach Mahalanobis distance in detection. Code is available: https://github.com/deeplearning-wisc/knn-ood.

Under the same model trained on ImageNet-1k, our method substantially reduces the false positive rate (FPR@TPR95) by 24.77% compared to a strong baseline SSD+, which uses a parametric approach Mahalanobis distance in detection. Code is available: https://github.com/deeplearning-wisc/knn-ood.

paragraphs: A deployed model may receive inputs unlike the data it was trained to handle. Distance-based out-of-distribution detection flags inputs that lie relatively far from familiar data in a learned feature space. Earlier approaches often assume a particular distributional structure in that space, and those assumptions may not hold.

This paper investigates nonparametric nearest-neighbor distance as the detection signal. It compares an input's features with nearby in-distribution examples without imposing a distributional assumption on the feature space. This gives the approach flexibility when the geometry of the learned data does not fit the assumptions of a parametric distance method.

The authors demonstrate strong performance on several benchmarks. Using the same model trained on ImageNet-1k, they report a 24.77% reduction in FPR@TPR95 relative to SSD+, a strong baseline based on Mahalanobis distance. That measure evaluates false positives at a fixed 95% true-positive rate. The result supports nearest-neighbor distance as an effective detection method in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor distances in deep feature space provide effective OOD detection without imposing a feature-distribution assumption.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection with Deep Nearest Neighbors

abstract: We present a generic framework for creating differentially private versions of any hypothesis test in a black-box way. We analyze the resulting tests analytically and experimentally. Most crucially, we show good practical performance for small data sets, showing that at ε = 1 we only need 5-6 times as much data as in the fully public setting. We compare our work to the one existing framework of this type, as well as to several individually-designed private hypothesis tests. Our framework is higher power than other generic solutions and at least competitive with (and often better than) individually-designed tests.

paragraphs: The paper presents a general framework for turning hypothesis tests into differentially private versions. It works in a black-box manner, so the starting point can be an existing test rather than a separately designed private testing procedure. The aim is to make private hypothesis testing broadly available through one reusable framework.

The authors analyze the resulting tests theoretically and experimentally, with particular attention to practical performance on small datasets. At a privacy parameter of ε = 1, they report needing roughly five to six times the data required in the fully public setting. This quantifies the observed data cost of obtaining privacy in the evaluated comparisons.

They compare the framework with an existing generic approach and several private tests designed individually. The framework has higher statistical power than other generic solutions and is competitive with, often better than, the specialized tests. Higher power means a greater ability to detect the effects being tested. These findings support the practicality of a general conversion framework, with the reported sample overhead and performance coming from the study's evaluations.
summary.tldr: A black-box framework converts hypothesis tests into private tests with competitive power and practical reported data requirements.

title: The Test of Tests: A Framework for Differentially Private Hypothesis Testing

abstract: We study neural network loss landscapes through the lens of mode connectivity, the observation that minimizers of neural networks retrieved via training on a dataset are connected via simple paths of low loss. Specifically, we ask the following question: are minimizers that rely on different mechanisms for making their predictions connected via simple paths of low loss? We provide a definition of mechanistic similarity as shared invariances to input transformations and demonstrate that lack of linear connectivity between two models implies they use dissimilar mechanisms for making their predictions. Relevant to practice, this result helps us demonstrate that naive fine-tuning on a downstream dataset can fail to alter a model’s mechanisms, e.g., fine-tuning can fail to eliminate a model’s reliance on spurious attributes. Our analysis also motivates a method for targeted alteration of a model’s mechanisms, named connectivity-based fine-tuning (CBFT), which we analyze using several synthetic datasets for the task of reducing a model’s reliance on spurious attributes.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained on the same dataset can reach different parameter solutions connected by simple paths of low loss. This paper asks whether that geometric relationship says anything about how the models make predictions. In particular, it investigates whether solutions using different predictive mechanisms can remain connected in this way.

The authors define mechanistic similarity through shared invariances to input transformations: models are similar in this sense when they share patterns of insensitivity to changes in their inputs. They demonstrate that a lack of linear connectivity implies dissimilar predictive mechanisms. This is a directional implication, rather than a claim that linear connectivity by itself proves identical mechanisms.

The analysis helps show why ordinary fine-tuning on a downstream dataset can leave a model's mechanisms unchanged, including continued reliance on spurious attributes. It also motivates connectivity-based fine-tuning, or CBFT, for targeted changes to those mechanisms. The authors analyze CBFT on several synthetic datasets aimed at reducing spurious reliance, connecting loss-landscape geometry to the practical objective of changing what a model uses to predict.
summary.tldr: The paper connects loss-landscape geometry to predictive mechanisms and proposes fine-tuning designed to alter reliance on spurious attributes.

title: Mechanistic Mode Connectivity

abstract: We consider the neural contextual bandit problem. In contrast to the existing work which primarily focuses on ReLU neural nets, we consider a general set of smooth activation functions. Under this more general setting, (i) we derive non-asymptotic error bounds on the difference between an overparameterized neural net and its corresponding neural tangent kernel, (ii) we propose an algorithm with a provable sublinear regret bound that is also efficient in the finite regime as demonstrated by empirical studies. The non-asymptotic error bounds may be of broader interests as a tool to establish the relation between the smoothness of the activation functions in neural contextual bandits and the smoothness of the kernels in kernel bandits.

paragraphs: Neural contextual bandits use neural networks in a setting where decisions and learning proceed together. The paper broadens the activation functions considered in this problem: instead of concentrating on ReLU networks, it studies a general collection of smooth activations. This shift requires understanding how the resulting networks relate to their kernel counterparts.

The authors derive finite-size error bounds between an overparameterized neural network and its corresponding neural tangent kernel. These non-asymptotic bounds quantify the approximation rather than relying only on a limiting relationship. That analysis supports a proposed bandit algorithm with a provable sublinear regret bound, so cumulative regret grows slower than the decision horizon.

Empirical studies also demonstrate efficiency in the finite regime, connecting the theoretical development to practically sized settings. The authors suggest that their approximation bounds may have broader value for relating activation smoothness in neural bandits to kernel smoothness in kernel bandits. This potential use is an additional implication of the analysis, alongside the algorithm and its demonstrated performance.
summary.tldr: Finite-size neural-kernel error bounds support a smooth-activation contextual-bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and empirical efficiency.

title: Provably and Practically Efficient Neural Contextual Bandits

abstract: We present MAV3D (Make-A-Video3D), a method for generating three-dimensional dynamic scenes from text descriptions. Our approach uses a 4D dynamic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), which is optimized for scene appearance, density, and motion consistency by querying a Text-to-Video (T2V) diffusion-based model. The dynamic video output generated from the provided text can be viewed from any camera location and angle, and can be composited into any 3D environment. MAV3D does not require any 3D or 4D data and the T2V model is trained only on Text-Image pairs and unlabeled videos. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using comprehensive quantitative and qualitative experiments and show an improvement over previously established internal baselines. To the best of our knowledge, our method is the first to generate 3D dynamic scenes given a text description. Generated samples can be viewed at make-a-video3d.github.io

paragraphs: MAV3D generates a moving three-dimensional scene from a text description. The fourth dimension is time, so the output represents both a scene’s spatial structure and how it changes. The generated scene can be viewed from different camera locations and angles and composited into a three-dimensional environment.

The method uses a dynamic Neural Radiance Field and optimizes its appearance, density, and motion consistency by querying a text-to-video diffusion model. This makes the video model a source of guidance for constructing the dynamic scene. MAV3D requires no three-dimensional or four-dimensional training data; its guiding video model is trained using text-image pairs and unlabeled videos.

The authors evaluate the approach quantitatively and qualitatively and report improvements over their previously established internal baselines. The findings support using video-generation guidance to construct scenes that can be explored spatially as well as over time. The authors also describe the method, to their knowledge, as the first to generate dynamic three-dimensional scenes directly from text descriptions.
summary.tldr: MAV3D uses text-to-video diffusion guidance to generate dynamic, viewable 3D scenes from text without 3D or 4D training data.

title: Text-To-4D Dynamic Scene Generation

abstract: Training long-horizon robotic policies in complex physical environments is essential for many applications, such as robotic manipulation. However, learning a policy that can generalize to unseen tasks is challenging. In this work, we propose to achieve one-shot task generalization by decoupling plan generation and plan execution. Specifically, our method solves complex long-horizon tasks in three steps: build a paired abstract environment by simplifying geometry and physics, generate abstract trajectories, and solve the original task by an abstract-to-executable trajectory translator. In the abstract environment, complex dynamics such as physical manipulation are removed, making abstract trajectories easier to generate. However, this introduces a large domain gap between abstract trajectories and the actual executed trajectories as abstract trajectories lack low-level details and are not aligned frame-to-frame with the executed trajectory. In a manner reminiscent of language translation, our approach leverages a seq-to-seq model to overcome the large domain gap between the abstract and executable trajectories, enabling the low-level policy to follow the abstract trajectory. Experimental results on various unseen long-horizon tasks with different robot embodiments demonstrate the practicability of our methods to achieve one-shot task generalization.

paragraphs: Long robotic tasks require both a useful plan and the physical ability to carry it out. This paper separates those responsibilities to support generalization to unseen tasks from one example. Its central idea is to generate a trajectory in a simplified environment and then translate that trajectory into behavior the real task requires.

The method first constructs a paired abstract environment with simpler geometry and physics. Removing difficult dynamics, including physical manipulation, makes trajectories easier to generate. But those trajectories omit details needed for execution, and their individual frames do not line up with the executed motion. A sequence-to-sequence model addresses this mismatch by translating between whole sequences, enabling a low-level policy to follow the abstract plan.

Experiments on unseen long-horizon tasks and different robot embodiments support the practicality of this approach. The contribution is a way to connect easier planning with physically detailed execution despite a substantial gap between them, with experimental evidence for one-shot task generalization.
summary.tldr: Translating simplified plans into executable robot trajectories supports one-shot generalization to unseen long-horizon tasks.

title: Abstract-to-Executable Trajectory Translation for One-Shot Task Generalization

abstract: We study the problem of constrained efficient global optimization, where both the objective and constraints are expensive black-box functions that can be learned with Gaussian processes. We propose CONFIG (CONstrained efFIcient Global Optimization), a simple and effective algorithm to solve it. Under certain regularity assumptions, we show that our algorithm enjoys the same cumulative regret bound as that in the unconstrained case and similar cumulative constraint violation upper bounds. For commonly used Matern and Squared Exponential kernels, our bounds are sublinear and allow us to derive a convergence rate to the optimal solution of the original constrained problem. In addition, our method naturally provides a scheme to declare infeasibility when the original black-box optimization problem is infeasible. Numerical experiments on sampled instances from the Gaussian process, artificial numerical problems, and a black-box building controller tuning problem all demonstrate the competitive performance of our algorithm. Compared to the other state-of-the-art methods, our algorithm significantly improves the theoretical guarantees while achieving competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems require expensive evaluations both to measure performance and to check whether a candidate satisfies constraints. This paper studies that setting when the objective and constraint functions can be learned using Gaussian processes. Its proposed algorithm, CONFIG, seeks an optimal feasible solution while controlling the costs of learning through repeated evaluations.

Under regularity assumptions, CONFIG has the same cumulative regret bound as the corresponding unconstrained setting, together with similar upper bounds on accumulated constraint violations. For commonly used Matérn and Squared Exponential kernels, these bounds grow sublinearly. The authors use those results to derive a convergence rate toward the optimum of the original constrained problem.

CONFIG also provides a mechanism for declaring infeasibility when no feasible solution exists. Experiments cover functions sampled from Gaussian processes, artificial numerical problems, and tuning a building controller. The reported empirical performance is competitive with leading alternatives, while the theoretical guarantees improve significantly. The contribution therefore combines analysis of optimization progress and constraint violations with evidence from several kinds of test problems.
summary.tldr: CONFIG optimizes expensive constrained black-box functions with conditional convergence guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

title: Constrained Efficient Global Optimization of Expensive Black-box Functions

abstract: A fundamental problem in data management is to find the elements in an array that match a query. Recently, learned indexes are being extensively used to solve this problem, where they learn a model to predict the location of the items in the array. They are empirically shown to outperform non-learned methods (e.g., B-trees or binary search that answer queries in $O(\log n)$ time) by orders of magnitude. However, success of learned indexes has not been theoretically justified. Only existing attempt shows the same query time of $O(\log n)$, but with a constant factor improvement in space complexity over non-learned methods, under some assumptions on data distribution. In this paper, we significantly strengthen this result, showing that under mild assumptions on data distribution, and the same space complexity as non-learned methods, learned indexes can answer queries in $O(\log\log n)$ expected query time. We also show that allowing for slightly larger but still near-linear space overhead, a learned index can achieve $O(1)$ expected query time. Our results theoretically prove learned indexes are orders of magnitude faster than non-learned methods, theoretically grounding their empirical success.

paragraphs: A learned index predicts where an item is located in an array, helping answer queries about matching elements. Such indexes have shown large empirical speed advantages over conventional methods, but the theory described in this paper had previously established only logarithmic query time, alongside a constant-factor space improvement under distributional assumptions.

The authors prove a stronger result: under mild assumptions on the data distribution, a learned index can achieve O(log log n) expected query time while using the same asymptotic space complexity as non-learned methods. Here n is the array size. The result improves the growth rate of expected query cost, rather than merely changing a constant factor.

A second result permits slightly greater, but still near-linear, space use and obtains O(1) expected query time. Together, these guarantees provide a theoretical explanation for substantial learned-index speedups and show how extra storage can change the attainable query complexity. The claims are distribution-dependent and concern expected time, preserving the distinction between these guarantees and an unrestricted worst-case promise.
summary.tldr: Under distributional assumptions, learned indexes achieve doubly logarithmic expected query time, or constant expected time with slightly more space.

title: On Distribution Dependent Sub-Logarithmic Query Time of Learned Indexing

abstract: Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for learning from complex data and reasoning under uncertainty. It has been widely applied in machine learning tasks such as medical diagnosis, drug design, and policymaking. In these common applications, data can be highly sensitive. Differential privacy (DP) offers data analysis tools with powerful worst-case privacy guarantees and has been developed as the leading approach in privacy-preserving data analysis. In this paper, we study Metropolis-Hastings (MH), one of the most fundamental MCMC methods, for large-scale Bayesian inference under differential privacy. While most existing private MCMC algorithms sacrifice accuracy and efficiency to obtain privacy, we provide the first exact and fast DP MH algorithm, using only a minibatch of data in most iterations. We further reveal, for the first time, a three-way trade-off among privacy, scalability (i.e. the batch size), and efficiency (i.e. the convergence rate), theoretically characterizing how privacy affects the utility and computational cost in Bayesian inference. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm in various experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference supports learning and reasoning under uncertainty, but applications can involve sensitive data. This paper studies how to give Metropolis-Hastings, a fundamental sampling method, differential privacy guarantees while keeping it practical for large datasets. The challenge is that privacy protection in existing sampling methods often comes at the expense of accuracy and computational efficiency.

The proposed DP-Fast MH algorithm is described as exact and fast, while examining only a minibatch of data in most iterations. The qualification matters: the approach does not claim to use a minibatch on every iteration. Its contribution combines private inference with reduced data access during much of the sampling process.

The authors also establish a theoretical trade-off among privacy, batch size, and convergence rate. This explains how stronger privacy requirements interact with scalability and the speed of inference, rather than treating these as independent design choices. Experiments support the algorithm’s effectiveness and efficiency. Together, the algorithm and analysis clarify how private Bayesian sampling can remain accurate while managing computational costs.
summary.tldr: DP-Fast MH provides exact private Metropolis-Hastings sampling and characterizes the trade-off between privacy, batch size, and convergence.

title: DP-Fast MH: Private, Fast, and Accurate Metropolis-Hastings for Large-Scale Bayesian Inference

abstract: We propose training fitted Q-iteration with log-loss (FQI-LOG) for batch reinforcement learning (RL). We show that the number of samples needed to learn a near-optimal policy with FQI-LOG scales with the accumulated cost of the optimal policy, which is zero in problems where acting optimally achieves the goal and incurs no cost. In doing so, we provide a general framework for proving small-cost bounds, i.e. bounds that scale with the optimal achievable cost, in batch RL. Moreover, we empirically verify that FQI-LOG uses fewer samples than FQI trained with squared loss on problems where the optimal policy reliably achieves the goal.

We show that the number of samples needed to learn a near-optimal policy with FQI-LOG scales with the accumulated cost of the optimal policy, which is zero in problems where acting optimally achieves the goal and incurs no cost. In doing so, we provide a general framework for proving small-cost bounds, i.e. bounds that scale with the optimal achievable cost, in batch RL. Moreover, we empirically verify that FQI-LOG uses fewer samples than FQI trained with squared loss on problems where the optimal policy reliably achieves the goal.

paragraphs: Batch reinforcement learning learns a policy from a collection of data. This paper asks whether changing the loss used to train fitted Q-iteration can reduce the amount of data needed to learn a near-optimal policy. Its proposed method, FQI-LOG, replaces squared loss with log-loss.

The theoretical result connects sample requirements to the accumulated cost of the optimal policy. This is a small-cost guarantee: the bound adapts to how little cost a successful policy can achieve. In problems where acting optimally reaches the goal without incurring cost, that optimal accumulated cost is zero. This describes the cost-dependent quantity in the guarantee, rather than asserting that learning needs no samples.

The authors also provide a general framework for proving such small-cost bounds in batch reinforcement learning. Experiments verify that FQI-LOG needs fewer samples than squared-loss fitted Q-iteration on problems where the optimal policy reliably reaches the goal. The contribution shows that the training loss can affect sample efficiency in a way that reflects the achievable task cost, linking the theoretical improvement to a concrete empirical comparison.
summary.tldr: Using log-loss in fitted Q-iteration yields cost-sensitive sample guarantees and reduces sample needs in the reported goal-reaching experiments.

title: Switching the Loss Reduces the Cost in Batch Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Input space reconstruction is an attractive representation learning paradigm. Despite interpretability benefit of reconstruction and generation, we identify a misalignment between learning to reconstruct, and learning for perception. We show that the former allocates a model’s capacity towards a subspace of the data explaining the observed variance–a subspace with uninformative features for the latter. For example, the supervised TinyImagenet task with images projected onto the top subspace explaining 90% of the pixel variance can be solved with 45% test accuracy. Using the bottom subspace instead, accounting for only 20% of the pixel variance, reaches 55% test accuracy. Learning by reconstruction is also wasteful as the features for perception are learned last, pushing the need for long training schedules. We finally prove that learning by denoising can alleviate that misalignment for some noise strategies, e.g., masking. While tuning the noise strategy without knowledge of the perception task seems challenging, we provide a solution to detect if a noise strategy is never beneficial regardless of the perception task, e.g., additive Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Reconstructing inputs is an appealing way to learn representations, but accurately reproducing data need not prioritize the features useful for perception. This paper identifies a mismatch: reconstruction directs model capacity toward data subspaces that explain observed variance, even when those subspaces provide relatively little information for a perception task.

A TinyImagenet example illustrates the distinction. Images projected onto a leading subspace explaining 90% of pixel variance yield 45% supervised test accuracy, whereas a bottom subspace accounting for only 20% yields 55%. The authors also find that reconstruction learns perception-relevant features late, contributing to the need for long training schedules.

The paper proves that denoising can alleviate this mismatch for some noise strategies, including masking. Choosing an effective strategy without knowing the downstream perception task remains challenging. The authors also provide a way to identify strategies that are never beneficial regardless of the perception task, giving additive Gaussian noise as an example. The key implication is that the corruption strategy matters to what denoising learns.
summary.tldr: Reconstruction can prioritize high-variance features over useful perceptual ones, while denoising with certain noise strategies can alleviate that mismatch.

title: How Learning by Reconstruction Produces Uninformative Features For Perception

abstract: We study the capabilities of the transformer architecture with varying depth. Specifically, we designed a novel set of sequence learning tasks to systematically evaluate and comprehend how the depth of transformer affects its ability to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization. We show a transformer with only one attention layer can excel in memorization but falls short in other tasks. Then, we show that exhibiting reasoning and generalization ability requires the transformer to have at least two attention layers, while context generalization ability may necessitate three attention layers. Additionally, we identify a class of simple operations that a single attention layer can execute, and show that the complex tasks can be approached as the combinations of these simple operations and thus can be resolved by stacking multiple attention layers. This sheds light on studying more practical and complex tasks beyond our design. Numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings.
