title: Rethinking Thinking Tokens: LLMs as Improvement Operators

abstract: A goal-conditioned reinforcement learning agent acting in an environment will see a wealth of information throughout a trajectory, most of which is discarded when only considering the trajectory with respect to a single goal. All-goals learning, where each transition is used for learning off-policy with respect to every goal, allows agents to extract maximal information, however it is usually computationally infeasible when done via naive relabelling. This can be overcome by jointly outputting values and actions for every goal at once, allowing for efficient, parallel all-goals updates with a single pass through the network, in a process we call Learning Everything all at Once (LEO). We show that this approach significantly outperforms other methods on goal-conditioned Craftax and is competitive with existing baselines on continuous control environments, while achieving a 250x speed-up compared to all-goals relabelling. We hope that, by unlocking all-goals learning at scale, LEO can serve as a useful tool for RL practitioners in complex environments. We open source our code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CraftaxGC-D3E1.

paragraphs: A goal-conditioned agent can learn from an experience in relation to goals beyond the one it was pursuing. Restricting each trajectory to a single goal leaves much of that information unused. All-goals learning addresses this by learning from each transition with respect to every goal, but repeatedly relabeling experiences can make the computation impractical.

Learning Everything all at Once, or LEO, changes how the network produces its outputs. It jointly predicts values and actions for every goal, enabling parallel updates through a single network pass. This makes the organization of computation central to the method: the agent can use an experience across goals without performing the naive relabeling procedure separately for each one.

LEO significantly outperforms the compared methods on goal-conditioned Craftax and is competitive with existing baselines in continuous control. It also achieves a reported 250-fold speedup over all-goals relabeling. These results support the approach as a practical way to extract more learning information from trajectories, with different performance outcomes across the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: LEO learns about every goal in one network pass, achieving a 250-fold speedup over all-goals relabeling and strong results in the evaluated environments.

title: Goal-Conditioned Agents that Learn Everything All at Once

abstract: Transcendental functions, such as the exponential, are central to scientific computing, yet they cannot be natively calculated by digital hardware. Instead, computers must approximate these functions by combining basic operations, such as ${+, -, \times, \div}$, using methods like Taylor series. These methods were developed over centuries by mathematicians, who focused on approaches that could attain arbitrary accuracy. However, computers can handle most applications by using only finite-precision types, like float32, where any accuracy beyond the type’s precision is effectively discarded. We explore, therefore, whether forgoing arbitrary accuracy can lead to the discovery of more efficient approximations. The evolutionary method of symbolic regression is particularly suitable, as it can search for arbitrary operation combinations and can optimize non-differentiable objectives, such as the number of operations used. Our results show that evolution can discover computer programs that outperform established methods in this setting, despite having no prior mathematical knowledge beyond the calculation of the basic operations. Starting from empty code, symbolic regression constructs programs representing novel mathematical expressions. In particular, we discovered a 10-operation program that approximates the exponential function to 14 significant figures, exceeding the accuracy of previously known approximations of this size by more than 6 orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Computers approximate functions such as the exponential using combinations of basic arithmetic operations. Traditional mathematical constructions often support arbitrarily high accuracy, but finite-precision arithmetic cannot retain unlimited digits. This paper asks whether designing directly for finite precision can uncover more efficient expressions than approaches built around the possibility of ever-increasing accuracy.

AutoNumerics-Zero uses evolutionary symbolic regression to search over programs made from basic operations. Starting with empty code, it constructs mathematical expressions without prior mathematical knowledge beyond those operations. This search can optimize objectives that are not differentiable, including operation count, allowing it to consider computational cost alongside approximation accuracy rather than requiring a fixed formula family.

The authors report programs that outperform established methods in this setting. Their highlighted result is a ten-operation exponential approximation reaching fourteen significant figures, with accuracy more than six orders of magnitude beyond previously known approximations of that size. The finding shows how an explicit finite-precision target can open opportunities for automated mathematical program discovery.
summary.tldr: Evolutionary program search discovers efficient finite-precision function approximations, including a ten-operation exponential approximation accurate to fourteen significant figures.

title: AutoNumerics-Zero: Automated Discovery of State-of-the-Art Mathematical Functions

abstract: Evolution Strategies (ES) is a class of powerful black-box optimisation methods that are highly parallelisable and can handle non-differentiable and noisy objectives. However, naïve ES becomes prohibitively expensive at scale on GPUs due to the low arithmetic intensity of batched matrix multiplications with unstructured random perturbations. We introduce Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning (EGGROLL), which improves arithmetic intensity by structuring individual perturbations as rank-$r$ matrices, resulting in a hundredfold increase in training speed for billion-parameter models at large population sizes, achieving up to 91% of the throughput of pure batch inference. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of ES for high-dimensional parameter objectives, investigating conditions needed for ES updates to converge in high dimensions, revealing a linearising effect, and proving consistency between EGGROLL and ES as parameter dimension increases. Our experiments show that EGGROLL: (1) enables the stable pretraining of nonlinear recurrent language models that operate purely in integer datatypes, (2) is competitive with GRPO for post-training LLMs on reasoning tasks, and (3) does not compromise performance compared to ES in tabula rasa RL settings, despite being faster.

paragraphs: Evolution Strategies optimize objectives by evaluating parameter perturbations, making them applicable to noisy or non-differentiable problems. Although these evaluations can run in parallel, unstructured random perturbations make large GPU workloads inefficient. EGGROLL addresses this computational bottleneck by expressing individual perturbations as low-rank matrices, increasing the useful arithmetic performed by the resulting batched operations.

For billion-parameter models with large populations, the authors report a hundredfold training speed increase and throughput reaching up to 91% of pure batch inference. Their theoretical analysis examines conditions for Evolution Strategies updates to converge in high dimensions, identifies a linearizing effect, and establishes consistency between EGGROLL and Evolution Strategies as parameter dimension increases.

Experiments demonstrate stable pretraining of nonlinear recurrent language models operating entirely with integer datatypes. They also find EGGROLL competitive with GRPO for reasoning-oriented language-model post-training and report no performance compromise relative to Evolution Strategies in reinforcement learning from scratch. Together, these findings suggest that structured perturbations can substantially improve execution efficiency while retaining useful optimization behavior in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: EGGROLL uses low-rank perturbations to make large-scale Evolution Strategies substantially faster while preserving performance in the reported experiments.

title: Evolution Strategies at the Hyperscale

abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often train slowly or fail to converge on challenging partial differential equations (PDEs), a behavior recently linked to severely ill-conditioned loss landscapes inherited from the underlying differential operator. We study PINNs augmented with a pointwise data-fidelity term, added at a few points in the domain to the standard residual and boundary losses. We show that this supervision term acts as an operator-level preconditioner: for suitable weights, our comparison bounds guarantee a substantially smaller condition number than under the standard PINN loss, independently of how the pointwise labels are obtained. For a broad class of PDEs admitting a Feynman-Kac (FK) representation, we generate such labels by Monte Carlo averages of the FK functional, resulting in what we call "FK-PINNs", and using the excess risk decomposition approach, we derive non-asymptotic $L^2(\Omega)$-error bounds for FK-PINNs with $\tanh$ activation trained by finitely many steps of gradient descent. Along the way, we establish pseudo-dimension bounds for first- and second-order derivatives of $\tanh$ neural networks, which are of independent interest and, to the best of our knowledge, new. Numerical experiments on Poisson, Schrödinger, mean exit time, and committor problems corroborate the theory, and show that FK-PINNs can successfully solve PDEs for which standard PINNs exhibit severe failure modes.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions to differential equations by penalizing violations of the equations and boundary conditions. Difficult equations can create severely ill-conditioned training objectives, making optimization slow or unsuccessful. This paper studies adding solution-value supervision at a few points to improve the geometry of that objective.

For suitable weights, the authors prove comparison bounds guaranteeing a substantially smaller condition number than the standard loss. This preconditioning effect does not depend on how the pointwise labels are obtained. For equations admitting a Feynman–Kac representation, they generate noisy labels using Monte Carlo averages, producing the FK-PINN method. They also derive finite-sample solution-error bounds for tanh networks trained with finitely many gradient-descent steps.

The analysis includes bounds on the complexity of first and second derivatives of tanh networks. Experiments on Poisson, Schrödinger, mean exit time, and committor problems support the theory, including cases where standard PINNs fail severely. The findings show how limited, noisy supervision can improve optimization through an operator-level effect, while connecting that improvement to explicit solution-error guarantees.
summary.tldr: Sparse pointwise supervision improves PINN conditioning, with Feynman–Kac sampling supplying noisy labels and supporting finite-training error bounds.

title: Taming the Loss Landscape of PINNs with Noisy Feynman–Kac Supervision: Operator Preconditioning and Non-Asymptotic Error Bounds

abstract: SWE-bench has emerged as the premier benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models on complex software engineering tasks. While these capabilities are fundamentally acquired during the mid-training phase and subsequently elicited during Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), there remains a critical deficit in metrics capable of guiding mid-training effectively. Standard metrics such as Perplexity (PPL) are compromised by the "Long-Context Tax" and exhibit weak correlation with downstream SWE performance. In this paper, we bridge this gap by first introducing a rigorous data filtering strategy. Crucially, we propose the Entropy Compression Hypothesis, redefining intelligence not by scalar Top-1 compression, but by the capacity to structure uncertainty into Entropy-Compressed States of low orders ("reasonable hesitation"). Grounded in this fine-grained entropy analysis, we formulate a novel metric, HE-SNR (High-Entropy Signal-to-Noise Ratio). We validate our approach on models with up to 560B parameters across different context windows (32K/128K). This work provides both the theoretical foundation and practical tools for optimizing the latent potential of LLMs in complex engineering domains.

paragraphs: This paper targets the problem of measuring progress during the mid-training stage that develops software engineering capabilities in language models. It argues that standard perplexity is a weak guide to downstream SWE-bench performance, partly because of what the authors call the Long-Context Tax. A useful metric should expose latent capabilities before supervised fine-tuning elicits them.

Alongside a data-filtering strategy, the authors propose the Entropy Compression Hypothesis. It shifts attention from compression into a single top prediction toward the structure of the model’s remaining uncertainty. Their notion of reasonable hesitation treats uncertainty concentrated into low-order, entropy-compressed states as informative. From this finer-grained analysis, they construct High-Entropy Signal-to-Noise Ratio, or HE-SNR.

The approach is validated on models with up to 560 billion parameters and context windows of 32K and 128K. The stated contribution is a theoretical perspective and practical measurement tools for guiding mid-training in complex engineering tasks. The entropy-based account remains a proposed hypothesis; the reported validation supports studying structured uncertainty as a training signal rather than reducing progress to one scalar compression score.
summary.tldr: HE-SNR uses the structure of predictive uncertainty to guide software-engineering mid-training beyond standard perplexity.

title: HE-SNR: Uncovering Latent Logic via Entropy for Guiding Mid-Training on SWE-bench

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL) seeks to optimize long-term performance while ensuring adherence to safety constraints. However, most existing approaches address safety in a simplified manner, typically by linearly combining rewards and costs, which provides limited guidance when safety and performance interact in complex, nonlinear ways. We present USB-RL (Unsupervised Score-Balanced Reinforcement Learning), a model-based framework that learns implicit safety–performance preferences directly from experience. Our approach infers a monotone partial-order score through unsupervised pairwise comparisons of long-horizon outcomes, capturing nuanced trade-offs without relying on manually tuned cost weights. The learned score guides model-based policy optimization by dynamically balancing safety and performance, enabling flexible and adaptive multi-step planning in imagination-based control. Across diverse safety benchmarks, USB-RL achieves strong returns while substantially reducing safety violations, demonstrating stable and interpretable safety–performance trade-offs.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must pursue useful long-term behavior while respecting safety constraints. A common approach combines reward and cost with a linear weighting, which offers limited guidance when their relationship is nonlinear. USB-RL instead learns an implicit preference over safety and performance from experience, avoiding manually tuned cost weights.

The method compares pairs of long-horizon outcomes without external supervision to infer a monotone partial-order score. This score provides a learned way to evaluate trade-offs rather than relying on one fixed linear formula. It then guides policy optimization inside a world-model framework, allowing multi-step planning over imagined outcomes with a dynamically learned balance.

Across diverse safety benchmarks, the authors report strong returns alongside substantially fewer safety violations, with stable and interpretable trade-offs. These results support learning how to compare safety and performance outcomes as part of model-based control. The empirical finding is improved behavior under the evaluated constraints; the abstract does not present the method as eliminating all safety violations.
summary.tldr: USB-RL learns safety–performance preferences from long-term outcomes to guide world-model planning without manually tuned cost weights.

title: Learning Reward–Cost Balance in Safe RL via Score-Based World Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that bypass safety guardrails. Existing approaches overwhelmingly operate within the prompt-optimization paradigm; the resulting prompts typically retain malicious semantic signals that modern guardrails are primed to detect. In contrast, we identify a deeper vulnerability stemming from the highly interconnected nature of an LLM’s internal knowledge. This structure allows harmful objectives to be realized by weaving together sequences of benign sub-queries, each of which individually evades detection. To exploit this loophole, we introduce the Correlated Knowledge Attack Agent (CKA-Agent), a dynamic framework that reframes jailbreaking as an adaptive, tree-structured exploration of the target model’s knowledge base. The CKA-Agent issues locally innocuous queries, uses model responses to guide exploration across multiple paths, and ultimately assembles the aggregated information to achieve the original harmful objective. Evaluated across SOTA commercial LLMs, CKA-Agent consistently achieves over 95% success rates even against strong guardrails, underscoring the severity of this vulnerability and the urgent need for defenses against such knowledge-decomposition attacks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Graph-COM/CKA-Agent.

paragraphs: This paper examines a safety weakness arising from connections between pieces of a language model’s knowledge. A harmful objective can be supported by information spread across questions that each appear benign. The concern is that a guardrail evaluating an individual request may fail to recognize what several responses enable when considered together.

The authors introduce CKA-Agent to study this knowledge-decomposition vulnerability. At a high level, it organizes interaction as an adaptive tree of queries and uses model responses to guide exploration across multiple paths. The collected information is then combined toward the original objective. This reframes the evaluation from optimizing a single suspicious prompt to examining the cumulative effect of locally innocuous interactions.

Across the tested state-of-the-art commercial models, the authors report attack success rates consistently above 95%, including against strong guardrails. These results highlight a gap between the apparent safety of individual exchanges and the purpose served by their aggregation. The paper argues for defenses that address knowledge-decomposition attacks, since locally acceptable responses can collectively support an outcome the model would otherwise be expected to refuse.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how individually benign queries can collectively bypass tested LLM guardrails, exposing a vulnerability to knowledge-decomposition attacks.

title: The Trojan Knowledge: Bypassing Commercial LLM Guardrails via Harmless Prompt Weaving and Adaptive Tree Search

abstract: While CLIP has achieved strong performance across vision–language tasks, fine-grained image–text alignment remains challenging. Recent efforts improve textual granularity by leveraging long, detailed descriptions and replacing CLIP’s text encoder with LLM, but often overlook the visual-side bottleneck: achieving finer alignment requires region- and pixel-level visual grounding. To address it, we propose PixCLIP, a framework that jointly enhances both sides by accommodating visual prompt regions and long-form text within a unified training objective. Firstly, to support training at this granularity, we develop an automated annotation pipeline that produces long-form descriptions with pixel-level localization, and use it to construct LongGRIT, a large-scale dataset with 1.5M samples. Furthermore, we introduce a three-branch pixel–text alignment framework that aligns image regions with corresponding textual descriptions across multiple granularities. Experiments show that PixCLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance on pixel- and region-level alignment tasks while preserving strong results on standard global image–text retrieval benchmarks, even with arbitrarily shaped region prompts and long texts. Our code is available at https://github.com/StuHude/PixCLIP.

paragraphs: PixCLIP addresses the difficulty of matching detailed language to precise parts of an image. Longer descriptions and stronger text encoders can improve the language side of alignment, but the paper argues that visual grounding must improve too. Fine-grained matching requires identifying the regions and pixels described by the text.

The authors build an automated annotation pipeline that pairs long descriptions with pixel-level localization. They use it to create LongGRIT, a dataset containing 1.5 million samples. PixCLIP then uses a three-branch alignment framework and a unified training objective to connect image regions with corresponding descriptions at multiple granularities. Its inputs accommodate both visual region prompts and long-form text.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on pixel- and region-level alignment while preserving strong performance on global image–text retrieval. The framework also handles arbitrarily shaped region prompts and long descriptions. These findings support improving the spatial specificity of visual representations alongside textual detail, allowing the same framework to connect language with whole images and with more precisely localized visual content.
summary.tldr: PixCLIP aligns long descriptions with image regions and pixels, improving fine-grained matching while retaining strong global retrieval performance.

title: PixCLIP: Towards Fine-grained Vision-Language Understanding via Any-granularity Pixel-Text Alignment

abstract: Adaptive rounding techniques in Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enable the efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) with low resource and data dependencies. While learning-based rounding methods are accurate yet costly, compensation-based approaches offer a highly efficient alternative. However, synergizing these two to realize their full potential is hindered by spatiotemporal misalignment in the decoupled paradigm. Key challenges include temporal parameter conflict, the invalidation of the initial Round-to-Nearest (RTN) assumption, and spatially-inconsistent optimization objectives. This paper introduces STLA, a novel rounding-optimized PTQ framework that achieves both fast and accurate LLM quantization. STLA resolves temporal inconsistency through cluster-wise integrated rounding optimization, which collocates the learning and compensation phases. STLA achieves spatial alignment through a unified global objective derived from the Schur Complement, enabling the solver to look ahead and align local rounding decisions with the optimal future compensation of remaining weights. Furthermore, we propose a Hessian-guided clustering strategy that exploits both diagonal and off-diagonal information to maximize intra-cluster error cancellation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that STLA establishes a new state-of-the-art for low-bit PTQ while maintaining high computational efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/AI2C-Lab/STLA.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the precision of model weights for efficient deployment. Learning how to round weights can be accurate but costly, while compensation-based methods offer efficiency. STLA addresses conflicts that arise when these operations are separated, including incompatible parameter updates, invalidated initial rounding assumptions, and objectives that disagree across weights.

The framework optimizes rounding within clusters while integrating the learning and compensation phases. A global objective derived from the Schur complement lets local rounding decisions account for the optimal future compensation of remaining weights. This lookahead connects a decision made now to how later adjustments can absorb its error. A Hessian-guided clustering strategy uses both diagonal and off-diagonal information to encourage error cancellation within clusters.

Experiments report a new state of the art for low-bit post-training quantization while retaining high computational efficiency. The result supports aligning rounding and compensation both in timing and across weights. STLA’s contribution is the coordinated optimization of these operations, rather than treating their decisions as independent.
summary.tldr: STLA coordinates weight rounding with future error compensation to deliver fast, accurate low-bit post-training quantization.

title: STLA: Spatiotemporal Lookahead Alignment for Post-Training Quantization

abstract: Data heterogeneity is a fundamental challenge in Federated Learning (FL), where induced model drift often results in "negative gains" for global models on data-abundant clients, with performance falling below that of local training. To address this issue, we propose FedGain, a novel framework that optimizes collaborative client clustering to mitigate the negative gain. We are the first to develop a modified Scaling Law (SL) to quantify the reduction in data utility caused by heterogeneity and define Effective Federated Capacity to align clients with the highest potential collaboration gains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our modified SL strictly adheres to the power-law learning discipline in non-IID scenarios. FedGain effectively suppresses negative gains to a negligible level across various FL algorithms and outperforms other Clustered FL methods.

To address this issue, we propose FedGain, a novel framework that optimizes collaborative client clustering to mitigate the negative gain. We are the first to develop a modified Scaling Law (SL) to quantify the reduction in data utility caused by heterogeneity and define Effective Federated Capacity to align clients with the highest potential collaboration gains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our modified SL strictly adheres to the power-law learning discipline in non-IID scenarios. paragraphs: Federated learning does not always benefit every participant. When clients have different data distributions, their contributions can pull the shared model in conflicting directions. For clients that already have abundant data, the resulting global model may perform worse than a model trained locally. FedGain targets this negative gain by reconsidering which clients should collaborate.

The framework develops a modified scaling law to quantify how heterogeneity reduces the usefulness of combined data. It also introduces Effective Federated Capacity, a quantity used to align clients with strong potential collaboration gains. These ideas guide client clustering, making the expected value of collaboration central to how groups are formed.

Experiments show that the modified scaling law follows power-law learning behavior under non-identically distributed data. Across several federated learning algorithms, FedGain reduces negative gains to a negligible level and outperforms other clustered approaches. This is an empirical result about suppressing harmful collaboration, rather than a claim that every possible client grouping can be made beneficial.
summary.tldr: FedGain groups clients using estimates of collaboration value, reducing negative gains from heterogeneous data to negligible levels in experiments.

title: FedGain: Toward Negative-Gain-Free Client Collaboration in Federated Learning

abstract: Text-guided texture editing aims to modify object appearance while preserving the underlying geometric structure. However, our empirical analysis reveals that even SOTA editing models frequently struggle to maintain structural consistency during texture editing, despite the intended changes being purely appearance-related. Motivated by this observation, we jointly enhance structure preservation from both data and training perspectives, and build TexEditor, a dedicated texture editing model based on Qwen-Image-Edit-2509. Firstly, we construct BlenderTex, a high-quality SFT dataset generated with Blender, which provides strong structural priors for a cold start. Secondly, we introduce StructureNFT, a RL–based approach that integrates structure-preserving losses to transfer the structural priors learned during SFT to real-world scenes. Moreover, due to the limited realism and evaluation coverage of existing benchmarks, we introduce TexBench, a general-purpose real-world benchmark for text-guided texture editing. Extensive experiments on existing Blender-based texture benchmarks and our TexBench show that TexEditor consistently outperforms strong baselines such as Nano Banana Pro. In addition, we assess TexEditor on the general-purpose benchmark ImgEdit to validate its generalization.

The authors find that even leading image-editing models frequently alter structure during edits intended to affect appearance alone. The stages connect controlled training examples with an objective that continues to favor structural consistency outside those examples.

title: TexEditor: Structure-Preserving Text-Driven Texture Editing

abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning (CTRL) provides a natural framework for sequential decision-making in dynamic environments where interactions evolve continuously over time. While CTRL has shown growing empirical success, its ability to adapt to varying levels of problem difficulty remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the instance-dependent behavior of CTRL and introduce a simple, model-based algorithm built on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) with a general function approximator. Unlike existing approaches that estimate system dynamics directly, our method estimates the state marginal density to guide learning. We establish instance-dependent performance guarantees by deriving a regret bound that scales with the total reward variance and measurement resolution. Notably, the regret becomes independent of the specific measurement strategy when the observation frequency adapts appropriately to the problem’s complexity. To further improve performance, our algorithm incorporates a randomized measurement schedule that enhances sample efficiency without increasing measurement cost. These results highlight a new direction for designing CTRL algorithms that automatically adjust their learning behavior based on the underlying difficulty of the environment.

paragraphs: Continuous-time reinforcement learning studies decisions in environments that evolve continuously, even though observations occur at selected times. This paper asks how learning performance can reflect the difficulty of a particular environment. It proposes a model-based algorithm using maximum likelihood estimation with a general function approximator.

The distinctive choice is to estimate the marginal distribution of states rather than directly estimate the system's dynamics. The analysis derives a regret bound, measuring accumulated performance shortfall, that depends on total reward variance and measurement resolution. These dependencies connect the guarantee to properties of the specific problem and to how finely the learner observes it.

The regret becomes independent of the particular measurement strategy when observation frequency adapts appropriately to problem complexity. That independence is conditional on the adaptation, rather than an unrestricted claim about all observation schedules. The algorithm also introduces randomized measurement timing to improve sample efficiency without increasing measurement cost. Together, the results suggest a route toward learners whose observation and learning behavior adjust to environmental difficulty.
summary.tldr: The paper develops continuous-time reinforcement learning guarantees that adapt to problem difficulty through state-density estimation and measurement scheduling.

abstract: In this paper, we propose two new support vector approaches for ordinal regression, which optimize multiple thresholds to deﬁne parallel discriminant hyperplanes for the ordinal scales. Both approaches guarantee that the thresholds are properly ordered at the optimal solution. The size of these optimization problems is linear in the number of training samples. The SMO algorithm is adapted for the resulting optimization problems; it is extremely easy to implement and scales eﬃciently as a quadratic function of the number of examples. The results of numerical experiments on benchmark datasets verify the usefulness of these approaches.

paragraphs: The paper proposes two support-vector methods for ordinal regression, where the prediction categories have an order. Both approaches learn multiple thresholds that define parallel discriminant hyperplanes for the ordinal scales. The thresholds therefore organize the model’s decisions according to the ordering that the prediction task requires.

A central property is that both methods guarantee correctly ordered thresholds at the optimal solution. This ties the optimization result to the intended ordinal structure. The authors also state that the size of each optimization problem grows linearly with the number of training examples, an important distinction from the time needed to solve it.

To perform the optimization, the paper adapts the SMO algorithm. The adapted solver is described as very easy to implement, with computational scaling quadratic in the number of examples. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets support the usefulness of both approaches. Together, the contributions combine an ordering guarantee, a stated optimization size, and a practical procedure for fitting the proposed ordinal models.
summary.tldr: Two support-vector ordinal regression methods guarantee ordered thresholds at the optimum and use an adapted SMO solver.

title: New approaches to support vector ordinal regression

abstract: We consider the problem of selecting a subset of m most informative features where m is the number of required features. This feature selection problem is essentially a combinatorial optimization problem, and is usually solved by an approximation. Conventional feature selection methods address the computational challenge in two steps: (a) ranking all the features by certain scores that are usually computed independently from the number of specified features m, and (b) selecting the top m ranked features. One major shortcoming of these approaches is that if a feature f is chosen when the number of specified features is m, it will always be chosen when the number of specified features is larger than m. We refer to this property as the "monotonic" property of feature selection. In this work, we argue that it is important to develop efficient algorithms for non-monotonic feature selection. To this end, we develop an algorithm for non-monotonic feature selection that approximates the related combinatorial optimization problem by a Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) problem. We also present a strategy that derives a discrete solution from the approximate solution of MKL, and show the performance guarantee for the derived discrete solution when compared to the global optimal solution for the related combinatorial optimization problem. An empirical study with a number of benchmark data sets indicates the promising performance of the proposed framework compared with several state-of-the-art approaches for feature selection.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a specified number of informative features. A common shortcut ranks features once and takes the highest-ranked ones. This produces nested selections: any feature selected for a smaller set remains selected when the requested set grows. The authors call this the monotonic property and argue for methods that can reconsider earlier choices.

Their approach approximates the underlying combinatorial selection problem with a Multiple Kernel Learning problem. It then converts the approximate solution into a discrete feature subset. This matters because the relaxed optimization is an intermediate step; the final result still needs to be an actual selection of features.

The authors provide a performance guarantee for the derived discrete solution relative to the global optimum of the associated combinatorial problem. They also report promising benchmark results against several state-of-the-art feature-selection approaches. Together, these contributions offer theoretical and empirical support for selecting features in a way that depends on the requested subset size, rather than forcing every subset to follow one fixed ranking.
summary.tldr: The method uses Multiple Kernel Learning to select feature subsets that can change non-monotonically as the requested subset size changes.

title: Non-monotonic feature selection

abstract: Online optimization has emerged as powerful tool in large scale optimization. In this paper, we introduce efficient online algorithms based on the alternating directions method (ADM). We introduce a new proof technique for ADM in the batch setting, which yields a linear rate of convergence of ADM and forms the basis of regret analysis in the online setting. We consider two scenarios in the online setting, based on whether the solution needs to lie in the feasible set or not. In both settings, we establish regret bounds for both the objective function as well as constraint violation for general and strongly convex functions. Preliminary results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper develops efficient online optimization algorithms based on the alternating directions method. Its analysis begins with the batch setting, where the authors introduce a new proof technique yielding a linear convergence rate. That technique then provides the foundation for studying performance as optimization proceeds online.

The online analysis separates two scenarios according to whether the solution must lie in the feasible set. This distinction matters because objective quality and satisfaction of constraints are separate concerns. The authors establish regret bounds for both the objective function and constraint violation, covering general convex functions as well as strongly convex functions.

Regret provides a way to assess accumulated online performance, so the results address how the algorithms behave over a sequence of optimization steps. Tracking constraint violation alongside the objective makes the analysis relevant to constrained problems in both feasibility scenarios. Preliminary experiments illustrate the proposed algorithms' performance. The main contribution is the connection between the batch proof technique and online guarantees covering both optimization quality and constraints.
summary.tldr: Online alternating-direction algorithms come with regret bounds for objective values and constraint violations under two feasibility settings.
